Title: The Banque centrale du Luxembourg and the financial centre
text: THE BANQUE CENTRALE DU LUXEMBOURG AND THE FINANCIAL CENTRE -YVES MERSCH on the occasion of the 1999 Economics Awards Ceremony at the Chamber of Commerce of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg Luxembourg, 6 July 1999 Only the word spoken is authentic. Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, I would like to thank you for this invitation. As you have certainly noticed, we are keenly interested in all events related to economics and business. In this presentation, I will talk mainly about the Banque centrale du Luxembourg in the context of the Luxembourg financial centre. However, I would like to begin my speech by briefly recalling the reason for a single European currency. The introduction of the euro is part of the desire to complete and strengthen the single market already characterised by the free movement of persons, goods, services and individuals. The introduction of a single currency, in addition to its political significance, has simple fundamental economic objectives which we shall explain briefly below: price transparency, exchange rate savings and the advantages of an international currency. Price transparency is one of the most noticeable points. Indeed, it is difficult to compare, during a transaction, the prices from one country to another, since they can vary daily in relation to each other according to the evolution of exchange rates. With the introduction of the euro, this hazard disappears for the countries that are part of the euro area. Whether you buy a good in Luxembourg or in any other country that has adopted the single currency, prices are expressed in the same unit, the euro, and are therefore easily comparable. This new transparency thus created is likely to activate competition between companies and, consequently, to promote a downward trend in prices. Secondly, economic actors are witnessing exchange rate economies. As the euro is used in all the countries that have adopted the single currency, economic actors save exchange fees, so that buyer and ask prices are equal. The phenomenon is beneficial for both individuals and companies. The introduction of the euro also allows companies to avoid the costs of hedging foreign exchange risk. With the euro, this risk disappears and companies no longer need to hedge themselves by using financial instruments specially designed for this purpose, such as options and futures. The profitability of some projects therefore becomes less uncertain and investments are boosted. As far as the future of the euro is concerned, there is a consensus that it will become an international currency, both commercially and financially. In international trade, about half of world trade is in dollars, while the United States accounts for only about 15% of world trade. The gradual switch from the dollar to the euro as the billing currency in international contracts allows European companies to settle their exchanges increasingly in their own currency, which eliminates the constraint of exchange rate risk. Other aspects relate to the use of the euro as a reserve currency as well as the increased interest in the financial markets for new products denominated in euro. The establishment of Economic and Monetary Union has had the effect of bringing about adjustments in institutional matters, particularly marked in Luxembourg, leading to amendments to the statutes relating to the Luxembourg Monetary Institute (IML). All Member States have had to adapt their legislation to the requirements of achieving EMU. Luxembourg legislation in this area consisted of the Act of 15 March 1979 on monetary status and the Act of 20 May 1983 which created the Luxembourg Monetary Institute. The Statute of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) and of the European Central Bank (ECB) states in its first article that "The Luxembourg Monetary Institute is the central bank of Luxembourg". The transition to EMU meant the gradual transformation of a virtual monetary authority" into a central bank similar to the other national central banks, members of the ESCB under the aegis of the ECB. The Luxembourg Monetary Institute has never played the role of a real central bank, luxembourg benefiting from these services through the branch of the National Bank of Belgium located in the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, within the framework of the monetary association grafted on the Belgoluxenburg Economic Union (BLEU). The missions of the IML were summarized in the following points: issue monetary signs and manage their circulation, promote the stability of the currency and ensure the proper functioning of the financial markets, to perform obligations and exercise rights arising from international agreements in the monetary field and financial supervise the financial sector. With the establishment of the European System of Central Banks on 1 June 1998 and pursuant to the Maastricht Treaty, Luxembourg set up an independent national central bank (NCB). Articles 107 and 108 of the Maastricht Treaty emphasise respectively the independence of each national central bank from any political power and the compatibility of each national legislation with that principle at the latest with the establishment of the European System of Central Banks. The independence of central banks is essential for the credibility of EMU. The Banque centrale du Luxembourg, which plays the role of a central bank in its own right, a unique fact in the history of our country, was thus born on the same day as the European Central Bank. At that time, the IML, mainly active in the prudential field, ended its existence. Through the central bank, Luxembourg thus gains monetary sovereignty by participating in the European System of Central Banks. By having one vote among seventeen in the Governing Council of the European Central Bank, which defines the guidelines and decisions to be taken in the field of monetary policy at the level of the euro area, the Grand Duchy is on an equal footing with the other countries participating in Economic and Monetary Union. The latest development we have just witnessed is the separation of supervisory activity from central banking activity stricto sensu. The independence that a central bank must have in monetary matters is considered incompatible with the administrative status of a prudential supervisory authority which carries out its activities under the hierarchical supervision of the Minister responsible for the financial sector. The Government has remedied this situation by two new laws: the Law of 23 December 1998 on the Monetary Status and the Central Bank of Luxembourg and the Law of 23 December 1998 establishing a Commission for the Supervision of the Financial Sector (CSSF). The CSSF takes over and exercises all the powers that the legal texts had conferred on the Banque centrale du Luxembourg in the field of prudential supervision as well as on the Commissariat aux Bourses of which it takes legal succession. The scope of supervision covers credit institutions, other professionals in the financial sector, UCIs, stock exchanges and financial markets. In states with a banking supervisory body separate from the central bank, cooperation between the two authorities is useful. On the one hand, the central bank may provide the supervisory authority with the macroprudential information necessary for the supervisory authority to understand and assess developments in the banking and financial systems. On the other hand, the central bank, through its presence as a market participant, can be a useful source of information on the financial condition of individual market agents. Conversely, the supervisory authority may have information relevant to the central bank for the performance of its task in the field of monetary policy. In this context, Article 105 of the Treaty imposes an obligation on the ESCB and the national central banks to make their contribution to the supervision and stability of the financial system. However, the Luxembourg Government has not laid down a legal obligation for cooperation and mutual exchange of information between the CSSF and the BCL. The main task of the BCL is to participate in the performance of the tasks of the ESCB, of which it is an integral part, in the pursuit of its objectives. The objectives and tasks of the ESCB are set out in Article 105 of the treaty on European Union. The main objective of the ESCB, as underlined in the first paragraph of that Article, is to maintain price stability. However, while this is often the sole purpose of the ESCB, the same paragraph also states that, without prejudice to the main objective, the ESCB shall support the general economic policies in the Community. The purpose of this second objective is to contribute to the achievement of the Community's objectives: the promotion of a harmonious and balanced development of economic activities throughout the Community sustainable and non-inflationary growth that respects the environment, a high degree of convergence of economic performance, a high level of employment and protection, raising the standard of quality of life, economic and social cohesion, solidarity between Member States. Article 105 lists the fundamental tasks of the ESCB, of which there are four: to define and implement the Monetary Policy of the Community, to conduct foreign exchange operations, define and manage the official foreign exchange reserves of the Member States, promote the proper functioning of payment systems. The establishment of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg as a full shareholder operating within the ESCB was thus accompanied by the establishment of a series of instruments, including a national payment system and the monetary policy instruments of the euro area. As part of the performance of its tasks within the ESCB, the BCL ensures the implementation of these instruments in Luxembourg's financial centre. In order to facilitate the management of the single monetary policy conducted by the ECB from the beginning of Phase III, the various national central banks decided in 1995 to set up a system which could optimise cross-border payments of large amounts in euro. The result of this reflection was the birth of the system called "TARGET". Behind this English acronym hides the name "Trans-european Automated Real-Time Gross Settlement Express Transfer System". The French term, no less technical, is "trans-European automated express transfer with real-time gross settlement". It is in fact an interbank means of payment that promotes the integration of money markets and, at the same time, the management of the single monetary policy. All payments related to monetary policy must go through this system. The aim of this system is to carry out cross-border transfers efficiently and quickly (in real time, i.e. immediately) as if it were happening at a national level. 1 January 1999 was the deadline for the establishment of TARGET. As a constituent element of the operational framework of the common monetary policy, TARGET therefore pursues the following main objectives: provide support for monetary policy operations within the ESCB, contribute to the reduction of systemic risks in payment systems, increase the efficiency of cross-border payments within the European Union. TARGET is not only a tool used for international payments. It links national real-time gross settlement (RTGS) systems, which already existed in most of the countries participating in EMU. Since Luxembourg did not yet have a national RTGS, considerable work was required to develop such an operational system: on the one hand the implementation of an RTGS at national level and on the other hand the connection of this RTGS to the TARGET network. This connection (INTERLINKING) takes place through a communication network that uses common formats and procedures when exchanging payment messages. With a view to EMU and with a view to having payment systems operational on 1 January 1999, an Economic Interest Grouping (RTGS-L Gie) had already been set up at the end of 1996. The purpose of this grouping, founded jointly by the Luxembourg Monetary Institute and 11 credit institutions in the Luxembourg financial centre, was to set up a real-time gross settlement system called LIPS-Gross (Luxembourg Interbank Payment System). After finalizing the preparatory work in mid-December 1998, Target has been operational since 4 January 1999. The introduction of the TARGET system was a great success, with transactions worth an average of 1 trillion being carried every day. The securities settlement system is the second major project carried out in the financial centre within the framework of payment systems. As a complementary element to TARGET in the execution of credit operations and in the integration of the European money market, the Securities Settlement System aims primarily to protect the central banks forming part of the ESCB against any credit risk. Within each country of the European Union, a central securities depository has been designated. In Luxembourg, the central depository is Cedelbank Luxembourg. As already mentioned earlier, let us now turn to the monetary policy instruments of the euro area, which the Banque centrale du Luxembourg is responsible for implementing in the Luxembourg financial centre. In order for the ESCB to achieve the objective of monetary stability, certain instruments have been developed. They fall into three main categories: open market operations, standing facilities and minimum reserves. Without wanting to go into too much detail, open market operations have three purposes: First: steering interest rates, Second: managing liquidity, Thirdly, to send a signal about the stance of monetary policy. Open market operations include four types of instruments. First of all, the two most important are the main refinancing operations, of weekly frequency and with a maturity of 2 weeks, as well as the operations of longer-term refinancing, monthly frequency and quarterly maturity. In addition to these two categories, fine-tuning operations and structural operations are added. The main refinancing operations, applied on a decentralised basis by the NCBs, are carried out on a regular basis and thus play a key role in the pursuit of the objectives of the ESCB. As their name suggests, the operations in question provide the bulk of the refinancing of the financial sector and are a key factor in steering interest rates and in reporting on the stance of monetary policy. The second set of instruments at the disposal of the ESCB consists of the Standing Facilities, the role of which is as follows: allow the provision and withdrawal of cash on a day-to-day basis, indicate the general stance of monetary policy, frame overnight market rates. For this purpose, there are two types of permanent facilities: the marginal lending facility and the marginal deposit facility. These two instruments constitute respectively the ceiling of 3.5% and the floor of 1.5% of the corridor within which the overnight interest rate moves. In this context, it should be noted that, since the beginning of January, the market has seen the birth of Eonia, the overnight rate of the euro zone. Through the marginal lending facility, counterparties in the financial centre receive overnight liquidity from the BCL against the delivery of eligible assets. Advances are made at 24 hours and on the basis of a predetermined rate which is currently 3.5%. In this way, the temporary needs of counterparties can be met. Counterparties in Luxembourg's financial centre have access to this facility at any time from the BCL. The rate applied to the marginal lending facility is the ceiling rate of the overnight market rate. As a symmetric of the previously processed facility, the deposit facility allows counterparties to invest their excess liquidity with the ESCB. As with the marginal lending facility, operations are 24 hours and at a pre-set rate of 1.5% currently. The rate applied to deposited cash is the floor rate of the overnight market rate. Access to this facility shall be permanent with the NCB concerned. Finally, the third instrument implemented by the BCL in the financial centre concerns minimum reserves. The purpose of minimum reserves is to: favour the stabilisation of interest rates on the money market, create or amplify a structural liquidity deficit. These reserves, the application of which is uniform within the euro area, shall be set up in the accounts opened in the books of the national central banks. Establishments subject to the system shall be listed on a list available to the public. These reserves, which are built up on average and whose remuneration is made at the rate of the main refinancing operations, currently 2.5%, are calculated on the basis of a balance sheet base to which a rate applies, currently 2%. Taxable persons have the possibility to deduct a lump sum of EUR 100,000 from the calculated amount. In the event of non-compliance with the obligations imposed by the system, the ECB may apply sanctions either in the form of penalties or in the form of unremunerated deposits. Another possible means of pressure is to suspend access to open-market operations and standing facilities to counterparties at fault. During this speech I drew your attention to some major changes that have taken place following the advent of the 3rd stage of EMU and which the BCL has ensured the application of in the financial centre. These developments underline the importance of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg's presence in the financial centre in order to ensure the effective implementation of the common monetary policy. Thank you for your attention.

Mesdames, Messieurs, Tout d'abord, je tiens  vous remercier pour cette invitation. Cependant, je me permets d'entamer mon expos en rappelant brivement le pourquoi d'une monnaie unique europenne. L'introduction de l'euro s'inscrit dans la volont de complter et de renforcer le march unique dj caractris par la libre circulation des personnes, des biens, des services et des particuliers. L'instauration d'une monnaie unique, en sus de sa porte politique, vise des objectifs conomiques fondamentaux simples que nous allons expliquer brivement par la suite: la transparence des prix, les conomies de change ainsi que les atouts d'une monnaie internationale. La transparence des prix est un des points les plus perceptibles. Cette nouvelle transparence ainsi cre est susceptible d'activer la concurrence entre les entreprises et, en consquence, de favoriser une tendance  la baisse des prix. Deuximement, les acteurs conomiques assistent  des conomies de change. Comme l'euro est utilis dans l'ensemble des pays ayant adopt la monnaie unique, les acteurs conomiques pargnent les commissions de change, les cours acheteurs et vendeurs tant alors gaux. Le phnomne est bnfique aussi bien pour le particulier que pour les entreprises. L'introduction de l'euro permet, en sus, aux entreprises d'chapper aux frais de couverture du risque de change. Avec l'euro, ce risque disparat et les entreprises n'ont par consquent plus besoin de se couvrir en ayant recours  des instruments financiers spcialement conus  cet effet, tels que les options et les futures. La rentabilit de certains projets devient donc moins alatoire et les investissements s'en trouvent dynamiss. En ce qui concerne l'avenir de l'euro, il y a un consensus pour dire qu'il deviendra une monnaie internationale, aussi bien au niveau commercial qu'au niveau financier. Dans le commerce international, environ la moiti des changes mondiaux s'effectuent en dollar alors que les Etats-Unis ne reprsentent qu'environ 15% du commerce mondial. Le basculement progressif du dollar vers l'euro comme devise de facturation dans les contrats internationaux permet aux entreprises europennes de rgler leurs changes de faon croissante dans leur propre monnaie ce qui limine la contrainte de risque de change. D'autres aspects ont trait  l'utilisation de l'euro en tant que devise de rserve ainsi qu' l'intrt accru sur les marchs financiers pour les nouveaux produits libells en euros. La mise en place de l'Union conomique et montaire a eu pour consquence d'entraner des adaptations en matire institutionnelle, particulirement marques au Luxembourg engendrant des modifications statutaires ayant trait  l'Institut Montaire Luxembourgeois (IML). Tous les Etats membres ont d adapter leur lgislation aux exigences de la ralisation de l'UEM. La lgislation luxembourgeoise en la matire consistait dans la loi du 15 mars 1979 relative au statut montaire et dans la loi du 20 mai 1983 qui a cr l'Institut Montaire Luxembourgeois. Les Statuts du Systme europen de banques centrales (SEBC) et de la Banque centrale europenne (BCE) prcisent dans leur premier article que "L'Institut Montaire Luxembourgeois est la banque centrale du Luxembourg". Le passage  l'UEM signifiait la transformation progressive d'une autorit montaire virtuelle" en une banque centrale analogue aux autres banques centrales nationales, membres du SEBC sous l'gide de la BCE. L'Institut Montaire Luxembourgeois n'a jamais jou le rle d'une vritable banque centrale, le Luxembourg bnficiant de ces services par le truchement de la succursale de la Banque nationale de Belgique installe dans le Grand-Duch du Luxembourg, dans le cadre de l'association montaire greffe sur l'Union conomique belgoluxembourgeoise (UEBL). Les missions de l'IML se rsumaient aux points suivants: mettre des signes montaires et grer leur circulation, promouvoir la stabilit de la monnaie et veiller  cet effet au bon fonctionnement des marchs financiers, excuter des obligations et exercer des droits rsultant d'accords internationaux dans le domaine montaire et financier, exercer la surveillance du secteur financier. Avec la mise en place du Systme europen de banques centrales, au 1er juin 1998, et en application du Trait de Maastricht, le Luxembourg s'est dot d'une banque centrale nationale (BCN) indpendante. En effet, dans ses articles 107 et 108, le Trait de Maastricht insiste respectivement sur l'indpendance de chaque banque centrale nationale par rapport  tout pouvoir politique et sur la compatibilit de chaque lgislation nationale avec ce principe au plus tard avec l'instauration du Systme europen de banques centrales. L'indpendance des banque centrales est essentielle pour la crdibilit de l'UEM. La Banque centrale du Luxembourg, qui joue un rle de banque centrale  part entire, fait unique dans l'histoire de notre pays, est ainsi ne le mme jour que la Banque centrale europenne. A ce moment, l'IML, principalement actif dans le domaine prudentiel, a fini d'exister. Par le truchement de la banque centrale, le Luxembourg gagne ainsi en souverainet montaire en participant au Systme europen de banques centrales. En ayant une voix parmi dix-sept au sein du conseil des gouverneurs de la Banque centrale europenne, conseil qui dfinit les orientations et les dcisions  prendre en matire de politique montaire au niveau de la zone euro, le Grand-Duch est  pied d'galit avec les autres pays partcipant  l'Union conomique et montaire. La dernire volution  laquelle nous venons d'assister est la sparation de l'activit de surveillance de l'activit de banque centrale stricto sensu. L'indpendance qu'une banque centrale doit possder en matire montaire est considre comme incompatible avec le statut administratif d'une autorit de surveillance prudentielle qui exerce ses activits sous la tutelle hirarchique du ministre ayant dans ses attributions le secteur financier. Le gouvernement a remdi  cette situation par deux nouvelles lois: la loi du 23 dcembre 1998 relative au statut montaire et  la Banque centrale du Luxembourg ainsi que la loi du 23 dcembre 1998 portant cration d'une Commission de surveillance du secteur financier (CSSF). La CSSF reprend et exerce toutes les comptences que les textes lgaux avaient confrs  la Banque centrale du Luxembourg dans le domaine de la surveillance prudentielle ainsi qu'au Commissariat aux Bourses dont elle prend la succession juridique. Le champ d'application du contrle englobe les tablissements de crdit, les autres professionnels du secteur financier, les OPC, les bourses, ainsi que les marchs financiers. Dans les Etats disposant d'un organisme de contrle du secteur bancaire distinct de la banque centrale, une collaboration entre les deux autorits s'avre utile. D'autre part, la banque centrale, de par sa prsence comme acteur dans le march, peut tre une source d'informations utile sur la condition financire d'agents individuels du march. Inversment, l'autorit de surveillance peut disposer d'informations utiles  la banque centrale pour l'excution de sa mission dans le domaine de la politique montaire. Dans ce contexte, l'article 105 du Trait impose au SEBC et aux banques centrales nationales une obligation de fournir leur contribution  la surveillance et  la stabilit du systme financier. Le gouvernement luxembourgeois n'a cependant pas prvu une obligation lgale de coopration et d'change mutuel d'informations entre la CSSF et la BCL. La mission principale de la BCL est de participer  l'excution des missions du SEBC, dont elle fait partie intgrante, dans la recherche de ses objectifs. Les objectifs et les missions du SEBC sont abords dans l'article 105 du mme Trait sur l'Union europenne. L'objectif principal du SEBC, comme le souligne le premier paragraphe du dit article, est de maintenir la stabilit des prix. Nanmoins, alors qu'on a souvent tendance  en faire le seul et unique but du SEBC, le mme paragraphe prcise galement que, sans prjudice de l'objectif principal, le SEBC apporte son soutien aux politiques conomiques gnrales dans la Communaut. La finalit de ce second objectif est la contribution  la ralisation des objectifs de la Communaut: la promotion d'un dveloppement harmonieux et quilibr des activits conomiques dans l'ensemble de la Communaut, une croissance durable et non inflationniste respectant l'environnement, un haut degr de convergence des performances conomiques, un niveau d'emploi et de protection lev, le relvement du niveau de la qualit de vie, la cohsion conomique et sociale, la solidarit entre les Etats membres. L'article 105 numre les missions fondamentales du SEBC, qui sont au nombre de quatre: dfinir et mettre en oeuvre la politique montaire de la Communaut, conduire les oprations de change, dfinir et grer les rserves officielles de change des Etats membres, promouvoir le bon fonctionnement des systmes de paiement. La mise en place de la Banque centrale du Luxembourg en tant que part entire oprant au sein du SEBC s'est ainsi accompagne de la mise en place d'une srie d'instruments parmi lesquels un systme de paiement national ainsi que les instruments de la politique montaire de la zone euro. Dans le cadre de l'excution de ses missions au sein du SEBC, la BCL assure la mise en oeuvre de ces instruments sur la place financire du Luxembourg. Afin de faciliter la gestion de la politique montaire unique mene par la BCE ds le dbut de la phase III, les diffrentes banques centrales nationales ont, ds 1995, dcid de mettre en place un systme qui puisse optimiser les paiements transfrontaliers de montants importants en euros. La rsultante de cette rflexion a t la naissance du systme baptis "TARGET". Derrire cet acronyme anglais se cache le nom "Trans-european Automated Real-Time Gross Settlement Express Transfer System". Le terme franais, non moins technique, est "transfert express automatis transeuropen  rglement brut en temps rel". Il s'agit en fait d'un moyen interbancaire de paiement qui favorise l'intgration des marchs montaires et, par la mme occasion, la gestion de la politique montaire unique. Tous les paiements lis  la politique montaire passent obligatoirement par ce systme. Le but de ce systme est de raliser des transferts transfrontaliers de faon efficace et rapide (en temps rel, c'est--dire immdiat) comme si cela se passait  un niveau national. Le 1er janvier 1999 tait la date butoir pour la mise en place du TARGET. Elment constitutif du cadre oprationnel de la politique montaire commune, TARGET poursuit donc principalement les objectifs suivants: constituer un support aux oprations de politique montaire effectues au sein du SEBC, contribuer  la rduction des risques systmiques dans les systmes de paiement, augmenter l'efficience des paiements transfrontaliers au sein de l'Union europenne. TARGET n'est pas seulement un outil utilis pour des paiements internationaux. Il relie des systmes de rglement brut en temps rel nationaux RTGS (Real-Time Gross Settlement), qui existaient dj dans la plupart des pays participant  l'UEM. Dans la mesure o le Luxembourg ne disposait pas encore d'un RTGS national, des travaux considrables ont t ncessaires pour l'laboration d'un tel systme oprationnel: d'une part l'implmentation d'un RTGS au niveau national et d'autre part le raccordement de ce RTGS au rseau TARGET. Cette connexion (INTERLINKING) s'opre  travers un rseau de communication qui utilise des formats et des procdures communs lors de l'change de messages de paiement. Dans la perspective de l'UEM et en vue d'avoir des systmes de paiement oprationnels au 1er janvier 1999, un Groupement d'Intrt Economique (RTGS-L Gie) avait dj t cr  la fin de l'anne 1996. L'objet de ce groupement, fond conjointement par l'Insitut montaire luxembourgeois et 11 tablissements de crdit de la place financire luxembourgeoise, tait la mise en exploitation d'un systme de rglement brut en temps rel appel LIPS-Gross (Luxembourg Interbank Payment System). Aprs finalisation des travaux prparatifs vers la mi-dcembre 1998, Target est oprationnel depuis le 4 janvier 1999. Title: Nine months of experience in the European System of Central Banks
text: NINE MONTHS OF EXPERIENCE IN THE EUROPEAN SYSTEM OF CENTRAL BANKS -YVES MERSCH Luxembourg Financial Market Forum Luxembourg, 14 October 1999 Reproduction is authorized, provided the source is acknowledged Table of contents - Preparatory work - Assessment - Requirements 1. Preparatory work Taking stock of the first nine months of the euro without mentioning the ECB's six-month start-up period would be a bit unfair in my view. The preparatory work already carried out in the European Monetary Institute, particularly on an institutional, organisational and regulatory basis, fits seamlessly into the first months of the operational appearance of the euro. 1. About exactly one year ago, the institutional substructure of the decision-making body of the Board of Governors was adopted. This substructure is also largely the one that works for the General Council. It is supported by 13 committees. Most committees are chaired by ECB Headquarters. However, the Budget Committee, the International Relations Committee and the Banking Supervision Committee are chaired by representatives of the national central banks. These committees, in turn, have a whole series of sub-working groups. For example, 2 working groups are active in the legal and banking supervisory areas, 3 working groups in the area of accounting and monetary income, 6 each for the Monetary Policy Committee, the Payment and Clearing Systems Committee and the Internal Audit Committee, 7 in the statistical field and the same number in the Committee on Market Operations, 8 in the Information Technology Committee, and even 12 in the Banknotes Committee. A number of these working groups are of course double-staffed or are joint working groups of 2 different committees. In total, this results in around 80 working groups and sub-working groups, which are staffed by the national central banks together with the ECB. If I now include the working groups in the monetary field at EU level, in the BIS, as well as additional internal working groups, I come to more working groups for a national central bank like luxembourg than we have staff, namely well over 170. Therefore, it is not surprising that the European Central Bank has increased from just over 400 to now over 700 employees over this initial phase, and that this growth is also considered to be pointing further north. For Luxembourg, where a large proportion of decision-makers still do not really know what to do with a central bank, we naturally have an above-average number of employees per capita with 160 employees. However, if one compares the number of employees with the balance sheet total of the central banks, Luxembourg is far at the lower end of the employment scale. 2. A year ago, the course was also set in the organizational area. At the first Governing Council meeting, for example, it was stated that the seating arrangements in the Governing Council should not be based on the alphabetical order of the euro area countries, but on the names of the members of the Governing Council, since everyone bears responsibility for the entire euro area and not only for their own country. A second decision concerned the number of meetings. The frequency frequency of 14 days has proven itself to this day and allows to do justice to Article 12 of the statutes: "12.1. The Governing Council shall adopt the guidelines and decisions necessary to ensure the performance of the tasks entrusted to the ESCB. The Governing Council shall determine the monetary policy of the Community, including, where appropriate, decisions on intermediate monetary policy objectives, key interest rates and the provision of central bank money in the ESCB, and shall adopt the guidelines necessary for their implementation."; Towards the end of the year, various decisions concerning the transparency of the Governing Council's decisions were also taken, giving rise to a number of comments and also some polemics. The aim of the Governing Council in this respect has never been to provide less information, but to ensure collegiality and uniform decision-making by the Council. From this insight, the euro system provides more and faster information than other central banks, which find it difficult to publish the minutes of meetings with individual voting behaviour with some delay, and probably somewhat cleaned up. The regular press conferences following the meetings of the Governing Council of the ECB, with clear communication of the decisions that have just been taken and the linking of these decisions to a previously communicated strategy, should meet the requirement for transparency and accountability, especially if these decisions continue to be substantiated in the monthly bulletins. However, it should not be underestimated that the euro system must make decisions accessible to 11 different nations according to their respective economic and cultural environments, and motivation can be influenced by different currency histories and traditions. That is why it was important that a year ago we found a viable solution as to what constitutes communication, i.e. the use of languages within the Governing Council. In this respect, I am glad that, as a Luxembourger, I can do without headphones in these sessions. The idea behind this organisational structure was therefore a very strong individualisation in the Governing Council of the ECB, in contrast to an organisational structure that would have placed more emphasis on the institutional representation of various national central banks, which would have run counter to the spirit of the Treaty insofar as the personal responsibility of the individual members would have been integrated into the responsibility towards national bodies and national orders of magnitude. The principle of "one man, one vote" has therefore been fully taken into account in this respect. 3. Also at the regulatory level, the first 6 months were fully used to pour the necessary foundations. This work has, of course, been reflected in the general regulations published in September 1998, which contained significant innovations compared to the version produced by the EMI. In this context, I would like to remind you that the minimum reserve system introduced by the ECB, which was a major innovation for Luxembourg, is primarily intended to serve 2 monetary policy functions: 1. to stabilise money market rates and (2) to reinforce the structural liquidity shortage in the banking system. The stabilisation function is intended to give credit institutions more flexibility in their day-to-day liquidity management and to allow them to take advantage of short-term arbitrage opportunities on the money market. Average compliance will also require less central bank intervention in the market to fine-tune. On 1 December 1998 the Governing Council issued a mandate for the imposition of minimum reserves, which lays down in a legally binding manner the broad lines of the minimum reserve system applied, which bears interest at the average rate for the main refinancing operations of the euro system and thus operates in line with market conditions. Furthermore, the main types of open market operations were retained. On the one hand, the main refinancing operations, which are carried out weekly and have a maturity of two weeks, and on the other hand, the longer-term refinancing operations with a term of three months, which are settled monthly. These main operations will be complemented by two standing facilities, the marginal lending facility and the deposit facility. Exactly one year ago, on 13 October 1998, the Governing Council presented the main elements of the eurosystem's stability-oriented monetary policy strategy, which, incidentally, are described in detail in the ECB's first Monthly Bulletin: with the publication of a quantitative definition of the primary objective of monetary policy, price stability, and the two pillars of the strategy aimed at achieving this objective. The first pillar is the money supply, which is given a prominent role, which is reflected in the announcement of a reference value for the growth of a broad monetary aggregate. The second pillar is the comprehensive assessment of future price developments and risks to price stability in the euro area. Thus, the Eurosystem has clearly not advocated an inflation objective, but a symmetrical objective of price stability that must counteract both inflationary and deflationary tendencies in order to contribute to healthy longer-term growth in the medium term. The statistical requirements for the design of the single monetary policy and the conduct of foreign exchange market operations had already been made available by the EMI to the banking associations in July 1996. These requirements included monetary and banking statistics as well as balance of payments statistics and financial accounts as well as other economic and financial statistics. However, the biggest requirement at the end of last year was the implementation of the target system. The last series of tests of the transition to test operation took place in November and December 1998. However, the assessment of EU securities settlement systems under certain directives as to their suitability for the conduct of Eurosystem credit operations and the assessment of the links between European securities settlement systems are still not fully completed. And the implementation of the correspondent central bank model for the cross-border use of collateral between central banks, which is supposed to have a transitory character, has now been extended again for the time being. 2. Assessment If one now proceeds to the assessment of this structure for the initial phase, one must admit to the system that the enormous preparatory work in the operational part has largely proven itself. Although not all links have yet been examined in the target, the various decisions of the initial phase are already partly considered for the need for adjustments. 1. If I apply the same grid as before, and first deal with the institutional, then probably only a change in the institutional is possible through an amendment of the Treaty, in the discussion on the enlargement of the EU. In this context, of course, the question must arise as to whether deepening European integration before enlargement, as has always been called for, would not contribute to the consolidation of the single currency, rather than a hasty enlargement that could call into question the institutional efficiency that exists at the moment and at the same time could also affect the objective of price stability. From another point of view, one could question whether various statements in the direction of institutional adjustments do not have to be located outside the Eurosystem's competence framework. In any event, the Eurosystem's principle of solidarity and collegiality can no longer be applied to these statements. In this respect, one would just like to recall that, on the one hand, if one warns of the difficulties that could affect the efficiency of a system through multi-statehood, one must also point out that multi-statehood in Europe has already led to a directorate of the great powers, which has led Europe through alliances, alliance amendments and ultimately conflicts, and that the basis of the EU idea is not based on supremacy nor population, but the engine of integration was also oiled by the small states. So one must both prevent the relapse into sacred and unholy alliances, as well as find an answer to petty statehood. If one calls for functional efficiency as the only criterion, then it would probably be better to leave the European Central Bank to a single country that does not need to consult with anyone. In this discussion, the basic elements of the Idea of European Integration, including the idea of representativity, are to be incorporated. Especially if one shares the conviction that a monetary union will only last in the long term if it is also underpinned by progress in political integration. 2. From an organizational point of view, the future will also show two opposing tendencies: the first towards centralization and the second the resistance of decentralization. While markets should normally finally see the benefits of a single European market through the introduction of a single currency, centralisation of markets could also be driven by over-regulation of financial institutions. The tendency towards disintermediation is, of course, also guided by the efforts of globalisation. In this respect, it is interesting to take a closer look at the progress made in the financial sector. In terms of outstanding borrowings worldwide, EMU has a market share that is about as large as that of the euro zone in the world's gross national product, namely 22.5%. In Europe, however, the share of foreign liabilities is higher, and domestic liabilities or bond market capitalisation lag significantly behind the development in the USA and Japan with around 6.4 trillion euros for EMU, compared to 12.5 trillion euros for the USA and 4.7 trillion euros for Japan. In the first 9 months, however, it can be seen that the broadened investor base has been used to expand the issuance activity of capital demand in the euro area. Companies have thus taken advantage of the opportunities to raise funds directly in the increasingly integrated financial markets of the euro area faster than expected. As an international issuing currency, the euro has now caught up with or even exceeded the dollar in terms of new issues. The potential of the EMU region is also still in the future for the equity markets. Although measurements in this area are difficult due to the high volatility on the stock exchanges, it can be noted that in Europe the market capitalization accounts for less than 70% of the gross domestic product with about 4 trillion euros, while in America this figure is about 16 trillion euros, which makes up a market capitalization, compared to the gross domestic product, of almost 200%. In Japan, the market capitalization is nominally at about the same level as in Europe, but compared to a gross national product that is significantly lower. The recent decisions of the stock exchanges in the euro area remind me of the stock market picture of Germany 15 years ago. When I was a Commissioner at the Luxembourg Stock Exchange, a family friend gave me old engravings depicting the stock exchanges of the German Economic Area. The pictures ranged from floor to ceiling. Whether this landscape will persist in the euro area without exchange rate risk remains to be seen. On the settlement side, there are at least two models in the room at the moment: on the one hand, a centralized system with a uniform platform; on the other hand, a system that combines national clearing plans with each other, which is sometimes described as a "spaghetti factory". In other areas, centralization is demonstrated to Europeans by Americans (see example CLS). One should therefore not underestimate the resistance to centralisation efforts. In this respect, one can also see how the bank mergers are mainly carried out at national level, even if it may only indicate a first step for cross-border banking constellations. Globalisation alone has made the boundaries between previously separate national capital markets obsolete. This should also lead to a rethinking of the supervisory function of the financial sector, taking into account the possibility of regulatory arbitrage. It is in this context that the discussion on the separation of central bank functions and surveillance functions should be seen, which has not yet been completed in various countries, and is already being called into question again in countries where it has been carried out. As long as this discussion at national level is not concluded, I think it is also premature to worry about a transfer to the European level. An even easier way to observe the trend towards centralization will, of course, be to follow the increase in the number of employees of the European Central Bank. With this number, the number of meetings and the number of working groups will also increase. However, the approach to centralisation at the institutional level should already come from the market. The faster a truly European market emerges, the greater the pressure to provide it with suitable solutions at the central level. But even in this context, one must not forget that there are advantages in the various areas of carrying out the decision-making mechanism or the implementation of decisions in the greatest possible geographical proximity. 3. Requirements It should not be forgotten that the primacy of subsidiarity corresponds to a fundamental principle of the European idea and that a truly equal treatment of all market participants, regardless of their size, is only possible with a decentralised structure. One could well imagine that the path to the future is not a linear one to more centralization, but a modular one, depending on the different functions that a central bank performs. 1. If one approaches the problem from this point of view, the primary work of the central bank is, of course, monetary policy, which is already largely centrally decided and decentralised. In this context, it should be noted that probably only a few amendments will be made on the basis of previous experience and no radical upheavals. With its implementation, the minimum reserve system has contributed to smoothing the development of the overnight money market, so that the implementation of fine-tuning measures could be dispensed with. Changes could only come in the area of adjusting the lump sum. There were some discussions about liquidity management. In principle, the Eurosystem must meet the liquidity needs of the banking system, the reserves and the liquidity required in addition. Over the first 9 months, experience has shown that, on average, the system has held higher liquidity holdings than is needed for minimum reserves, or that there is a surplus of demand for reserves in Europe. However, this surplus has halved from the beginning of the year to the middle of the year, which can also be inferred from a more efficient liquidity management of the banking system. Although higher liquidity can be expected to result in lower overnight interest rates, it has been observed on several occasions that this relationship between price and quantity has not always been true. Nevertheless, an additional observation period should be given in this context in an initial phase. There have been discussions in connection with the bidding behaviour of financial institutions. Stable allocation rates are of course desirable, but not the primary objective of liquidity management. Any action in this sense must first be weighed against the side effects for the management of short-term interest rates, which is why very great caution is required in this area. In order to solve the overbidding problem, the possibility of a transition from a volume tender to an interest rate tender has been discussed for some time. If different options were to lead to increased fluctuations in overnight interest rates as a result, the system would be forced to introduce fine-tuning instruments with which central banks in smaller countries in particular have gained experience in the past, but which cannot easily be transferred to another monetary policy area. The latest findings clearly show that with a volume tender, the precision of the liquidity supply is more accurate and therefore the overnight interest rates are stabilized. Of course, this advantage is lost with a 100% allocation policy. The same advantages can also be achieved with an interest rate tender if the interest rate tender is accompanied by an advance publication of the allocation quantity and an indication of the operational objective of the interest rate. The transparency and clarity of the signals are generally better with a volume tender, but again the same results can be achieved with an interest rate tender through a targeted publication policy. The Governing Council will continue to deepen the issue and will not come to a hasty conclusion on this delicate issue. The stabilization of the interest rate due to the average fulfilment in the minimum reserve system naturally decreases towards the end of the "maintenance period". In this context, too, consideration is being given to the extent to which the greater use of the standing facility towards the end of the reserve period and thus also the greater volatility in overnight interest rates is a disruptive factor that may or may not have to be counteracted by fine-tuning mechanisms. A third element, which was more discussed in academic circles, is the monetary policy strategy, in particular as it was pointed out that the existing strategy offers a relatively wide margin of manoeuvre in connection with the insufficient statistical depth of euro area statistics. Even if the reference value for M3 will be discussed after one year of experience, there is currently no reason to rethink the 2-pillar strategy. The reference value will be decided on the basis of data on medium-term trend growth in real GNP and the velocity of money in circulation. This monetary analysis will also take into account price developments based on a wide range of indicators and inflation forecasts within and outside the Eurosystem. As for the publication of such forecasts, I would like to quote here Professor Remsperger, who recently wrote: "The belief in the predictability of an interest rate hike through the publication of inflation forecasts is similar to the attempt in football to predict from the exact position speed of the players, from their stride length, from the wind speed, the nature of the football field and from the angular momentum of the ball in the first half. want a goal to fall into the left corner of the goal in the 12th minute of the second half." The second function of the European Central Bank is to ensure the smooth functioning of the payment system. I recall that Target was founded with 3 main objectives: to offer a secure and reliable mechanism for the processing of cross-border payments, to increase the efficiency of cross-border payments and to meet the requirements of the Eurosystem's monetary policy. After a week, the system had settled down to about 20-30,000 transactions per day with a volume between 300 and 400 billion euros. After the first 9 months, cross-border target traffic corresponds to 10% of all payments made in "large value Euro payment systems" and 27% of the total value, provided that the larger amounts in particular are processed via Target. The average value of individual payments in July 1999 was almost 12 million euros, which is 3-5 times higher than the values for other systems. From this one can conclude that Target does justice to the objective of monetary policy. 34,000 banks or bank offices can be reached via Target, and measurements have shown that a payment can be processed in an average of one and a half to 6 minutes. This, too, should meet market demands, even if the end user sometimes has questions about factors beyond Target's control, such as the settlement times of intermediaries or liquidity management. A third function of the ESCB is the collection of statistical data. Much and more work has been done in this area in the first 9 months of this year, especially in the area of money and banking statistics and balance of payments statistics. It will be necessary to free up further resources for this work, both in the European Central Bank and in the national central banks. A final task of central banks is to issue banknotes and coins. With a view to the introduction of the euro, this work will be meticulously continued in order to achieve a smooth introduction of the 13 billion banknotes in Europe. In Luxembourg, 46 tonnes of banknotes are imported in euro, equivalent to the 46 million notes in euros, and approximately up to 40 million existing banknotes are withdrawn. In addition to these notes, there are the coins, which represent 120 million in Luxembourg, which corresponds to a weight of 553 tons. These figures correspond to the introduction of euro coins and must be supplemented by the figures for the return of national coins, i.e. 160 million coins, which corresponds to a weight of 658 tonnes. In total, more than 1,300 tons of money will have to be transported in Luxembourg during the weeks of the "changeover", which will require close to 8,000 transports. If these Luxembourg figures do not impress you, consider that the Luxembourg financial centre represents one twentieth of the euro area in terms of liquidity, but the ratio of Luxembourg banknotes in the euro area is in a ratio of 1:250. Of course, the whole thing is a requirement for logistics and for the interaction of transport companies, financial institutions and the central bank. In Luxembourg, we are in the process of drawing up a detailed staff plan with the available special wagons of the transport companies, the loading capacity, the insurance limit and the most efficient use of the available logistics. Our current calculations suggest that we need about 7 theoretical days to return and enter new notes, while the size of the coins could take 50 to 60 days. In this context, we try to return this last theoretical figure through an optimal organization. Although the Banknotes Working Group has the largest number of sub-groups at Eurosystem level, the main burden of implementation remains at national level. In this area, I am particularly pleased to note that the newly established Luxembourg Central Bank has been able to cope with the rapid development at European level and, as in all other functions, has integrated seamlessly into the Eurosystem.

Deshalb ist auch nicht verwunderlich, dass die Europische Zentralbank ber diese Anfangsphase von etwas ber 400 auf jetzt ber 700 Mitarbeiter angestiegen ist, und dass dieses Wachstum auch als tendenziell weiter nach Norden zeigend erachtet wird. Fr Luxemburg, wo ein groer Teil der Entscheidungstrger noch immer nicht so richtig weiss was sie mit einer Zentralbank anfangen soll, haben wir natrlich pro Kopf der Bevlkerung mit 160 Mitarbeitern einen berdurchschnittlich hohen Personalbestand. Wenn man jedoch die Zahl der Mitarbeiter mit der Bilanzsumme der Zentralbanken vergleicht, liegt Luxemburg weit am unteren Ende der Beschftigungsskala. 2. Vor einem Jahr wurden auch die Weichen im organisationnellen Bereich gesetzt.
