text_original: LA PLACE FINANCIRE: ACTUALITS -YVES MERSCH  l'occasion de la crmonie d'inauguration de la Banque industrielle et commerciale de Chine  Luxembourg  l'Htel Le Royal Luxembourg, le 16 dcembre 1999 Seule la parole prononce fait foi. La reproduction est autorise si la source est cite. Table des matires La place financire : chiffres rcents Somme des bilans des IFM (Institutions financires montaires) luxembourgeoises Etablissements de crdit luxembourgeois Somme des bilans des banques Evolution des comptes profits et pertes des banques Rserves obligatoires Evolution de la valeur nette d'inventaire des OPC (Organismes de placement collectif) Evolution de l'effectif global dans le secteur financier Le rle international de l'euro Conclusion Bienvenue  Luxembourg C'est un plaisir pour moi d'accueillir  Luxembourg la nouvelle succursale de la Banque industrielle et commerciale de Chine. Votre banque qui comporte environ 500 000 personnes, est la bienvenue dans ce pays d'un nombre d'habitants  peu prs quivalent. Aprs l'tablissement d'une filiale  Francfort, l'ouverture d'une succursale  Luxembourg marque votre volont de contribuer au dveloppement de l'conomie chinoise et d'intensifier les relations avec l'Europe. Je ne doute pas que cet tablissement puisse fournir  sa clientle engage dans le commerce international, des services adquats et accder aux marchs internationaux pour y lever les fonds ncessaires au financement de ses activits. Je salue la dlgation spcialement venue de Chine, pays ayant bien rsist  la crise financire frappant depuis 1997 divers pays asiatiques. Il est encourageant d'observer que l'conomie chinoise continue sa forte croissance depuis 1998 (8% environ). Le Fonds montaire international (FMI) a pu relever les problmes relatifs aux secteurs financier et des entreprises publiques : il encourage les autorits  continuer leurs efforts en matire de renforcement du secteur financier et de rformes des entreprises publiques. J'espre que l'exprience recueillie  Luxembourg puisse contribuer au bon dveloppement de ce secteur. Selon le FMI, dans les domaines de politique macro-conomique et de cours de change, la Chine a suivi une direction approprie en maintenant la stabilit de la monnaie et en fournissant des incitants pour l'conomie. Ces mesures ont jou un rle important dans les ajustements conomiques rgionaux et la reprise conomique. Nous saluons les efforts d'intgration de la Chine aux marchs commerciaux et financiers internationaux. Le Luxembourg, n'a jamais pratiqu une politique de centre off-shore. Au contraire, un grand atout de la place financire de Luxembourg est l'adaptation continue de sa lgislation bancaire et financire aux circonstances nouvelles et au dveloppement du droit communautaire. L'introduction de l'euro  Luxembourg s'est faite rapidement et sans problmes. A ce jour, plus de la moiti des tablissements de crdit de la place ont bascul vers la monnaie unique. L'introduction de l'euro a entran une rnovation de la structure institutionnelle au niveau europen avec la cration de la Banque centrale europenne et au niveau luxembourgeois avec la cration de la Banque centrale du Luxembourg et de la Commission de surveillance du secteur financier. La mission principale de la Banque centrale est de raliser les missions de l'Eurosystme. Celles-ci consistent d'abord en la mise en oeuvre de la politique montaire de l'Eurosystme mais impliquent aussi d'autres missions, notamment de surveillance des systmes de paiement et de rglement sur titres. Il appartient exclusivement  l'Eurosystme d'organiser la surveillance des systmes de paiement et de rglement sur titres si importants pour la politique montaire et les marchs financiers en gnral. 1. La place financire : chiffres rcents 1.1. Somme des bilans des IFM (Institutions financires montaires) luxembourgeoises Les IFM comprennent les tablissements de crdit au sens du droit communautaire et d'autres tablissements financiers rpondant  la dfinition des fonds d'investissement montaires. Ce secteur produit les donnes significatives pour la politique montaire de l'Eurosystme. La somme de bilan provisoire des IFM luxembourgeoises au 31 octobre 1999 s'lve  629 524 millions d'euros. Au cours du mois sous revue, la somme des bilans des IFM a tmoign d'une hausse de 14 891 millions d'euros par rapport au 30 septembre 1999 o elle se situait  614 633 millions d'euros. 1.2. Etablissements de crdit luxembourgeois 1.2.1. Somme des bilans des banques A la fin du mois d'octobre 1999, la somme des bilans provisoire des tablissements de crdit luxembourgeois s'lve  584 266 millions d'euros. La somme des bilans des tablissements de crdit luxembourgeois a par consquent connu, au cours du mois d'octobre 1999, une hausse de 12 979 millions d'euros soit 2,27% par rapport au 30 septembre 1999. L'analyse du bilan agrg des tablissements de crdit luxembourgeois montre que la hausse de la somme de bilan agrge s'explique essentiellement par l'augmentation trs nette des actifs et des passifs interbancaires. Du cot de l'actif, on constate un accroissement des dpts interbancaires, mais galement des crances sur la clientle. Alors que ces dernires affichent un faible taux de croissance de 0,5% par rapport au mois de septembre 1999, on notera qu'en glissement annuel leur taux de croissance est de 10,8%. A noter galement l'volution favorable du portefeuille-effets et valeurs mobilires  revenu fixe qui n'a cess d'augmenter rgulirement au cours des dernires annes. Avec un poids relatif de 24,5% dans la somme des bilans, ce poste consolide son importance dans la structure de l'actif du bilan agrg. Au niveau du passif, on notera que les dpts de la clientle ont volu de manire favorable avec une lgre hausse de 0,15% par rapport au mois prcdent; ils se situent dsormais  189 923 millions d'euros. 1.2.2. Evolution des comptes profits et pertes des banques L'analyse du compte de profits et pertes au 30 septembre 1999 et la comparaison des rsultats atteints par les banques luxembourgeoises ne peuvent pas tre effectues sans procder  la neutralisation des revenus sur divers exceptionnellement levs et non rcurrents observs en 1998. Compte tenu de cette neutralisation, les rsultats bruts dgags par les tablissements de crdit luxembourgeois au 30 septembre 1999 se situent  un niveau similaire  celui observ  la mme date de l'anne prcdente. Nanmoins, les diffrentes composantes du rsultat brut montrent des volutions particulires qui sont brivement dcrites ci-dessous. Rsultats sur intrts La baisse en termes bruts des intrts perus et bonifis en glissement annuel, dj observe au 30 mars ainsi qu'au 30 juin 1999, s'est maintenue galement au cours du troisime trimestre de l'anne en cours. Malgr une somme de bilan moyenne suprieure  celle observe au cours des trois premiers trimestres de l'anne prcdente, les comptes de profits et pertes des tablissements de crdit luxembourgeois, arrts au 30 septembre 1999, tmoignent d'une baisse des intrts perus et bonifis. Cette volution dfavorable qui trouve son explication dans la baisse continuelle des taux d'intrt sur les marchs, prsente nanmoins une caractristique rjouissante pour les tablissements de crdit luxembourgeois. La tendance, entame depuis le dbut de l'anne 1998, qui consistait dans un accroissement plus rapide des intrts bonifis par rapport aux intrts perus, s'est retourne au cours de l'anne 1999; en effet, face  une baisse de 8,3% des intrts bonifis, on retrouve une baisse de 7,2% seulement des intrts perus. La marge sur intrts s'est par consquent accrue de 4,8% par rapport au 30 septembre 1998 et reprsente dsormais 52,1% du rsultat brut total. Rsultats hors intrts En ce qui concerne les rsultats hors intrts, on remarquera une baisse notable des revenus sur la ralisation de titres. Le rsultat sur titres, qui se situe plus ou moins au mme niveau que celui observ au 30 septembre 1997, est de 32,7% infrieur  celui observ  la mme date de l'anne prcdente. Le rsultat sur commissions quant  lui continue  constituer la principale source de revenus hors intrts malgr un taux de croissance infrieur  celui observ au cours de l'anne 1998. Ce taux de croissance annuel est de 12,8% au 30 septembre 1999, alors qu'en date du 30 septembre 1998 il tait de 20,2% en glissement annuel. Toutefois, en raison de la diminution du rsultat sur divers, le solde sur commissions gagne en importance relative dans le total du rsultat hors intrts et reprsente dsormais 34,9% de ce dernier. Le rsultat sur oprations de change volue galement d'une manire positive et, avec une augmentation de 12,75% en glissement annuel, est mme suprieur au niveau atteint le 30 septembre 1998. Cette volution est de nature  dmontrer que les banques luxembourgeoises ont su compenser les manques  gagner dus  l'introduction de la monnaie unique en tendant leurs activits sur des units montaires autres, essentiellement le USD, le JPY mais galement le CHF, que celles des pays de la zone euro. Finalement, on notera particulirement la baisse importante des rsultats sur divers. Dans ce contexte, il y a lieu de rappeler que l'anne 1998 tait caractrise par des rsultats sur divers exceptionnels due  la ralisations de plusvalues importantes sur des titres de participation (cfr. galement rapport annuel de la BCL). En raison de l'importance exceptionnelle des revenus nets sur divers au cours de l'anne 1998, la marge sur intrts ne reprsentait, en moyenne, plus que 45% du rsultat brut. Au cours de l'anne 1999 le poids relatif de la marge sur intrts est nanmoins revenu au niveau "normal"; bien que l'importance relative du rsultat sur intrts soit en dcroissance depuis quelques annes son niveau s'est nanmoins rtabli autour de 52% au cours des trois premiers trimestres de l'anne en cours. Frais Au 30 septembre 1999, les frais de personnel montrent un accroissement de 9,6% en glissement annuel. Cette volution est  voir en relation avec la croissance considrable de l'emploi dans le secteur bancaire, mais galement en relation avec l'augmentation des cots salariaux. L'augmentation des frais d'exploitation devrait tre vue d'une part en relation avec des investissements au niveau informatique (an 2000) et d'autre part par des quipements supplmentaires, indispensables en raison de l'accroissement de l'effectif. 1.2.3. Rserves obligatoires Le montant provisoire de l'exigence de rserve pour la priode de maintenance qui a dbut le 24 novembre s'lve  6 190 millions d'euros, soit 72 millions d'euros de plus que lors de la priode de maintenance prcdente o le montant dfinitif tait de 6 118 millions d'euros. 1.3. Evolution de la valeur nette d'inventaire des OPC (Organismes de placement collectif) D'aprs les explications fournies par la Commission de surveillance du secteur financier, la hausse de la valeur nette d'inventaire totale des OPC luxembourgeois rsulte de l'effet conjugu de la hausse du cours du dollar et des marchs boursiers au cours du mois d'octobre (60%) et de l'investissement net en capital (40%). 1.4. Evolution de l'effectif global dans le secteur financier D'une manire gnrale, l'volution de l'effectif dans le secteur financier est plus que satisfaisante. Au 30 septembre 1999, l'emploi dans le secteur financier s'levait  23 618 units, ce qui reprsente une progression de 520 units (+ 2,25%) par rapport au 30 juin 1999 et de 1 451 units (+ 6,55%) par rapport  la mme date de l'anne prcdente. L'emploi dans le secteur financier reprsente dsormais 10,4% de l'emploi total au Luxembourg contre 9,8% au 30 septembre 1998. La rpartition entre Luxembourgeois et trangers continue  voluer en dfaveur des Luxembourgeois qui ne reprsentent plus que 35,0% de l'emploi dans le secteur financier contre 37,8% au 30 septembre 1998. Au cours du dernier trimestre, le nombre de Luxembourgeois employs dans le secteur financier est stagnant, alors que le nombre des employs trangers a augment de 410 units. Au 30 septembre 1999, l'effectif total dans les tablissements de crdit s'lve 20 947 units, soit une progression de 505 units (+ 2,47%) par rapport au 30 juin 1999 et de 1 285 units (+ 6,64%) par rapport au 30 septembre 1998. Au 30 septembre 1999, l'emploi dans les autres professionnels du secteur financier qui s'levait  2 671 units, reste stable par rapport au 30 juin 1999. Par rapport au 30 septembre de l'anne prcdente, l'emploi total augmente de 166 units ce qui reprsente une hausse de 6,63%. 2. Le rle international de l'euro Le rle international de l'euro dcoule naturellement des liberts garanties,  l'intrieur comme  l'extrieur en matire de capitaux. L'euro a pour vocation, depuis son lancement de servir de monnaie internationale ; ce rle est appel  crotre progressivement, au gr d'une part de l'intgration, et de l'amlioration des marchs financiers europens et d'autre part, des mesures politiques suivies,  l'intrieur comme  l'extrieur. On peut relever que plus d'une trentaine de pays ont des rgimes de taux de change impliquant l'euro. L'euro est sans conteste,  prsent, la deuxime monnaie internationale la plus utilise et ce dans ces diffrentes fonctions de financement, d'investissement, de rserve ou d'unit de rfrence. Il est prvisible que l'usage international de l'euro ira croissant mme si cette volution ne peut tre que progressive ; il contribue  l'amlioration des marchs financiers en euro. L'euro a aussi pour vocation de servir d'actif de rserve, ce qui vient encore d'tre reconnu par le prsident de l'Autorit montaire de Hong Kong M. Joseph Yam. 3. Conclusion Le dmarrage de l'Union montaire a t un succs et les effets sur la place financire de Luxembourg ne peuvent tre que bnfiques pour ses perspectives d'avenir. De nombreux dfis sont sans aucun doute encore  relever. Cependant, l'euro a la vocation de devenir une monnaie largement utilise  l'chelle mondiale ; il apparat comme un facteur dynamique dans le dveloppement si important pour nous, des relations financires entre l'Europe et l'Asie. L'action de l'Eurosystme s'inscrit dans la dure ; elle vise  garantir la stabilit et contribue au dveloppement des services et marchs financiers, ainsi que de l'conomie globale. C'est dans ce contexte gnral que s'attache un prix particulier  l'installation de votre banque  Luxembourg  laquelle nous souhaitons plein succs. Annexe: Liste des tableaux 1. Title: The role of the Central Banks in Euroland
text: THE ROLE OF THE CENTRAL BANKS IN EUROLAND -YVES MERSCH Prague, 28th March 2000 Seule la parole prononcee fait foi. Introduction "Prague is a famous, ancient, kingly seat. In situation and in state complete, in architecture stately". So wrote an English volunteer who fought at the battle of the White Mountain in 1620, John Taylor. Ladies and Gentlemen, it is a privilege to have been invited to this historical, beautiful and charming city of Prague, in the heart of Europe. Much of the beauty of this lovely city is due to building work commissioned by members of the House of Luxembourg, notably Charles IV. I am delighted to speak before such a distinguished audience of the role of the Central Banks in Euroland. Such a title could be ambiguous. My purpose is not to describe the general functions entrusted to Central Banks. We know that most of the Central Banks in Europe were set up in their home countries as early, in many cases, as the 19 th century. Their main function was to issue banknotes. Progressively their role has changed profoundly: they were just issuing banks, but now they have been transformed into institutions charged with the definition and implementation of monetary policy. From 1 st January 1999 the euro has been introduced in eleven of the fifteen EU Member States. The former national currencies remain as temporary expressions of the single currency. Apart from introducing the euro, the Eurosystem has been set up primarily to conduct monetary policy. Its first objective is, as we know, to maintain price stability. Let me remind you that if the Treaty refers to the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) as a new institution and the ECU as a new currency, the terms which have been used since last year, are the Eurosystem and the euro respectively. The Eurosystem is composed of the newly created European Central Bank (ECB) together with the national central banks (NCBs) of the States participating in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). For these countries this is a new challenge and it provides them with a new framework in which to develop their activities. In this context the Luxembourg situation is specific: the Banque centrale du Luxembourg (BCL) had to be established ( together with the ECB on 1 st June 1998) in order to comply with a specific provision of the Maastricht Treaty. The new law establishing the BCL is dated 23 rd December 1998. It entered into force at the beginning of the activities of the Eurosystem on 1 st January 1999. So undoubtedly the BCL is the most recently born NCB; its statute was drafted so as to comply fully with the requirements of EMU. If the BCL is the youngest NCB, it is not really the smallest one. The relative weight is not to be judged only in view of the number of staff members or by the key of capital subscription of the European Central Bank (ECB). This gives the BCL 0,15% of the capital of the ECB. At the Board its Governor is represented with an equal vote alongside 10 other Governors of NCBs and 6 members of the Executive Board. This voting weight of 1/17 th is sometimes depicted in the media of larger countries as an example of overrepresentation of small countries. They forget to mention that a Central Bank is about liquidity in the economy and Luxembourg represents far more than 1/17 th of the total liquidity of the euro area. I now wish to comment more specifically on the institutional framework, leaving to other speakers the discussion of the practical organisation of the Eurosystem and the division of labour between the ECB and the NCB's. The dual capacity of the NCBs The NCB's are legal entities set up by the laws of their respective States. They are, at the same time, an integral part of the ESCB. The Treaty imposes basic tasks on the Eurosystem. Among the main priorities the first is to define and implement the monetary policy of the Community. The Treaty conferssome competences on the ECB, others on the NCBs. Article 14 of the Statute of the ESCB-ECB, refers specifically to the national central banks as Members of the Eurosystem. The statutes of NCBs themselves must be compatible with the Treaty, and have to that extent been partially harmonised in the process of legal convergence. The cohesion inside the system is guaranteed: "the NCBs are an integral part of the ESCB and shall act in accordance with the guidelines and instructions of the ECB". This applies of course to the functions of Central banks transferred to ESCB, mainly monetary policy, payment systems, reserve management, exchange rate operations, banknote issuance and advisory functions, but not prudential supervision since the Treaty limits the role of the ECB to contribute to the work of national authorities in this area. If NCBs are independent from Governments, the Eurosystem is also independent from individual NCBs in the area of transfer of sovereignty to the European level. In other areas NCBs remain independent from the Eurosystem and subject to the rules of national organisations of constitutional power. NCBs have thus a dual capacity at national and European level. This is true for the division of competence according to functions of Central Bank transferred to the Eurosystem and functions that remain of national competence according to the European Treaties like prudential surveillance. But this dual capactiy applies also to the implementation of monetary policy and to the decision making process involving Governors of NCBs in the Governing Council of the ECB in their personal capacity. The NCBs and the decision-making process of the ECB Personal independence of members of the Governing Council Each Governor enjoys a dual capacity, acting both as Chief Executive of his NCB and as Member of the Governing Council. As a Member of the Governing Council the Governor acts in his personal capacity and not as the representative of his NCB. Each Governor contributes to the work of the Governing Council through his personal participation but in such a way that the Eurosystem can benefit from the work done in his NCB. In fact, it is quite simply not appropriate to consider the participation of the Governors of NCBs in the Governing Council as protection of national interests in the decision-making process of the ECB. The Governors do not represent their own NCB. Indeed, the participation of Governors from countries of very different sizes provides an element of independence and, even more, of cohesion. Even though Governors are not appointed according to a common procedure but according to separate national procedures, the mandate of each Governor is protected, under the Statute for the duration of his term of office. His removal during his term of office (which shall be not less than five years) is subject to Community procedure and, eventually to a judgement by the Court of Justice of the European Communities. The basic voting procedure is one man, one vote. Weighted voting is limited to financial (as opposed to monetary) decisions where the NCB Governors are representatives of the ECB. Comparisons should not be made with the Council of Ministers of the EU where qualified weighted voting is becoming the normal voting method. The EU procedure takes into account of the importance of each Member State. On its side, the Governing Council of the ECB should not be seen, legally, as a body in which national interests are debated. Thus, even the enlargement of the European Union will not lead to a "re-nationalisation" of the ECB. The Governing Council of the ECB is empowered to take the most important and strategically significant decisions affecting the Eurosystem. "The Governing Council shall formulate the monetary policy of the Community including, as appropriate, decisions relating to intermediate monetary objectives, key interest rates and the supply of reserves in the ESCB, and shall establish the necessary guidelines for their implementation". The role of a Governor should not be compared with that of "Landeszentralbankprasident" in the Deutsche Bundesbank, neither with that of the Governor of a US regional Reserve Bank. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is composed of eight permanent members, seven members of the Federal Reserve Board (FRB) and the President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. This committee also includes four members from among the other eleven Governors of the Regional Reserve Banks on a rotating basis. The US approach is more centralist. The presence of the Governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York is explained by the fact that the New York Bank has exclusive competence for the operational implementation of policy. This structure is quite different from that of the Eurosystem. At the Deutsche Bundesbank the nine "Landeszentralbankprasidenten" are members of the "Zentralbankrat" together with the President, the Vice-President and up to eight further members of the "Direktorium". The "Landeszentralbanken" are fully integrated into the Deutsche Bundesbank. They have no legal personality. The former principle, under which each "Land" enjoyed the presence of its own "Landeszentralbank" no longer applies. Committees of the ESCB The decision making process of the Governing Council benefits also from the ESCB "committees". These committees are composed of representatives of the ECB and of the NCBs of each participating Member State. They provide for technical analysis, contribute to the preparation of decisions, and help to follow up the implementation of these decisions. Thus forecasts developed inside some committees and involving staff from both the ECB and NCBs have contributed to the decision-making process. Nevertheless, it should be recalled that the work of the ESCB committees is preparatory. The committees help the decision-making bodies of the Eurosystem but they are not part of these bodies and they do not take any binding decisions. The Governing Council remains sovereign. NCB preparatory analysis Beyond their participation in the Committees, the NCBs also contribute directly to the decisionmaking process in the Eurosystem insofar that each NCB has to prepare the analysis of the relevant problems so as to enable its Governor to take part in the discussions of the Governing Council. In the area of statistics, euro area figures are not published nationally, but aggregated at the ECB to prepare decisions on the ground of common euro area wide statistics. Other statistical material is prepared by NCBs to assist their Governor for the Governing Council meeting; yet other statistics are required for national purposes. In the Eurosystem research work remains largely decentralised but is co-ordinated. Much research is conducted in the various departments of NCBs, in the economic, financial, legal and technical fields. The single voice policy which is a basic requirement, does not imply the absence of decisions inside the system. The implementation of monetary policy Decentralised implementation The Statute contains the general principle that "to the extent deemed possible and appropriate" it is up to the NCBs to carry out those operations that are required to perform the tasks of the system. There is a presumption that the operational activities of the system, which have been decided upon by the ECB, take place at decentralised level. Usually, for commentators, this provision relates to the principle of subsidiarity. It is true that according to the Treaty this principle applies only in areas "which do not fall within the exclusive competence of the Community". Although monetary competences have been definitively transferred from the NCBs to the ECB, the implementation of monetary policy decisions is conducted on a "shared" basis within the Union. For the implementation of monetary policy, the NCBs are responsible for maintaining relations with their counterparts, which are local credit institutions. A centralised approach is not necessarily ruled out, but any decision in this field has to be taken by the ECB on a case-by-case basis according to the discretion of its decision-making bodies. The operations required to implement decisions of the ECB are conducted at national level under national legislation. Contrary to other operations in the field of payment and security settlement systems there is so far no "remote access" for the credit institutions. These must make use of the facilities provided by their own central bank. In the event of a default on a part of a credit institution, the sanction procedure is initiated by the relevant NCB, on behalf of the ECB. In implementing its monetary policy, the Eurosystem bears in mind principles such as equal treatment, decentralisation, cost-benefits ratio and harmonisation. The Eurosystem is not comparable with the FED in which the Federal Reserve Bank of New York conducts operations according to decisions taken at federal level. The NCBs also contribute to the communication policy of the Eurosystem in the monetary field. Until there is a complete integration of financial, economic and social policies the single monetary policy has different consequences in the different Member States. The monetary authorities not only have to keep the market informed but must also keep in touch with policy-makers, to contribute to an adequate policy mix in view of the needs of national and regional authorities. The NCBs will be responsible for issuing the euro banknotes as from 1 st January 2002. They are actively involved in the preparatory work for this operation. The manufacture of euro banknotes has already started. The Treaty provides for the exclusive right of the ECB to authorise the issue of such notes. An intensive information campaign will be conducted by the Eurosystem from August this year. The Treaty provides that some areas shall be treated through joint actions on the part of the ECB and the NCBs, for example international cooperation where improvements are expected. The NCBs have provided the ECB with foreign reserve assets totalling an amount to 50 000 million euros. This amount will probably be increased when the regulation "on further calls of foreign reserve assets" is adopted. These assets are managed on behalf of the ECB by those NCBs which have transferred them. The other foreign reserve assets held by NCBs are managed by them according to common rules. Direct implementation Some specific functions are entrusted exclusively to the ECB under EU rules (legal acts, sanctions, external representation, opinions . . . ). In most cases it is up to the discretion of the decision-making bodies of the Eurosystem to decide on the way in which such functions should be carried out, either on a centralised basis or on a decentralised one. So theoretically the ECB has a choice between direct or indirect implementation, but any centralised implementation must be justified in view of the principle of subsidiarity. Such centralisation can be expected with respect to the external representation of the ESCB -for instance relations with international organisations and third countries. The objective is to achieve operational efficiency inside the Eurosystem. Generally this efficiency is to be enhanced with local proximity. National procedures may be used. Common policy can tolerate some divergence, in order to cope with particularities of national banking systems, historical and structural differences. Smooth functioning is compatible with decentralisation as long as it does not lead to a new fragmentation of the single market of financial services. The monetary policy is single. This is an overriding principle. It must therefore be implemented without discrimination ensuring a level playing field. This principle has to be borne in mind when the opportunity for some operations of the system to be centralised either totally or partially is debated. The other functions of NCBs The NCBs perform functions other than those directly related to monetary policy. Some of these functions are mixed, carried out in accordance with decisions of the ECB. The Statute permits NCBs to carry out, also, non-Eurosystem functions unless these interfere with the objectives and tasks of the Eurosystem. Mixed functions I will not discuss the involvement of NCBs in matters which complement the implementation of monetary policy. The ESCB decides how the ECB shall be represented in measures of international cooperation concerning the tasks entrusted to the Eurosystem. Most important, we must remember the significance of the role of NCBs in the fields of payment systems, communication policy and statistics. As far as statistics are concerned, the Statute assigns to the NCBs the task of assisting the ECB to collect the necessary statistical information. May I draw your attention to an important competence mentioned in the Statute: "the ECB and national central banks may provide facilities, and the ECB may make regulations, to ensure efficient and sound clearing and payment systems within the Community and with other countries". The payment systems oversight is one of the core competences attributed to the NCBs. That an adequate distinction between prudential supervision and oversight of payment systems is made is a matter for national legislation. This is the reason why the ECB has recently adopted a critical opinion on draft legislation in a Member State because that State failed to make a distinction between the two tasks. The main focus of prudential supervision, however, is the safety and soundness of individual financial institutions, whereas the primary focus of oversight is placed on the clearing and payment systems themselves in order to ensure their smooth operation, to avoid systemic risk within or between such systems and to ensure the efficient and sound transmission of monetary policy impulses. National functions "National central banks may perform functions other than those specified in this Statute unless the Governing Council finds, by a majority of two thirds of the votes cast, that these interfere with the objectives and tasks of the ESCB. Such functions shall be performed on the responsibility and liability of national central banks and shall not be regarded as being part of the functions of the ESCB". One of the main activities assumed by NCBs outside the Eurosystem is that of prudential supervision. In this field the ESCB has an advisory function and has to contribute to the stability of the financial system. The Treaty also provides for the possibility of assigning to the ECB specific tasks in prudential supervision of credit institutions and other financial institutions with the exception of insurance undertakings. In the long run one might imagine that certain functions developed with success at one national level might encourage the NCBs of other countries to develop them. Discussions have already begun, for instance, concerning certain central bank services such as: credit registers, databases on annual accounts, research and analysis of national economy, fight against money laundering, investment advisor and manager for governments or other public bodies, communication, and so on. Conclusion At present, there are nearly 60 000 staff members in the different NCBs which participate in the ESCB and less than 800 at the ECB. Such figures are not to be seen as the expression of some balance of power. The Eurosystem is composed of the ECB together with the NCBs. It is a complex architecture which has avoided a difficult legal merger between different legal entities. The NCBs, on their side, contribute effectively to the smooth functioning of the system as a whole. The NCBs enjoy legal, financial and social autonomy, but they must comply with decisions of the ECB, in particular with guidelines and instructions relating to operational tasks. The present situation is not final. The organisation of the system is still in progress. A number of studies are in progress, aimed at providing a blueprint of the future organisation of the system and the full participation of both present and future members of the Eurosystem. Many important problems, such as income distribution and social policy, and the external representation of the Eurosystem will need consideration in the future. These subjects are not for today. Thank you, Ladies and Gentlemen.

Title: The dangers of inflation for Luxembourg - Yves Mersch
text: THE DANGERS OF INFLATION FOR LUXEMBOURG -YVES MERSCH Speech by Yves Mersch at the lunch-debate organised by the Economist Club Luxembourg Luxembourg, 6 October 2000 Only the word spoken is authentic. Ladies and Gentlemen, In the art of describing risks, identifying dangers, predicting crises, economists do not give it to anyone. It is not without reason that their profession is sometimes described as the science of disasters; they are often seen as inveterate skeptics. There are probably also economists who associate their prestige so closely with the making of pessimistic forecasts that they see the absence of disasters as disenchantment and personal bankruptcy. In normality, however, economists hope that politicians will take their formal notice seriously and thus avoid misadventures to the Nation. Why would a central banker speak out about the dangers of inflation? The most obvious answer is, of course, that in the final analysis everyone now agrees that inflation is a monetary phenomenon, and that considerable deviations from the objective of price stability are the consequence of a certain degree of laxity in the conduct of monetary policy in the face of exogenous shocks. Do we not now have almost unanimity, which is extremely rare among economists, to support the view that the best contribution that monetary policy can make is to ensure price stability? The pursuit of this objective is not only the best contribution of monetary policy to growth in the face of the wealth of evidence on the negative impacts of inflation on economic activity in general, but price stability is also the best contribution of monetary policy to social policy since it is the poorest who are least able to protect themselves against inflation. In a monetary economy, price stability allows markets to function effectively and prices to be correctly perceived. The thesis that monetary policy should have price stability as a priority objective therefore stems not only from the conservatism of central banks, but defines one of the few recognized axioms of economic discipline. If there is agreement on the objective of price stability, the facade consensus begins to crack when it comes to giving a numerical definition to this concept. In Europe we have adopted a definition of considering stable prices if they are compatible with a year-on-year increase in the harmonised index of consumer prices of less than 2%. The word "increase" makes it clear that decreases in consumer prices are not compatible with the definition of price stability: the definition is therefore symmetrical in that it excludes both inflation and deflation. On the other hand, we must insist on the word "medium-term" which recognizes the existence of short-term price developments that are outside the control of monetary policy. This medium-term orientation also allows for a graduated and measured response to economic shocks to avoid introducing unnecessary volatility into interest rates or real economic activity. The numerical definition of price stability can be discussed. Some central banks have not adopted a precise figure. The decision taken within the European System of Central Banks reflects above all the desire to remain controllable, since a numerical definition gives an order of magnitude that makes it possible to measure performance. In addition, the figure of 2% is in line either implicitly or explicitly as most of the central banks participating in the euro had given themselves in their national monetary policy before the advent of the euro. This figure can also be found already in a recommendation of the Council of the European Union as early as July 1995. Finally, for a new central bank a numerical definition gives a clear anchor for the long-term expectations of economic agents, while for an institution with a past reputation and performance, this definition may be more implicit. In Europe, monetary policy has been pooled and decisions are taken on the basis of European aggregates and not on the basis of national figures. A country that moves into an exceptional position in relation to European aggregates exposes itself to the risks of inadequate monetary policy for its own economy. It is therefore up to it to react by re-establishing an appropriate policy mix through structural or fiscal policies. This reaction by other areas of national policy is all the more necessary since this country is unable to influence by its own weight the common monetary aggregates. Inflation in Luxembourg, which exceeds that of its neighbouring countries and that of the euro zone, will quickly have negative consequences on competitiveness, especially since the country has the greatest economic opening. Moreover, Luxembourg is the country where factor mobility plays a role within the greater region probably more perfectly than elsewhere in monetary union; this means that a deterioration in our economic performance will ultimately lead to a loss of part of our human capital, since cross-border workers will turn away from Luxembourg in favour of countries with a better economic situation. This is why the Banque centrale du Luxembourg noted with concern the phenomenon of a sharper acceleration of inflation in Luxembourg than elsewhere in the euro area, to the point of leading to a reversal of the relative position in the sense that Luxembourg inflation generally tended to move more slowly than the average of its partners. Since the second quarter of 1999 it has been growing at a higher rate. The rise in oil prices and the level of the exchange rate against the US dollar of the single currency are the main factors explaining the acceleration of inflation in Luxembourg. It should be noted, however, that apart from these two elements, we have also seen a number of increases in administrative prices of which we can ask ourselves the question of expediency, perhaps not from the point of view of economicity, but from the point of view of timing in a context characterized by accelerating inflation. August inflation in the euro area, as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, was 2.3% on an annual basis. In Luxembourg it exceeded this figure by 1.4%. Only Ireland, with an annual rate of 5.7%, experienced higher inflation than Luxembourg in August 2000. The figures for September still show inflation of 4.2% according to the harmonised index or 3.4% depending on the national way of measuring. It is true that energy products are more strongly represented in the harmonised index of consumer prices in Luxembourg, namely 12.08%, than in the other countries of the euro area (average weight: 8.98%). Secondly, the sensitivity of the prices of energy products to consumption in relation to world oil prices is also highest in Luxembourg due to lower taxation. But let's look elsewhere. The price of food also rose from 1.24% in January to 2.84% in July. Prices for industrial goods rose 7.32% in July, partly explained by the surge in the energy subcomponent. The evolution of the prices of non-energy industrial goods also increased by 1.63% in July. Slowly energy prices will make their way through the prices of intermediate goods and wage costs via indexation to lead to the prices of final goods. If the competitive situation of companies has led them in the first stage to absorb this increase in profit margins, this absorption becomes implausible given the persistence over time of the increase in oil prices and its translation into wage costs. The latest figures indicate an increase in wage costs in industry of 4.4% compared to 1.8% in 1999. As regards services, it should be noted that the increases observed by the HICP were of the order of 2.5% to 2.8% during the current year, which is mainly the result of the index tranches due in August 1999 and July 2000 respectively, which are most felt at the level of labour-intensive services. Core inflation (IPCN version) increased in pace to 2% in Luxembourg in September, well above core inflation in the euro area. This increase is explained by the impact of index brackets, the dynamism of the economic situation as well as the appearance of the repercussions of oil price increases on the price of other goods and services. I would like to take a moment to draw your attention to the inflation of real estate asset prices in Luxembourg dealt with in the most recent Bulletin of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg. While it is true that there is no direct link between asset price inflation and consumer prices because the former do not appear in the household basket used to measure consumer price inflation, there is an indirect link through the wealth effect with consequences for consumer price inflation. This study will be a first contribution, and the analysis will be continued in subsequent Bulletins. I would like to return to my analysis of inflation in Luxembourg and the consequences of this exogenous inflation. Is this observation of external origin synonymous with impotence? Does the Luxembourg economy have no instrument at its disposal to counteract exogenous shocks? I would say that even if the means of action of economic policy are limited in Luxembourg to the whole month, the policy should not tend to reinforce external shocks. Thus, in 1974 during the first oil shock, we experienced the largest increase in budgetary spending since the Second World War. This timid attempt to finance an external shock, however, quickly yielded to the recognition of the need for adjustment. This year it still seems that the first reaction was a desire to finance the external shock. Is there insufficient knowledge of the phenomena of transmission of price increases in Luxembourg in the particular institutional framework that it has, particularly in terms of wage formation? That is why I thought it necessary to draw attention to the principles agreed at Community level with regard to the need to avoid a pro-cyclical fiscal policy. If tax reforms in Europe are part of the necessary structural reforms, they should be part of a withdrawal of public spending, while we have seen in Luxembourg an extraordinary increase in this same expenditure. It is true that a large part of this increase translates into a strengthening of investment funds, but does not automatically translate into investment expenditure. Investment funds have technical limitations due to existing human resources in the public service as well as to the ability of the private sector to intervene in the field of activity of certain investment funds. We can speak of public savings rather than a strengthening of investment activity. However, in the current context of the use of public savings in term accounts, this saving has a remuneration lower than inflation. The money set aside decreases in value. What is the intrinsic value of increased state intervention in the economy if we look at the composition of growth for 1999, which amounted to 7.5%, almost a third of which was due to general government consumption? This consumption increase of 12.8% was due to 4 recurring factors: the expenditure on the newly introduced long-term care insurance; some additional family allowances; one increase in the expenditure of health insurance funds; one increase in pension expenditure. In addition, the draft budget for 2001 provides for an increase in inflation of 2.0% and a further injection of purchasing power through a reduction in the tax scale, while the increase in final consumption of households reached 4.1% last year and shows no signs of weakness this year. It is true that the national scenario partly echoes the behaviour of our neighbours. Are we repeating the mistakes of the past described by the IMF as follows: Competitive exchange rate positions encourage the start of the European economy. Driven by external demand, the exchange rate should appreciate as the cycle matures. But the lack of counter-cyclical economic policies and outright pro-cyclical fiscal policies is encouraging inflationary pressures during the recovery forcing real wages to respond to improved cyclical conditions and further strengthening inflationary pressures. This leads the monetary authorities to respond to these increased risks by tightening financing conditions. Thus, in times of recovery, there is a masking of rigidities in economies that prevent rapid adjustment to external shocks. Thus, the comfortable situation in terms of public finances should be used to attack policies that are better oriented towards a more efficient supply in both product and factor markets, through structural reform policies in these markets, policies to reform the tax system, a review of subsidies in public spending. If these reforms are not implemented, the policy mix could become problematic again in the euro area as the cycle matures. And the Monetary Fund continues that especially in countries where risks of overheating arise specific efforts should be made to accelerate structural reforms aimed at encouraging growth potential. In Luxembourg, beyond the political debate and without wanting to enter into a partisan discussion, this would mean abandoning policies to stimulate demand and moving towards policies to broaden supply. Shouldn't the real resource base, including labour resources, be broadened in order to maintain current exponential growth rates and avoid inflationary bottlenecks and infrastructure bottlenecks in the future? The Monetary Fund also insists that tax cuts should be limited to taxes with the greatest impact on supply, and that for the surplus public savings could be formed to accompany social security financing reforms. Unfortunately, the history of cycles in Europe over the last three decades leads us to caution. Almost always the inadequacy of counter-cyclical policies or even outright pro-cyclical policies has strengthened inflexible markets to break the recovery and project growth into a downward phase. The inability in the past of structural reforms to revitalize the supply side to the extent required to meet expanding demand raises questions about sustained and sustained growth, which alone will be able to sustainably reduce unemployment levels that remain at unacceptably high levels. In this regard, the Fund also notes that wage formation at national level has become much more sensitive to competitiveness within the euro area, and I believe that it would be useful for the main actors to reflect on the consequences of our institutional functioning in a changed environment. In conclusion, we can be worried about the dangers of inflation in Luxembourg. At the fiscal level, public consumption is experiencing a very high structural dynamic, the numerous subsidies are not necessarily intended to broaden supply, some of them rather aimed at stimulating demand. The high level of public investment intentions in the face of a record level of private investment can also lead to price pressures. Even if capital goods are imported, existing domestic resources must keep pace. The reduction of the tax burden is still targeted at demand. The formation of certain administrative prizes is part of an outdated philosophy. While we have been well informed about the size and color of the eyes of Luxembourgers for 150 years, our knowledge of the channels of transmission and price formation is lacking. We do not seem to have the resources or the will to try to spot the signs of a new economy at home. Yet one thing is certain: if we believe we can live with inflation higher than those of our neighbors, it is the entire future of our economic and social well-being that we are putting at stake. It is not too early for an awareness to be raised about the functioning of our economy in Economic and Monetary Union.

Et le Fonds Montaire de continuer que surtout dans les pays o des risques de surchauffe se prsentent des efforts spcifiques devraient tre faits pour acclrer les rformes structurelles destines  encourager le potentiel de croissance. Au Luxembourg, au-del du dbat politique et sans vouloir entrer dans une discussion partisane, cela voudrait dire de se dpartir des politiques de stimulation de la demande pour s'orienter vers des politiques d'largissement de l'offre. Ne faudrait-il pas largir la base de ressources relles, notamment de ressources de main d'oeuvre dans le pays afin de maintenir les taux de croissance exponentiels actuels et d'viter des goulots d'tranglement inflationnistes ainsi que des engorgements d'infrastructure  l'avenir ? Title: Speech on the occasion of the presentation of the PartnershipBank centrale du Luxembourg - Ministre des Finances
text: SPEECH BY MRS ANDReE BILLON, DIRECTOR OF THE BCL, ON THE OCCASION OF THE PRESENTATION OF THE PARTNERSHIPBANQUE CENTRALE DU LUXEMBOURG - MINISTeRE DES FINANCES Minister, ladies and gentlemen, dear partners, colleagues and friends, it is a privilege for me to present to you what is the cornerstone of the Central Bank's Euro 2002 information campaign, namely its partnership programme. Here at the BCL, we are actively preparing this formidable operation known as cash changeover, replacing the current notes and coins with euro banknotes and coins at the beginning of 2002. The logistical, technical and security problems are considerable, but we are facing them within the framework of the Eurosystem, which, as you know, brings together the European Central Bank and the Central Banks of the 12 States participating in the euro area. However, this event affects the entire population. Our duty is to inform him. Communication is in no way a luxury or an advertising toy, it is an essential element for the effective achievement of a central bank public service mission: namely to give everyone, professionals and individuals, young and old, new payment instruments. We know that the public, especially in Luxembourg, is generally in favour of the new currency, which will be very useful to them. Nevertheless, a recent survey conducted in the twelve countries of the euro zone reveals that about 56% of the Luxembourg population think that euro banknotes will have a national face, which, of course, is not the case. We therefore need to inform and raise awareness. The public must also have confidence in these new notes, which will replace the old monetary signs in one fell swoop. To this end, it must have adequate and timely information on the visual and tactile aspects of euro banknotes and coins; he must know the precise graphics, the dimensions, the dominant colors. He must also, of course, know the new names of the 7 banknotes and 8 coins. In due course, i.e. from 1 September 2001, we will make public the security features incorporated in these monetary signs. To this presentation of the new monetary signs, information on the practical modalities of the cash changeover is attached. In this regard, we are already beset by many questions: how will professionals be frontloaded, how will the public be able to benefit from coin kits, how will the harmonious exchange be carried out during the period of dual circulation in January  February 2002, as well as after this period? In addition, the BcL is developing a training program specifically for its traditional privileged interlocutors, its customers bankers, in particular cash handling cash management staff, cash carriers and law enforcement. Our Central Bank is the youngest but also the smallest in the Eurosystem. It needs partners to reach the entire population and pay particular attention to those who are difficult to approach by the traditional banking world. Ticket information must also reach, for example, the visually impaired, the elderly or the disabled. No exclusion is possible. To reach such groups, in an effective way, we need privileged relays. The BCL's information campaign beats are full. May I recall the inauguration of the Euro-clock here on 4 January. This clock on Boulevard Royal marks the easily followed countdown in Luxembourg. Throughout the year, the Central Bank will continue its communication activities. First of all, it will ensure a presence in the written press, radio and television. It is a pleasure to be able to thank especially our friends in the written press, who have agreed to publish on a weekly basis, Euro-news prepared by our Bank giving general information on banknotes and coins, and their conditions of issue. The Central Bank will be present in shopping centres, it will participate in major fairs in Luxembourg later this year; it is preparing a major event, a "euro showcase" to be held in Luxembourg in July next, as in other European capitals. The campaign is thus designed to gradually expand to culminate in the autumn of 2001, when the safety features will be made public, the first species will be made available to professionals and the public will be aware of the imminence of change. However, the cornerstone of the campaign is the 2002 Partnership Programme, which was inaugurated today. The Partnership does not mean that we are looking to offload our communication tasks onto you: we remain associated for the coming months. We ourselves are fully involved in the Eurosystem campaign and you will benefit from its strengths. We are committed to providing you with all the necessary information material that you are invited to disseminate, subject to possible adaptations that are adequate to the audience you reach. Each partner is allowed to use the new internationally recognised and protected partnership logo at its best convenience, while associating its own logo with it. This logo evokes the theme of bridges, which serves as an emblem of euro banknotes, and which this time also symbolizes the link between the Central Bank and each partner, as well as the link between the partner and the privileged public that is its own. The partner also has exclusive access to the reserved part of the B.C.E.'s special website, dedicated to the campaign. He can download the information material and get the most up-to-date data and information. We need your help and even your imagination. You know better than we do the particular audience that is yours. We are pleased, after the conclusion of our agreements, to prepare together the conditions for the dissemination of information. Each of you is invited to stay in touch with our team, which is grouped into a Taskforce of Central Bank agents specially dedicated to this task; it also includes a Committee ensuring, under the authority of the Directorate, a follow-up of the progress of the campaign. We are confident that you will do everything you can to facilitate the final transition to the euro. Our joint efforts will allow everyone to prepare and familiarize themselves with the new currency. It is on behalf of the Central Bank that I thank you in advance for your activity as a partner. "Let's join forces" is the theme of the campaign, which is now taking off again. Thank you for your attention.
