Title: On the European monetary policy strategy and practice
text: ON THE EUROPEAN MONETARY POLICY STRATEGY AND PRACTICE by Mr. Yves Mersch, Member of the European Central Bank Governing Council Tokyo, 23 October 2001. Seule la parole prononcee fait foi Ladies and Gentlemen, Speaking on strategy reminds me of the following quotation from the "Recorded Sayings" of the Founder of Kencho-Ji Temple in Kamakura, Rankei Doryu: "If you have lost your true self, all phenomena bring you nothing but annoyance. If you discover your essence of mind, you can follow nothing but the true path." Before starting with the main content of my speech, I would like to make some brief remarks concerning the common mistake to compare the US and European area economies with regard to both their cyclical position and their medium-term growth outlook. The euro area economy has been affected by the international economic climate and, in particular, by the sharp slowdown of the US economy. This is a natural effect of the growing interdependence of regional economic areas, brought about by increase in international trade and financial flows. Nonetheless, it would be a mistake to draw excessive parallels between economies, which exhibit non-synchronised economic cycles, different structural characteristics, and hence unequal long-term growth prospects. In fact, many of the macroeconomic and financial disequilibria, which have built up in the US, cannot be found in the euro area. Although investment has remained buoyant in recent years in the Euro area, there is no sign of surplus accumulation in capital stock. Moreover, although the European savings ratio has declined in recent years, it is still appreciably higher than in the US. Lastly, the private sector, with the likely exception of the telecom sector, is in a less vulnerable position, being characterised by lower relative debt and less exposure to fluctuations in financial asset prices. The policy-mix in the United States is the result of a one-to-one relation between one monetary policy and one fiscal policy. The European monetary area displays an asymmetric relation in this respect. The policy mix is composed of a single monetary policy for the twelve participating member states, with fiscal policies remaining to a large extent in the hands of national authorities. Against this background, it should come as no surprise that European monetary policy has been, is and will be different from the monetary policy of the Federal Reserve System. This discrepancy is, I believe, not so much due to differences in the statutory remit of the respective central banks but rather to economic situations departing from different bases and requiring different measures. Having clarified -once more -the differences between the US and the Euro area economies, and hence the appropriate monetary policy, I shall concentrate on the strategy adopted by the Eurosystem in the remainder of my speech, without making too many references to the US. The Eurosystem Monetary Policy Strategy 1. The Need for a Monetary Policy Strategy Quite naturally, monetary policy decision-makers operate in a world of uncertainty. Information or knowledge of economic activity and structures are necessarily imperfect. Complete descriptions of economic activity are only available after a significant time lag. Usually, they become available after the monetary policy decisions have been taken. This simple fact has several implications being of particular importance for the conduct of monetary policy. A large academic literature has also addressed the question of optimal monetary policy in an uncertain environment. Together with the long-standing practical experience of Euro area national central banks, this literature has shaped the design of the Eurosystem monetary policy strategy. It is of fundamental importance to ensure, as far as possible, that monetary policy itself does not become an additional source of uncertainty. Hence the ECB's monetary policy strategy announcement attempts to address the issue of uncertainty in providing a very clear and concise systematic framework for the analysis of information and the taking of policy decisions, without specific policy conclusions being predetermined in a mechanical manner. The design of the Eurosystem monetary policy strategy also recognises that any specific economic framework is incomplete and cannot capture the full complexity of the monetary transmission process in the 12 Euro area economies. This is done in employing different analytical frameworks, commonly referred to as the two-pillar strategy, and in relying on long-standing professional experience, rather than to solely rely on one single monetary or economic indicator. This considerably reduces the risk of making substantial policy errors, disciplines policy choices and keeps decisions consistently anchored to the mandated objectives. ECB's Definition of Price Stability In contrast to the FED's mandate, the Maastricht Treaty establishing the European Union states that "the primary objective of the European System of Central Banks shall be to maintain price stability". The Treaty thus assigns a clear mandate to the newly created central banking system, while leaving open a more precise and operational definition of the price stability objective, as well as the design of the monetary strategy to be adopted in order to fulfil this objective. Making use of its independence to decide how to fulfil the mandate given by the Maastricht Treaty, the Governing Council announced its "stability-oriented monetary policy" in October 1998 and laid out how it intended to interpret and make operational the price-stability mandate. Several elements of that announcement are worth reminding and discussing here. Firstly, the Governing Council stated that the "monetary policy strategy will focus strictly on this objective of price stability". In addition, a quantitative definition of price-stability was announced. "Price stability shall be defined as a year-on-year increase in Harmonised Index of Consumer Price (HICP) for the Euro area of below 2%", with price stability having to be maintained "over the medium term." Hence the existence of short-term price volatility, which cannot be controlled by monetary policy, was explicitly recognised. The announcement contained an explicit and quantitative definition of price stability  which the Fed, among other central banks, lacks. This feature improves accountability and helps to anchor economic agents' expectations. Do We Need a Quantitative Definition? Monetary policy could target a constant price level, a zero inflation rate, an upward drifting price level or a low but nonzero rate of inflation (Fisher, 1996; Goodhart and Vinals, 1994). An advantage of a price level target is that it keeps uncertainty about price levels in the distant future smaller than it would with zero inflation target, which entails a base drift. The main disadvantage is that it puts a greater strain on monetary policy, because variations in the inflation rate are required to reverse the effects of previous shocks on the price level. There are in addition several reasons for aiming for a small positive inflation rate instead of a zero rate: According to Debelle (1997) the true rate of inflation is below the measured rate, which is due to measurement problems, As Akerlof, Dickens and Perry (1996) point out, if nominal wages are rigid downward, then reductions in real wages will involve less employment loss when brought about through inflation. Very low inflation therefore effectively reduces real-wage flexibility and may worsen the allocative efficiency of the labour market, With a zero targeted inflation rate, there is a greater danger of deflation. As pointed out in the literature on financial crises, persistent deflation can create serious problems for the financial system. The lower bound of zero on the nominal interest rate arises because cash carries a zero nominal interest rate, which imposes problems for monetary policy with a zero targeted inflation rate (Summers, 1991). If the expected inflation rate is zero, it is very difficult to engineer a negative short-run real interest rate (which may be needed during recessions). These arguments led the Governing Council of the Eurosystem to conclude that price stability is the best way to insure an endurable growth in the euro area and to adopt a quantified definition of price stability which accepts a rate of inflation of up to 2%. Important to note is also that, in addition to the quantitative specification of the price stability objective, the monetary policy strategy announcement emphasised very clearly from the very beginning that strategy and decisions will aim at stabilising inflation in the Euro area as a whole, irrespective of inflation developments in any of its constituent members. 2. The Eurosystem's Monetary Policy Strategy The Two-Pillar Strategy Let me go back to the "stability-oriented monetary policy strategy". In addition to the quantitative definition of the price stability objective, a clear commitment to the goal variable which I have just discussed, the announcement contained a description of the strategy to be implemented. The monetary policy strategy consists of two key elements, the famous two pillars. To recapitulate briefly, under the first pillar, "money will be assigned a prominent role [a] signalled by the announcement of a quantitative reference value for the growth of a broad monetary aggregate". In addition, and in parallel with that analysis of monetary growth, a major role is assigned to "a broadlybased assessment of the outlook for price developments and the risks to price stability in the Euro area" -the second pillar. We thus recognise different existing models of the structure of the economy and the nature of the monetary transmission mechanism. The first pillar represents a group of models and analytical frameworks which embody a view of price level determination that accords an important role to money. The second pillar encompasses a range of alternative models of the inflation process, predominantly those which emphasise the interplay between supply and demand in the goods and labour markets, as well as information useful for monetary policy stemming from financial variables, such as bond yields, asset prices (including exchange rates), credit developments and balance sheet positions. First Pillar: The prominent role for money reflects the monetary origins of inflation over the medium to longer term. One of the most remarkable empirical regularities in macroeconomics is the ubiquitous long-run relationship between the price level and money stock. A positive and often almost one-to-one relationship between monetary growth and inflation at longer horizons has been illustrated for a wide variety of economies, using a number of different analytical and empirical tools and employing various definitions of money data sets. There is a broad consensus in the literature that any well-specified model of a monetary economy should exhibit this feature. On both empirical and theoretical grounds, the literature provides ample justification for assigning money an important role in monetary policy making. This conclusion is particularly appropriate for the Euro area. In contrast to other countries where monetary developments during recent decades have been rather erratic, in the Euro area the available evidence continues to point towards the existence of a stable relationship between broad monetary aggregates  in particular M3  and price developments in the long term. Moreover, M3 and other monetary and credit aggregates appear to possess good leading indicator properties for future price developments, especially at medium-term horizons. The reference value of M3 growth is presently set at 4 % and will be revisited in December. This value is considered consistent with the long-run economic growth rate in the Eurozone, the inflation objective of below 2% in the medium term and the trend reduction in money velocity. However, deviations of M3 growth from the Eurosystems reference value of 4 % do not mechanically trigger interest rate changes. Rather, such deviations are to be seen as catalyst for further analysis, first searching for the causes of such deviations and thereafter assessing the implications for future price developments and the appropriate monetary policy. Therefore, the reference value for M3 is not an immediate or direct monetary target in itself. The Eurosystem does not attempt to control monetary growth in the short term so as to hit the reference value at a specific horizon. Rather the reference value acts as an analytical and presentational device, which constitutes an important benchmark for assessing risks to price stability in the medium term. The analysis under the first pillar is particularly important in making an evaluation of the magnitude of monetary impulses to the economy and may help in the assessment of possible bubbles in financial markets. Historically, booms and busts in asset markets have been strongly associated with large movements in monetary and credit aggregates in particular, and their implications on the economy may depend on the strength of the balance sheet position of the financial sector. This constitutes a further reason for the Eurosystem strategy to give special consideration to the analysis of monetary and credit aggregates and of financial intermediaries' balance sheets from which these aggregates are derived. Second Pillar: The second pillar of the monetary policy strategy is a broadly-based assessment of the outlook for price developments. Forecasts of crucial economic indicators, including inflation developments, play a significant role in this assessment. While inflation is ultimately a monetary phenomenon, monetary developments may, at least in the short term, not always be the only or even the most useful guide for assessing the economic disturbances threatening price stability. A monetary policy aimed at the maintenance of price stability must therefore rely on the analysis of a broad range of variables. Therefore, in parallel with the analysis of monetary developments, the Eurosystem also evaluates a wide range of other economic and financial indicators in broadly assessing the risks to price stability in the medium term. It is vital that these two pillars are not misinterpreted as targets or any form of monetary rule. On the contrary, the Governing Council has made it clear on numerous occasions that it will take its decisions on the basis of a detailed and comprehensive assessment of a broad range of economic indicators. Isolated developments of individual indicators, such as deviations of monetary growth from the reference value, will not prompt automatic and mechanistic monetary policy responses. The structure of the monetary policy strategy clarifies the much-discussed role of the exchange rate. Along with other indicators, the exchange rate of the Euro is a component of the second pillar. It is not regarded as a target of the Eurosystem's monetary policy, but it is given due consideration in actual monetary policy decisions. Nonetheless, an increasing weight will be attached to the exchange rate whenever its development threatens the medium term internal price stability in the Euro zone. In any other case, monetary policy decisions will be largely unaffected. This is also true of all the other indicators of the second pillar, such as wage developments. Ultimately, the Governing Council has to come to a monetary policy decision on the basis of its collective overall assessment of the economic situation and the risks to price stability. This decision will take into consideration all the available relevant information, and not just the information reflected in forecasts and/or deviations of M3 growth from its reference value. 3. The Monetary Policy Strategy in Practice A Closer Look at the Interest Rate Decisions by the Governing Council The first column in table 1 shows the dates at which the Governing Council decided to change the key policy rate while the second column displays the level of that rate. The third column reports the cumulative change in that interest rate since the onset of EMU. The fourth column shows the annual HICP inflation rate for the Euro area corresponding to the month preceding the decision (and hence, one that is likely to be available at the date of the meeting). The fifth column displays its cumulative change, the sixth column reports the level of M3 and the seventh the cumulative change in M3 growth at the same time. Interest Rate Changes, HIPC Inflation and M3 Growth ECB Interest rate Cumulative Change HICP Cumulative Change M3 Cumulative Change 22 December 98 3.00 0.80 5.70 09 April 99 2.50 -0.50 1.00 0.20 4.90 -0.80 05 November 99 3.00 0.00 1.40 0.60 6.20 0.50 4 February 99 3.25 0.25 1.90 1.10 6.20 0.50 17 March 00 3.50 0.50 2.00 1.20 6.50 0.80 28 April 00 3.75 0.75 2.10 1.30 6.50 0.80 09 June 00 4.25 1.25 1.90 1.10 5.40 -0.30 01 September 00 4.50 1.50 2.40 1.60 5.60 -0.10 06 October 00 4.75 1.75 2.70 1.90 5.30 -0.40 December 00 4.75 1.75 2.60 1.80 4.80 -0.90 11 May 01 4.50 1.50 2.90 2.10 5.30 -0.40 31 August 01 4.25 1.25 2.8 2.00 6.70 1.00 18 September 01 3.75 0.75 2.70 1.90 n.a. 1.00 Until May 2001 all decisions on interest rates, with the exception of the 50 basis point rate cut in April 1999, have taken the form of an increase of 25 or 50 basis points. By the end of EMU's second year, the interest rate has risen by 175 basis points, matching almost exactly the corresponding cumulative change in inflation. Hence the real interest rate was basically unchanged. Despite the negative cumulative change until May 2001, the annual rate of M3 growth continues to be above the fixed reference growth of the ECB. The recent three-month average annual growth rate during the period June-August 2001 increased to 6.4%. The corresponding growth rate during the period May-July 2001 was 5.9%. These developments partly reflect the relatively flat yield curve up to August and the weakness in stock markets, which made the holdings of short-term deposits and marketable instruments included in M3 more attractive. As pointed out previously, the eurosystem's surveys indicate that the data for M3 are distorted upwards by nonresident holdings of market paper and debt securities with a maturity up to two years issued by MFIs. These holdings may have contributed with three-quarters of percentage point to annual M3 growth over recent months. In fact, the subtraction of this amount reduces the excess with regard to the reference value of 4 %. The Governing Council kept interest rates unchanged until the 11 th of May 2001. This can be explained because the deterioration of the price outlook was due to temporary factors, such as the oil price and the exchange rate of the euro against the dollar. In addition, the slowdown in US economy and the subsequent deterioration in the world economic outlook lowered inflationary risks as from the third quarter of 2000, paving the way in October 2000 for a halt in the succession of official interest rates rises. On the basis of the evaluation of inflationary risks in the area and the development of the external environment, the Governing Council has always adopted a prudent stance, gradually modifying his assessment of macroeconomic conditions in the euro area. As a result, the Governing Council set the benchmark interest rate in May 2001 to 4.5%, estimating that the lower economic growth envisaged for the euro area should mitigate inflationary pressures in the medium term followed by a further cut of 25 basis points on August 31 st. On 17 September 2001, the Governing Council took the decision to lower the key interest rates by 50 basis points. This was done in concert with the Federal Reserve System, and a direct response to the increased uncertainty regarding the global economic environment following the terrorist attacks on the US. With the benefit of hindsight, this interest rate decision can be viewed as a "front loading", both in terms of timing and of magnitude, of a reduction which would have occurred under more normal circumstances in subsequent Governing Council meetings. The Governing Council monitors inflation developments in the euro area attentively. While the less expansionary economic climate tends to moderate inflation, risk factors remain. These are associated with uncertainty concerning wage developments as a consequence of price increases of energy and other imported inputs. While these factors could delay the reduction in inflation rates in the near future, the most recent developments allow one to expect further gradual reductions in recorded inflation. I think it has become apparent to you that decisions on the money policy stance do not mechanically follow from deviations of M3 growth from the reference value. More generally, the medium term focus recognises the presence of different transmission channels affecting price developments with long, variable and uncertain lags. Money growth, in particular, is associated with inflation at a medium to long term horizon. In fact, extracting information from monetary developments is not a mechanical process. Over policy-relevant horizons, money and credit may be influenced by many factors, including cyclical shifts in the demand for money and credit and regulation. The same applies in particular for the publication of most economic projections. So, a main task of monetary analysis is to understand and quantify these various possible effects, drawing out the key implications for inflation outlook. In addition, acknowledging that the inflation is the central goal of the Eurosystem, does not imply that its monetary policy should ignore significant output movements. Governing Council Decision on 31 August 2001 With regard to the first pillar, the increase in the growth rate of M3 of 5.9% must be interpreted carefully. In fact, it reflects both the weakness in stock markets and the relatively flat yield curve. In addition, there have been indications that monetary growth figures are distorted upwards by non-Euro area residents' purchases of negotiable paper included in M3. Regarding the second pillar, there are clear signals of lower inflationary pressures coming from the demand side. Recent economic indicators show that the Euro area's real GDP growth in this year will most likely be lower than was expected a few months ago. However, the growth outlook in the Euro area is better than the USA's growth perspective and the present level of the ECB interest rate conforms to its strategy. Finally, I think that financial and economic agents recognise that the monetary policy strategy of the Eurosystem has been implemented with a high degree of flexibility since the beginning of 1999. In the first few months of European Monetary Union, economists worried about threats of deflation and negative real effects following the international financial crisis. Then they worried about the strong US Dollar and the increases in oil prices and the generated inflation risk. Later they were concerned about the slowdown of economic growth in the USA and the much heralded new economy. Did it really exist, one may wonder? They worry about financial difficulties in Turkey and Argentina, as well as a prolonged recession in the USA, following the tragic events of 11 September, which is feared to spread around the globe. All these issues are also taken into consideration when deliberating about the appropriate monetary policy decision in order to achieve price stability in the medium term. 4. Future Challenges for the Eurosystem Despite this success, many challenges for monetary policy and the Eurosystem persist. Among these are: The introduction of notes and coins in January 2002 (to which I very much look forward), The mastering of inflation phenomena and persuasion of other policy making institutions to share the Eurosystem's policy and objectives, particularly in this economic period of stress. While short term deviations from budgetary targets appear acceptable in the present environment, they must not lead to delaying or even endangering the set medium term fixed policy objectives. The future EU enlargement and its implications on ECB future reform. Please allow me to elaborate on this point before closing my speech. Let me emphasise that the Eurosystem's attitude to EU membership of the accession countries is positive. However, it is important to realise that any political entry into the EU & into the EMU are fundamentally distinct. At the moment, accession countries are foremost interested in joining the EU. Once, these countries have joined the EU, there is a very specific procedure for joining EMU. In fact, accession to EU does not guarantee automatic acceptance into the monetary union. After joining the European Union, the newcomers are expected to join the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERMII). This is necessary to start the reporting period clock. The Maastricht treaty specifically requires that compliance with the debt, deficit, interest rates and inflation targets be evaluated over the year before the examination. However, the reporting period is 2 years for the exchange rate criterion (ERM membership without devaluation), so the evaluation can (theoretically) not be passed until a 2year track record exists. After the 2 nd accession anniversary to the EU, the Commission and ECB need about 2 months to receive the final economic data and to write their convergence reports. These reports assess the suitability of all non-EMU Member States for EMU membership based on compliance with the EMU-related acquis and the Maastricht economic convergence criteria. The Maastricht criteria require inflation rates, government deficits and debts, and long-term interest rates to have been low enough and exchange rates to have been stable enough during the reporting period. While there are other criteria, experience shows that if these are met, one can expect that the members will be judged to be fit to enter Eurosystem. The Ecofin Council will then deliberate on the reports for one month, suggesting that the Ecofin vote can come no sooner than 27 months after EU accession. If the answer is "yes" the EMU-members-elect may need some time to adopt the euro. It took the founding members 8 months, while it took Greece 6 months. Hence, voting rights in the Governing Council should come about 6 months after the Ecofin decision. If the rules are followed to the letter, the process should take at least 33 months. This represents enough time to the Governing Council to resolve the problem of necessary reform. This is of course the most rigid and swift entry scenario, which appears to be rather unlikely given the strong need for real convergence to set in. By real convergence we think mostly of convergence terms of GDP per capita and industrial structures, in order to minimise the risks and the effects of asymmetric shocks. Also, it is in the interest of 'in' and 'out' countries to enter EMU only when they are able to sustain the new monetary policy system. Let me explain why the nominal convergence is not sufficient to join the EMU. In the year 2000, the degree of real convergence remained limited, as Euro area growth was nearly as strong as growth in the accession countries. Furthermore, it is unlikely that the medium-term growth differential will be significantly higher than 1% in favour of the accession countries. Together with the huge current GDP per capita differential of about 56% in purchasing power parity terms or about 78% in terms of current exchange rates, it seems that the GDP per capita gap between Euro area countries and accession countries will remain large for the next few years. Therefore, it cannot be emphasised enough that substantial structural reform and prudent macroeconomic policies are crucial to enhance accession countries' growth potential, thereby fostering cohesion within the enlarged EU and hence minimising the risks and effects of asymmetric shocks. 5. Concluding Remarks My speech provided an overview of Eurosystem's monetary policy strategy in theory and practice. I have illustrated the monetary policy framework of EMU and its operation during its first two and a half years, and gave a brief outlook regarding the challenges that lie ahead of us. The Eurosystem has shown the capability to ensure price stability in the medium term, given the means at its disposal. Other instruments affecting price stability lie in the hands of national governments, and hence are outside the control of the Eurosystem. The task for national governments remains to adhere to the stability and growth pact and to continue driving forward the necessary structural reforms. Economic growth and the maintenance of price stability also and especially depend on appropriate wage agreements. I am heartened by developments in this area, which bear testimony to the emergency and consolidation of a stability culture in Europe. These developments are desirable from an economic angle and, given present times, also from a wider political standpoint. Thank you very much for your interest.

Title: The Banque centrale du Luxembourg in the euro area
text: THE BANQUE CENTRALE DU LUXEMBOURG IN THE EURO AREA Speech by Mr Yves Mersch, President of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg on the occasion of the 44th Engineer's Day Luxembourg, 8 February 2003 Only the word spoken is authentic Mr President Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, I would like to thank the organizers for inviting me to this 44th Engineer's Day. It is a pleasure for me to be in front of an assembly representing a profession that has always characterized pragmatism. Since the dawn of time, there have been optimists, those for whom the glass is half full and the pessimists, those for whom the glass is half empty. Then there are the engineers, those for whom the glass is twice too big. This pragmatism is undoubtedly a connivance with the profession of central banker. Science, which you shape, interacts in two ways with the sphere of central banks. First, central banks apply new technologies as part of their core business. Thus, advanced technology contributes to the execution of monetary policy, the flow of money flows, the settlement of securities transactions, the compilation and dissemination of statistics, the printing and circulation of banknotes, and the transfer and processing of information, all against the backdrop of two attributes that are at the heart of central banks' concerns: efficiency and safety. Second, technology influences the social, economic and financial environment. Technology is transforming consumption habits, expanding space and redefining the conditions of action of economic agents, expanding the range of increasingly complex financial instruments. The irrational exuberance of markets, based on the split between the unbounded progress of technology and the rational expectations of the profits generated, has proven to be a destructive phenomenon of this new economy and a challenge to economic and financial regulation. The global village of McLuhan is economic and financial, electronic speed is at the heart of the ongoing changes. As a result, the tasks of central banks, with price stability and financial stability as their main tasks, are becoming more complex while gaining in scope. The subject I have been invited to discuss with you today concerns the role of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg (BCL) within the euro area. Now a member of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB), composed of the national central banks (NCBs) of the 15 Member States of the European Union (EU) and the European Central Bank (ECB), the BCL has a recent existence, dating from 1 June 1998, concomitant with that of the ECB. The BCL is the only central bank whose birth is enshrined in the Treaty. Until then, Luxembourg did not have a central bank, delegating the burdens incumbent on such an institution to the National Bank of Belgium (NBB). As part of the monetary association grafted onto the Belgo-Luxembourg Economic Union (BLEU) concluded between Luxembourg and Belgium in 1921, the BNB had set up a branch in Luxembourg in 1935. The creation of the BCL was not, however, created ex nihilo, replacing the Luxembourg Monetary Institute (IML), as indicated in the Treaty. While the main task of the BCL is to participate in the performance of the tasks of the ESCB with a view to achieving its objectives, it also carries out the tasks entrusted to it by its own organic law or by other laws, regulations or conventions. The BCL is, by this institutional structure, a head of Janus operating both at a supranational level, that of the euro zone, and at a national level. In the first part, I will begin by presenting the fundamental tasks of the Eurosystem, artificial terminology without legal personality but determining the contours of the monetary area within the ESCB, and the role played by the BCL within it. The description of the BCL's participation in the work of the ESCB cannot be exhaustive, as the areas covered, often of a technical nature, are vast. In concrete terms, there are thirteen different committees, all of which ultimately aim to provide the Governing Council with detailed information enabling it to take its decisions under optimal conditions. They cover the following areas: accounting, banking supervision, budgeting, external communication, information systems, internal audit, international relations, legal, market operations, monetary policy, payment and securities settlement systems and statistics. In addition to these committees, there is a set of working groups and cells forming a comitological network of some 90 entities, each of which is participating with a number of 207 staff on 1 January 2003. I shall therefore confine myself to presenting to you the main objective of the Eurosystem, price stability, the definition and execution of monetary policy, its role as a contributor to financial stability and its role in the field of monetary signs. In a second part, I will set out the other tasks carried out by the Bank. The bcl's participation in the performance of the Eurosystem's tasks The Eurosystem, composed of the NCBs of the countries that have adopted the euro and the ECB, has several fundamental tasks: the definition and implementation of monetary policy, the conduct of foreign exchange operations, the holding and management of the official foreign exchange reserves of the Member States, and the promotion of the proper functioning of payment systems. In addition, it contributes to the sound conduct of the policies pursued by the competent authorities with regard to the prudential supervision of credit institutions and the stability of the financial system. It also collects the statistical information necessary for the performance of its tasks and the issue of banknotes in the euro area. In addition, the ECB is consulted on any proposed Community act in the areas within its competence. It shall also be consulted by the national authorities on any draft regulation in the areas within its competence. Finally, the ECB may take the initiative to issue an opinion, both at Community and national level, always under the constraint of its area of competence. Main objective: price stability While the Eurosystem's tasks are manifold, its main objective is unique, namely price stability. However, without prejudice to the main objective, the Eurosystem also supports the general economic policies of the Community, all within an overall framework of an open market economy with free competition and the efficient allocation of resources. Let me first clarify the concept of price stability before explaining how this main objective relates to that of support for general economic policies. Since the main objective of the Eurosystem is price stability, it is first necessary to consider the arguments justifying such an approach: In an environment of price stability, the market allocates resources efficiently. Indeed, price variability complicates the evaluation of prices. This uncertainty accentuates imperfect information and increases the probability of under-optimization in individual agent decisions, i.e. the probability of an inefficient allocation of resources; The Long-term interest rates incorporate an inflation risk premium. If the markets anticipate significant inflation, it is integrated in the form of a premium, leading to an increase in interest rates and consequently an increase in refinancing conditions making investment more expensive. Thus, a credible price stability policy, focused on the medium to long term, allows a concomitant anchoring of expectations, lowering long-term interest rates and thus promoting investment, growth and employment; The Limiting monetary erosion makes it possible to maintain the purchasing power of economic agents, promoting consumption, investment and in turn growth and employment. One of the key elements related to the notion of price stability is credibility. In order to establish its credibility in relation to its main objective, the Governing Council of the ECB, the decision-making body deciding on the stance of the single monetary policy and composed of the six members of the Executive Board of the ECB and the twelve Governors of the euro area NCBs, decided to quantify price stability. As a result, is price stability defined as an annual increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) of less than 2% for the euro area as a whole? Price stability is part of a medium-term perspective. The quantification of the main objective therefore allows economic operators to facilitate their assessment of the Eurosystem's performance in achieving its main objective. The fact that price stability is defined in relation to the euro area as a whole means that the Governing Council does not act on the basis of inflation rates in individual countries. Thus, the medium-term perspective underlines that monetary policy has no control over elements of short-term price volatility, such as the price of oil. It also points out that the impact of a change in the official interest rate on prices is through a transmission mechanism with a time lag of an average of 12 to 18 months. Subsequently, the short-term exceeding of the 2% threshold in no way constitutes a trigger for automatic intervention on the official interest rate determined by the Governing Council. Finally, the term "annual increase" in the definition of price stability symmetrically excludes the acceptance of deflation, characterized by a sustained and significant decrease in prices, a situation just as harmful as Japan is currently experiencing. In December 2002, the HICP grew by 2.3% annually and is expected to fall below the 2% mark in the coming months. While this increase is consistent with the governing council's objective, the current large differential between measured and perceived inflation, i.e. perceived by economic agents, is regrettable. The introduction of the euro cash has undoubtedly contributed to the rise in prices. This effect was estimated for the first half of 2002 at a maximum of 0.2% for the euro area as a whole. For Luxembourg, a study carried out jointly by the BCL and Statec put this cumulative effect between January 2001 and July 2002 at a maximum of 0.74% for the HICP. For the national consumer price index (NCPI), which filters the consumption of non-residents and is used as an indicator underlying the indexation mechanism, the maximum cumulative effect over the same period was estimated at 0.67%. Overall, real price growth in the euro area is out of all proportion to perceived inflation. This distortion is detrimental, biasing both investment decisions and wage negotiations because they are based on misperceptions. Price stability is an essential objective in the missions of any modern central bank, but is not classified in the same way in each central bank. While it is the main objective of the Eurosystem, in the United States for example, it is considered on an equal footing by the Federal Reserve System with the objective of maximum employment and moderate long-term rates. In linking our main objective with support for the Community's general economic policies, it should be stressed that price stability and support for the real economy should not be regarded as exclusive but, on the contrary, conjunctive. Indeed, as I explained earlier, price stability is the best contribution in the medium term to sustainable and job-creating growth. Monetary policy, by smoothing out external shocks, contributes to lower volatility in growth and employment. In order to achieve an objective, two phases are necessary: the implementation of a strategy, based on an adequate institutional framework, and an operational framework that allows its transposition. While the definition and decisions of monetary policy are centralised at the level of the Governing Council, the execution of decisions is decentralised at the level of the NCBs, the latter together forming, on an equal footing, the operational arm of the Eurosystem. The definition of monetary policy In December 1998 the Governing Council adopted a monetary policy strategy based on two pillars. The philosophy behind the strategy adopted is that inflation is a long-term monetary phenomenon, the subject of a broad consensus today. Thus, the first pillar of the strategy gives a predominant role to money, defined by a broad monetary aggregate called M3 consisting of the sum of fiat money, plus the outstanding amounts of certain highly liquid liabilities, in the broad sense of the term, of financial institutions. The reference value for the annual growth of this aggregate is 4 1/2%. This reference value is an indicator for the Governing Council and in no way implies a mechanical action by the Governing Council if the annual growth is above the reference value. In order to be able to take its decisions on the basis of the most comprehensive information possible, the Governing Council shall also rely on the second pillar of the strategy, which consists of the analysis of a wide range of economic and financial indicators that can provide guidance on future price developments. In determining the strategy of monetary policy as well as in making decisions on the official interest rate, the principle of "one man, one vote" is required, even if the Governing Council favours decision-making by consensus. The President of the BCL therefore represents one of eighteen voices in monetary policy decisions. However, I would make it clear that each governor takes part in these decisions, not as a representative of his Bank or his country, but in his personal capacity, with a view to making the best decision for the entire euro area. As already mentioned above, this strategy is part of a medium-term perspective. In addition to the two arguments already stated, in this case the impotence of monetary policy to have a grip on short-term price volatility and the time-shifted impact of monetary policy on prices, a third element should be added: the postulate of the neutrality of money in the long run. Expressed differently, there is no long-term trade-off between inflation and growth. Arbitrage, which exists in the short term, generates more inflation in the long term without additional growth and employment. The latest results from Eurosystem researchers support this thesis. While monetary policy inflections are having a short-term effect on overall output in the euro area, output will eventually return to a level very close to its initial level. In contrast, the impact of monetary policy on prices is more moderate in the short term, but persists over time. Any temptation to use monetary policy for fine-tuning purposes in the short term should therefore be avoided. It is for this reason that monetary policy must be entrusted to an independent central bank, since the political powers, in search of short-term votes in the electoral deadlines, can more easily give in to this temptation. Numerous studies have shown that countries that have delegated their monetary policy to an independent central bank show more moderate price increases over the long term. This independence comes in several forms: personal, institutional, operational and financial. While the first form enshrines the independence of the Governor as a member in his personal capacity of the Governing Council, materialized by the allocation of a fairly long mandate, six years in Luxembourg, the second relates to the governing bodies of an NCB which must neither seek nor accept instructions from institutions or bodies that are third, European or national or national governments. The other two forms must ensure that an NCB can equip itself with sufficient technical and financial resources to be able to fulfil its tasks. While some consider that this independence is anti-democratic in nature, it should be stressed that independence is not free, but counterbalanced by several counterparts. First of all, independence is based on a legal basis, enshrined in the Treaty and relayed in the organic law of the various NCBs. Secondly, the ECB, as a quasi-European institution, is subject to the judicial review provided for in Community law. Finally, independence has an essential counterpart, which is the responsibility, or more precisely the obligation of the ECB to be accountable to its objectives to the general public and the European Parliament. To this notion of accountability, those of transparency and communication are closely linked. Several communication channels are used, among others: press conference after each meeting of the Governing Council that has had a discussion on the official interest rate stance on the agenda, quarterly appearance of the President of the ECB before the European Parliament's Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs, monthly bulletin, annual report, speech. The BCL, mainly through publications and speeches, relays this information at a national level. The execution of monetary policy While the Governing Council sets the monetary policy guidelines on the basis of its two-pillar strategy, they are implemented and transposed by the NCBs in accordance with the principle of decentralisation. Thus, the BCL, as an intermediary between the Eurosystem and Luxembourg financial institutions, carries on average some 10% of all liquidity allocated by the Eurosystem during monetary policy operations. In these terms, the role of the BCL is proportionally more than sixty times greater than its share of capital held in the ECB, i.e. 0.15%. Every monetary policy operation within the Eurosystem is carried by a payment system called TARGET. This system is composed of an interconnection of national real-time gross settlement (RTGS) systems. In 2002, some 250 000 operations on average per day passed through TARGET for an average daily value of some EUR 1 500 billion. The Luxembourg component, set up between 1996 and 1998, is called LIPS-Gross and currently includes 31 direct participants. The BCL is the technical and liquidation agent of this system, which in 2002 ensured the payment of nearly 82,000 domestic transactions and 564,000 cross-border transactions, for a total value of some 7,600 billion euros. The BCL thus ensures both the follow-up of developments in existing systems and the execution of payments. In 2002, the availability rate was 99.92% for the LIPS-Gross component, the second best performance of the Eurosystem after Finland, and 99.77% for TARGET. In addition to the LIPS-Gross system, there is also a mass payment system in Luxembourg carrying transactions of small amounts called LIPS-Net. This tool, which allows the exchange of credit transfers and cheques at national level, recorded a total of 13.7 million transactions in 2002 for a total value of EUR 48.2 billion. Unlike the RTBR system where transactions are liquidated one by one in real time, the LIPS-Net system liquidates multilateral balances five times a day. The liquidation agent is the BCL, the technical agent being CETREL. In financial markets, and here more particularly during monetary policy operations, payment systems are inseparable from clearing and securities settlement systems. The settlement of securities transactions involves two flows: delivery of securities and payment (money flow). While initially, the delivery of securities was done in a physical form, the vast majority is now done in a dematerialized way, in the form of accounting entries. Securities are located with central securities depositories. Any credit transaction made by the Eurosystem to a counterparty must be against collateral in the form of eligible assets. This rule aims to protect the Eurosystem against potential losses and to ensure equality between counterparties. In Luxembourg, Clearstream Banking has become the national depository for the BCL to receive on deposit the securities pledged by commercial banks in order to be able to make their payments via the TARGET network or to receive credit from the BCL, both during monetary policy operations and during intra-day credit operations in payment systems. At 31 December 2002, total guarantees deposited by counterparties amounted to some EUR 87.1 billion. This abundance of guarantees explains the importance of the liquidity channelled through the BCL, making Luxembourg a platform for centralizing the management of banks' liquidity, with excess liquidity compared to local needs being sent abroad. The BCL also plays an essential role in the collection of statistics, which is indispensable in the strategy as well as in the execution of monetary policy. Thus, the BCL compiles the national data of the broad monetary indicator aggregated at the level of the euro area and constituting the analytical basis of the first pillar of the monetary policy strategy. The BCL therefore collects and provides a large number of economic and financial statistics to the Eurosystem, used under the second pillar. In the context of monetary policy, the calculation and monitoring of the minimum reserves to be set up by counterparties with the BCL is essential. Finally, it should be added that in the context of the determination of monetary policy, the analytical aspect is unavoidable. Thus, the BCL makes forecasts of the liquidity needs of Luxembourg counterparties, aggregated data at the level of the euro zone, and participates in the preparation of economic projections published twice a year. These projections are one analytical tool among others in the second pillar of the monetary policy strategy. Financial stability Price stability and financial stability are two inseparable poles, their relationship being symbiotic. Price stability, by anchoring agents' expectations, contributes to financial stability. This relationship is underpinned by the credibility and transparency of monetary policy, which has the effect of helping to reduce market volatility in a less uncertain environment. While the objective of price stability has been fulfilled in the medium term, the initial work on the predictability of monetary policy decisions by the Governing Council is very encouraging. Between the beginning of January 1999 and the beginning of June 2002, the market anticipated by 92% the twelve changes in key rates and by 94% the sixty-six status quo. While these results are similar to those found for the United States, they are all the more encouraging for a recent institution such as the ECB. Conversely, financial instability can undermine price stability by altering the various channels involved in the monetary transmission mechanism. Thus, for example, the bursting of a speculative bubble can contribute to a process of deflation through the deterioration of the wealth effect, a currency crisis can cause a depreciation of the exchange rate and generate imported inflation etc. While central banks' intervention downstream of financial crises is a controversial issue, mainly because of the debate on moral hazard, there is no doubt that their intervention upstream, at the level of prevention, is, unequivocally, crucial. The ESCB's stability tasks are twofold: to contribute to the policies of the competent authorities on the prudential supervision of credit institutions and the stability of the financial system and to promote the smooth functioning of payment systems. In this context, the BANKING Supervisory Committee (SB) of the ESCB plays a key role, bringing together those responsible for micro and macro-prudential supervision. The main task of this committee is to study the monitoring of the banking sector in Europe, which has entered a phase of integration and consolidation. In addition to monitoring and actively participating in European work, the BCL has set up macro-prudential indicators to monitor the overall evolution of the Luxembourg financial system. For six months, from June to December 1998, the BCL incorporated the activity of micro-prudential supervision, i.e. individual financial institutions, the latter having constituted the vast majority of the IML's tasks. It was the laws of 23 December 1998 on the BCL and the supervision of the financial sector that relocated micro-prudential supervision, the dominant mission of the IML, within the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF). In taking this step, the legislator probably did not imagine that Luxembourg would be the only country in the European Union where this separation would lead to a total lack of bilateral coordination between micro-prudential and macro-prudential supervision, the latter corresponding to the supervision of the financial system as a whole and traditionally the responsibility of a central bank. This institutional configuration has created an unpremeditated situation where financial stability no longer assumes the status of a public good, segmentation having taken precedence over coordination, against the current of financial globalization in general and further reducing Luxembourg's low weight on the international scene. Payment systems are the keystone in the irrigation of the economic fabric and financial circuits of an economy. By enabling payments made securely and on time, they contribute to good economic development and contribute to financial stability. Symmetrically, they are a significant source of financial instability. Because of the size of the amounts channelled through them, a default by a counterparty can cause a domino effect qualified as systemic risk. Therefore, the role of securities settlement systems is equally essential in transactions whose counterpart is the unwinding of a securities transaction. In view of the importance of these infrastructures for the financial system, the legislator conferred supervision in principle on the CSSF and by exception on the BCL in February 2001. Within the framework of the payment systems in which it participates, the BCL ensures that the systems comply with the international standards and recommendations in force. At ESCB level, an informal and non-binding agreement was concluded in 2000 between the supervisory authorities of payment systems and the banking supervisory authorities of the European Union. It covers cooperation and exchange of information on prudential arrangements affecting systemic stability and on aspects requiring cooperation between the ESCB and banking supervisors. The issuance and circulation of monetary signs Beyond the functions it performs, means of payment, store of value and unit of account, money is an element of social cement. Sharing the same currency implies a common cultural belonging, a role that the single currency, the euro, assumed on 4 January 1999 in its scriptural form. This role has become all the more tangible since it was put into cash circulation a year ago, a form that implicitly embodies an essential element inherent in money: trust, necessary for the acceptance of a currency. Thus, central banks have a primary function to play in the construction and maintenance of capital confidence linked to a currency: Guarantee a low monetary erosion in order to guarantee the purchasing power of a currency; Guarantee - as an issuer - the quality and incorporation of good security elements in the banknotes in order to to promote their longevity and ensure protection against counterfeiting and; Ensure an adequate supply of the economy in monetary signs. While the first imperative is, as we have seen, the main objective of the Eurosystem, the other two do not remain behind, on the contrary. The security features are the result of sophisticated techniques and make the euro at least as secure a banknote as the safest of the banknotes that have previously circulated in national monetary areas. As a result, the initial feeding of the euro banknotes, commonly known as "cash-changeover", was smooth. In Luxembourg, a survey carried out by the Eurosystem revealed that 90% of respondents felt that they were well or very well informed and prepared for the introduction of the euro. Compared with 31 December 2001, the date of the introduction of the euro cash, the ebb rate in value of Luxembourg franc banknotes was 90% a year later. For coins, the rate was 70.5%. The BCL issues and puts into circulation the euro banknotes, but only puts the coins into circulation, on behalf of and in the name of the State Treasury, the issuance of which is the responsibility of the latter to date. The BCL as an integral part of the Luxembourg institutional landscape As we have seen, the BCL's main mission within the Eurosystem is multifaceted. However, as provided for in its Organic Law, the Bank also carries out national tasks that do not contradict its European mission. Production of statistics As I have already mentioned, the BCL compiles and disseminates statistics within the framework of the Eurosystem's tasks. In addition, it produces statistics on the financial centre, the use of which is essentially confined to a national level. The BCL was therefore instructed by the legislator to set up, together with Statec, Luxembourg's balance of payments. Beyond a simple statistical record of the economic transactions of an economic zone with the rest of the world, the balance of payments is of major interest for economic policy. I would remind you that, before the preparation of a purely Luxembourg balance of payments, an aggregated balance of payments for Belgium and Luxembourg was produced by the Belgian-Luxembourg Exchange Institute (IBLC). Soon, the Bank will set up the necessary reporting structures to establish the financial accounts for which Luxembourg benefits from a derogation until 2005. Financial accounts cover all claims, debts, rights and liabilities in an economy. They make it possible to highlight how the different economic sectors affect their savings and from which sectors they find the necessary resources. The BCL strives to contribute to the transparency and improvement of the quality of statistics in Luxembourg, which are essential for good political and economic governance. Economic analysis The BCL, like any central bank, has a research department. As such, it participates in the national economic debate. Its independence allows it to make analyses without being subjected to political pressure. Studies produced by staff or teams of researchers are the result of research carried out within the framework of the ESCB or targeted in the light of current economic debates in Luxembourg. The recent study paper on the pension system is a perfect illustration of this. In addition to the study books, the BCL publishes its newsletter and its annual report. International cooperation and the provision of services to third parties The BCL also contributes to Luxembourg's representation at international level, like the other European central banks; this multilateral representation has long been the prerogative of the NBB. The BCL's action gives priority to multilateral monetary and financial contact with a Luxembourg presence as well as bilateral contact with the countries or regions of activity of national cooperation. Today, however, the voice of Luxembourg and the financial centre is still excluded from forums open to the central banks of all other European countries. The BCL's involvement covers two areas: technical assistance and the provision of services to central banks outside the ESCB and to international and even supranational institutions. Technical assistance activities can be carried out bilaterally, but also within a multilateral framework at both international (e.g. through the World Bank or the IMF) and national (e.g. Financial Technology Transfer Agency - ATTF). At the national level, the BCL has, for example, become, through its expertise, a regular active player and appreciated in the context of seminars organized by the ATTF. I would also add that the BCL, without wishing to become a training centre, has know-how hitherto unavailable in Luxembourg, which it intends to disseminate to interested targets. In terms of financial services, BCL offers its know-how in the management of reserves, securities and cash for the same categories of institutions. Finally, the BCL also acts as the State's fiscal agent vis-a-vis the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and accounts for all the Assets and Liabilities of the Grand Duchy in relation to the IMF. Cooperation with the actors of the Luxembourg financial centre As an intermediary with the Eurosystem and an institution anchored in the Luxembourg financial landscape, the BCL is keen to closely involve economic actors. In order to establish a dialogue for information and consultation purposes, the BCL has set up various working committees which it organizes in the fields of statistics, market operations, payment systems, monetary signs, legal issues and information technology. As you have seen, despite the desire to limit its scope of action, the tasks incumbent on the Banque centrale du Luxembourg are vast. On the eve of its fifth anniversary, it has managed to ensure its anchoring both within the Eurosystem and in the Luxembourg institutional landscape. However, we remain a young institution that must constantly question itself and strive to communicate with its counterparts, not only professional but also and above all with the general public. We are working on that. Thank you for your attention.
