L'arbitrage, qui existe dans le court terme, engendre dans le long terme plus d'inflation sans croissance et emploi supplmentaires. Les derniers rsultats auxquels ont abouti les chercheurs de l'Eurosystme soutiennent cette thse. Alors que les inflexions de la politique montaire induisent un effet dans le court terme sur la production globale de la zone euro, la production retourne  terme  un niveau trs proche de son niveau initial. En revanche, l'impact de la politique montaire sur les prix est plus modr dans le court terme, mais persiste dans le temps. Toute tentation d'utiliser la politique montaire  des fins de rglage fin dans le court terme doit donc tre vite. C'est pour cette raison que la politique montaire doit tre confie  une banque centrale indpendante, les pouvoirs politiques, en qute de suffrages dans le court terme aux chances lectorales, pouvant plus facilement cder  cette tentation. Maintes tudes ont dmontr que les pays ayant dlgu leur politique montaire  une banque centrale indpendante affichent des progressions de prix plus modres sur le long terme. Cette indpendance se dcline sous plusieurs formes : personnelle, institutionnelle, oprationnelle et financire. Tandis que la premire forme consacre l'indpendance du gouverneur en tant que membre en sa capacit personnelle du Conseil des gouverneurs, matrialise par l'attribution d'un mandat assez long, six annes au Luxembourg, la seconde a trait aux organes dirigeants d'une BCN qui ne doivent ni solliciter, ni accepter des instructions d'institutions ou d'organes tiers, europens ou nationaux ou de gouvernements nationaux. Les deux autres formes doivent garantir  une BCN de pouvoir se doter des moyens techniques et financiers suffisants afin de pouvoir rpondre aux missions qui lui incombent. Alors que d'aucuns considrent que cette indpendance revt une nature anti-dmocratique, il convient de souligner que l'indpendance n'est pas gratuite, mais contre-balance par plusieurs contreparties. Tout d'abord, l'indpendance repose sur une base lgale, inscrite dans le Trait et relaye dans la loi organique des diffrentes BCN. Ensuite, la BCE en tant que quasi-institution europenne est soumise au contrle juridictionnel prvu dans le droit communautaire. Finalement, l'indpendance a une contrepartie essentielle qui est la responsabilit, ou plus exactement l'obligation de la BCE de rendre compte par rapport  ses objectifs envers le grand public et le Parlement europen. A cette notion de rendre compte, celles de transparence et de communication sont troitement lies. Plusieurs canaux de communication sont utiliss, entre autres : confrence de presse aprs chaque runion du Conseil des gouverneurs ayant eu  l'ordre du jour une discussion sur l'orientation du taux d'intrt officiel, apparition trimestrielle du Prsident de la BCE devant la commission conomique et montaire du Parlement europen, bulletin mensuel, rapport annuel, discours. La BCL, par le biais essentiellement de publications et de discours, relaie cette information  un niveau national. L'excution de la politique montaire Alors que le Conseil des gouverneurs fixe, sur base de sa stratgie des deux piliers, les orientations de politique montaire, ces dernires sont excutes, transposes par les BCN, conformment au principe de dcentralisation. Ainsi, la BCL, en tant qu'intermdiaire entre l'Eurosystme et les institutions financires luxembourgeoises, vhicule en moyenne quelque 10% de l'ensemble des liquidits attribues par l'Eurosystme lors des oprations de politique montaire. En ces termes, le rle de la BCL est proportionnellement plus de soixante fois plus important que sa part de capital dtenue dans la BCE, soit 0,15%. Chaque opration de politique montaire au sein de l'Eurosystme est vhicule par un systme de paiement appel TARGET. Ce systme est compos d'une interconnexion de systmes nationaux de rglement brut en temps rel (RBTR). En 2002, quelque 250.000 oprations en moyenne journalire ont transit par TARGET pour une valeur moyenne journalire de quelque EUR 1.500 milliards. La composante luxembourgeoise, mise en place entre 1996 et 1998, s'appelle LIPS-Gross et comprend  ce jour 31 participants directs. La BCL est l'agent technique et de liquidation de ce systme qui au cours de l'anne 2002 a assur le paiement de prs de 82.000 oprations domestiques et 564.000 oprations transfrontires, pour une valeur totale de quelque 7.600 milliards d'euros. La BCL assure ainsi aussi bien le suivi des dveloppements apports aux systmes existants que l'excution des paiements. En 2002, le taux de disponibilit tait de 99,92% pour la composante LIPS-Gross, deuxime meilleure performance de l'Eurosystme aprs la Finlande, et de 99,77% pour TARGET. Outre le systme LIPS-Gross, il existe galement au Luxembourg un systme de paiements de masse vhiculant des oprations de petits montants appel LIPS-Net. Cet outil, qui permet l'change de virements et de chques au niveau national, a enregistr un total de 13,7 millions d'oprations en 2002 pour une valeur totale de EUR 48,2 milliards. Contrairement au systme RTBR o les oprations sont liquides une par une en temps rel, le systme LIPS-Net liquide des soldes multilatraux cinq fois par jour. L'agent de liquidation est la BCL, l'agent technique tant CETREL. Sur les marchs financiers, et ici plus particulirement lors des oprations de politique montaire, les systmes de paiement sont indissociables des systmes de compensation et de rglement-titres. Le rglement des oprations sur titres implique deux flux : livraison de titres et paiement (flux montaire).Alors qu'initialement, la livraison de titres se faisait sous une forme physique, la grande majorit se fait aujourd'hui de manire dmatrialise, sous formes d'critures comptables. Les titres sont localiss auprs de dpositaires centraux de titres. Toute opration de crdit faite par l'Eurosystme  une contrepartie doit se faire contre une garantie sous forme d'actifs ligibles. Cette rgle vise  protger l'Eurosystme contre des pertes potentielles et  assurer l'galit entre les contreparties. Au Luxembourg, Clearstream Banking est devenu le dpositaire national pour la BCL pour recevoir en dpt les titres gags par les banques commerciales afin de pouvoir effectuer leurs paiements via le rseau TARGET ou pour recevoir du crdit de la BCL, aussi bien lors des oprations de politique montaire que lors des oprations de crdit intra-journalier dans les systmes de paiement. Au 31 dcembre 2002, le total de garanties dposes par les contreparties s'levait  quelque EUR 87,1 milliards. Cette abondance de garanties explique l'importance des liquidits achemines par le biais de la BCL, faisant du Luxembourg une plate-forme de centralisation de la gestion des liquidits des banques, le surplus de liquidits par rapport aux besoins locaux tant envoy  l'tranger. La BCL exerce galement une fonction essentielle dans le cadre de la collecte de statistiques, indispensable dans la stratgie ainsi que dans l'excution de la politique montaire. Ainsi, la BCL compile les donnes nationales de l'indicateur montaire large agrges au niveau de la zone euro et constituant la base analytique du premier pilier de la stratgie de politique montaire. Aussi, la BCL collecte et fournit-elle un grand nombre de statistiques conomiques et financires  l'Eurosystme, utilises dans le cadre du deuxime pilier. Dans le cadre de la politique montaire, le calcul ainsi que le suivi des rserves obligatoires  constituer par les contreparties auprs de la BCL est primordial. Finalement, il convient d'ajouter que dans le cadre de la dtermination de la politique montaire, l'aspect analytique est incontournable. Ainsi, la BCL effectue des prvisions de besoin de liquidits des contreparties luxembourgeoises, donnes agrges au niveau de la zone euro, et participe  l'laboration des projections conomiques publies deux fois par an. Ces projections constituent un instrument d'analyse parmi d'autres dans le deuxime pilier de la stratgie de politique montaire. La stabilit financire La stabilit des prix et la stabilit financire sont deux ples indissociables, leur relation tant symbiotique. La stabilit des prix, en ancrant les anticipations des agents, contribue  la stabilit financire. A cette relation s'adossent la crdibilit et la transparence de la politique montaire mene, ayant pour consquence de concourir  la rduction de la volatilit des marchs dans un environnement moins incertain. Alors que l'objectif de la stabilit des prix a t rempli  moyen terme, les premiers travaux sur la prvisibilit des dcisions de politique montaire par le Conseil des gouverneurs sont trs encourageants. Entre dbut janvier 1999 et dbut juin 2002, le march a anticip  concurrence de 92% les douze modifications de taux directeurs et  concurrence de 94% les soixante-six statu quo. Alors que ces rsultats sont similaires  ceux trouvs pour les Etats-Unis, ils sont d'autant plus encourageants pour une institution rcente telle que la BCE. A l'inverse, l'instabilit financire peut compromettre la stabilit des prix en altrant les diffrents canaux enoeoeuvre lors du mcanisme de transmission montaire. Ainsi, par exemple, l'clatement d'une bulle spculative peut-elle contribuer  un processus de dflation par le biais de la dtrioration de l'effet de richesse, une crise de change peut-elle engendrer une dprciation du taux de change et gnrer une inflation importe etc. Alors que l'intervention des banques centrales en aval des crises financires est un sujet  controverse, essentiellement en raison du dbat sur l'ala moral, il est indubitable que leur intervention en amont, au niveau de la prvention est, sans quivoque, cruciale. La mission attribue au SEBC en matire de stabilit est double : contribuer aux politiques menes par les instances comptentes en matire de supervision prudentielle des tablissements de crdit et de stabilit du systme financier et promouvoir le fonctionnement sans heurts des systmes de paiement. Dans ce cadre, le Comit de surveillance bancaire (CSB) du SEBC joue un rle essentiel, rassemblant les responsables de la surveillance micro et macro-prudentielle. Ce comit a pour mission principale d'tudier le suivi du secteur bancaire en Europe, entr dans une phase d'intgration et de consolidation. Outre le suivi des, et la participation active aux travaux europens, la BCL a mis en place des indicateurs macro-prudentiels ayant pour objet de suivre l'volution globale du systme financier luxembourgeois. Durant six mois, de juin  dcembre 1998, la BCL a incorpor l'activit de surveillance micro-prudentielle, c'est-dire des institutions financires individuelles, cette dernire ayant constitu la grande majorit des missions de l'IML. Ce sont les lois du 23 dcembre 1998 portant sur la BCL et la surveillance du secteur financier qui ont dlocalis la surveillance micro-prudentielle, mission dominante de l'IML, au sein de la Commission de surveillance du secteur financier (CSSF). En franchissant ce pas, le lgislateur n'imaginait-il sans doute pas que le Luxembourg serait le seul pays de l'Union europenne o cette sparation engendrerait une absence totale de coordination bilatrale entre la supervision micro-prudentielle et macro-prudentielle, cette dernire correspondant  la surveillance du systme financier dans son ensemble et incombant traditionnellement  une banque centrale. Cette configuration institutionnelle a engendr une situation, non prmdite, o la stabilit financire ne revt plus le statut de bien public, la segmentation ayant pris le dessus sur la coordination,  contre-courant du processus de globalisation financire en gnral et diminuant encore le faible poids du Luxembourg sur la scne internationale. Les systmes de paiement constituent la cl de vote dans l'irrigation du tissu conomique et des circuits financiers d'une conomie.En permettant des paiements effectus de manire sre et dans les dlais requis, ils contribuent au bon dveloppement conomique et contribuent  la stabilit financire. Symtriquement, ils constituent une source importante d'instabilit financire. De par l'importance des montants achemins par leur biais, un manquement d'une contrepartie peut provoquer un effet domino qualifi de risque systmique. Aussi, le rle des systmes de rglement des oprations sur titres est-il tout aussi essentiel lors d'oprations ayant pour contrepartie le dbouclage d'une opration sur titres financiers. Au vu del'importance de ces infrastructures pour le systme financier, le lgislateur en a confr la surveillance de principe  la CSSF et par exception  la BCL en fvrier 2001. Dans le cadre des systmes de paiement auxquels elle participe, la BCL veille  la conformit des systmes aux normes et recommandations internationales en vigueur. Au niveau du SEBC, un accord informel et non contraignant a t conclu en 2000 entre les autorits de surveillance des systmes de paiement et les autorits de contrle bancaire de l'Union europenne. Il porte sur la coopration et l'change d'information ayant trait aux dispositifs prudentiels ayant une incidence sur la stabilit systmique et sur les aspects ncessitant une coopration entre le SEBC et les autorits de contrle bancaire. L'mission et la mise en circulation de signes montaires Au-del des fonctions qu'elle assure, moyen de paiement, rserve de valeur et unit de compte, la monnaie est un lment du ciment social. Partager une mme monnaie induit une appartenance culturelle commune, rle que la monnaie unique, l'euro, a endoss ds le 4 janvier 1999 sous sa forme scripturale. Ce rle est devenu d'autant plus tangible depuis sa mise en circulation fiduciaire il y a un an, forme qui incarne implicitement un lment essentiel inhrent  la monnaie : la confiance, ncessaire  l'acceptation d'une monnaie. Ainsi, les banques centrales ont une fonction primordiale  jouer dans la construction et la conservation du capital confiance lie  une monnaie : Garantir une rosion montaire faible afin de garantir le pouvoir d'achat d'une monnaie ; Garantir -en tant qu'metteur -la qualit et l'incorporation de bons lments de scurit dans les billets afin de favoriser leur longvit et d'assurer la protection contre la contrefaon et ; Assurer une alimentation adquate de l'conomie en signes montaires. Tandis que le premier impratif constitue, nous l'avons vu, l'objectif principal de l'Eurosystme, les deux autres n'en demeurent pas en retrait, au contraire. Les signes de scurit sont le fruit de techniques sophistiques et font de l'euro un billet au moins aussi sr que le plus sr des billets ayant circul prcdemment dans les espaces montaires nationaux. Aussi, l'alimentation initiale des billets en euros, appele communment  cash-changeover , s'est-elle faite sans heurts. Au Luxembourg, un sondage, effectu par l'Eurosystme, a rvl que 90% des sonds se sont estims bien, voire trs bien, informs et prpars  l'introduction de l'euro. Par rapport 31 dcembre 2001, date de l'introduction de l'euro fiduciaire, le taux de reflux en valeur des billets en francs luxembourgeois tait de 90% un an plus tard. Pour les pices, le taux tait de 70,5%. La BCL met et met en circulation les billets en euros, mais ne fait que mettre en circulation les pices, pour le compte et au nom du Trsor de l'Etat, dont l'mission incombe  ce dernier  ce jour. La BCL en tant que partie intgrante du paysage institutionnel luxembourgeois La mission principale de la BCL au sein de l'Eurosystme comporte, nous l'avons vu, de multiples facettes. Toutefois, comme prvu dans sa loi organique, la Banque accomplit galement des missions nationales n'tant pas en contradiction avec sa mission europenne. La production de statistiques Comme je l'ai dj voqu, la BCL compile et diffuse des statistiques dans le cadre des missions de l'Eurosystme. En sus, elle produit des statistiques sur la place financire dont l'utilisation est essentiellement cantonne  un niveau national. Aussi, la BCL a-t-elle t charge par le lgislateur de mettre en place, ensembleavec le Statec, la balance des paiements du Luxembourg. Au-del d'un simple relev statistique des transactions conomiques d'une zone conomique avec le reste du monde, la balance des paiements prsente un intrt majeur pour la politique conomique. Je rappelle qu'avant l'laboration d'une balance de paiement purement luxembourgeoise, une balance de paiement agrge de la Belgique et du Luxembourg tait produite par l'Institut belgo-luxembourgeois de change (IBLC). Bientt, la Banque mettra en place les structures de reporting ncessaires afin d'tablir les comptes financiers pour lesquels le Luxembourg bnficie d'une drogation jusqu'en 2005. Les comptes financiers couvrent l'ensemble des crances, des dettes, des droits et des engagements dans une conomie. Ils permettent de mettre en vidence la faon dont les diffrents secteurs conomiques affectent leur pargne et auprs de quels secteurs ils trouvent les ressources ncessaires. La BCL s'applique  contribuer  la transparence et  l'amlioration de la qualit des statistiques au Luxembourg, indispensables  une bonne gouvernance politico-conomique. L'analyse conomique La BCL, comme toute banque centrale, dispose d'un dpartement de recherche. A ce titre, elle participe au dbat conomique national. Son indpendance lui permet de faire des analyses sans subir de pression politique. Les tudes produites par des agents ou des quipes de chercheurs sont le fruit de recherches effectues dans le cadre du SEBC ou cibles en fonction des dbats conomiques d'actualit au Luxembourg. Le rcent cahier d'tudes sur le systme des pensions en est une parfaite illustration. Outre les cahiers d'tudes, la BCL publie son bulletin ainsi que son rapport annuel. La coopration internationale et l'offre de services  des tiers La BCL contribue galement  la reprsentation du Luxembourg au niveau international  l'instar des autres banques centrales europennes ; cette reprsentation multilatrale a longtemps t l'apanage de la BNB. L'action de la BCL donne la priorit au contact multilatral montaire et financier avec une prsence luxembourgeoise ainsi qu'au contact bilatral avec les pays ou rgions d'activit de la coopration nationale. Aujourd'hui, la voix du Luxembourg et de la place financire est toutefois encore exclue d'enceintes ouvertes aux banques centrales de tous les autres pays europens. L'implication de la BCL porte sur deux domaines : assistance technique et offre de services  des banques centrales ne faisant pas partie du SEBC ainsi qu' des institutions internationales, voire supranationales. Les activits s'inscrivant dans le cadre de l'assistance technique peuvent se faire de manire bilatrale, mais galement s'insrer dans un cadre multilatral aussi bien au niveau international (p.ex. par le biais de la Banque mondiale ou du FMI) que national (p.ex. Agence de transfert de technologie financire -ATTF). Au niveau national, la BCL est,  titre d'exemple, devenue de par son expertise un acteur actif rgulier et apprci dans le cadre des sminaires organiss par l'ATTF. J'ajouterai galement que la BCL, sans vouloir devenir un centre de formation, dispose d'un savoir-faire jusque l non-disponible au Luxembourg, qu'elle entend diffuser aux cibles intresses. En termes de services financiers, la BCL offre pour les mmes catgories d'institutions son savoir-faire en matire de gestion de rserves, de titres et de cash. Enfin, la BCL agit galement comme agent fiscal de l'Etat  l'gard du Fonds montaire international (FMI) et comptabilise tous les avoirs et engagements du Grand-Duch en relation avec le FMI. La coopration avec les acteurs de la place financire de Luxembourg En tant qu'intermdiaire avec l'Eurosystme et institution ancre dans le paysage financier luxembourgeois, la BCL tient  impliquer troitement les acteurs conomiques. Afin d'instaurer un dialogue  des fins d'information et de consultation, la BCL a mis en place divers comits de travail dont elle assure l'organisation dans les domaines des statistiques, des oprations de march, des systmes de paiement, des signes montaires, des questions juridiques ou encore de l'informatique. Comme vous avez pu le constater, malgr la volont de limiter son rayon d'action, les missions incombant  la Banque centrale du Luxembourg sont vastes. A l'aube de son cinquime anniversaire, elle est parvenue  assurer son ancrage aussi bien au sein de l'Eurosystme que dans le paysage institutionnel luxembourgeois. Cependant, nous demeurons une institution jeune qui se doit de se remettre en question de manire permanente et de s'efforcer  communiquer avec ses contreparties, non seulement professionnelles mais aussi et surtout avec le grand public. Nous nous attelons  cette tche. Je vous remercie pour votre attention.

Title: The Banque centrale du Luxembourg in the polls
text: THE BANQUE CENTRALE DU LUXEMBOURG IN THE POLLS Speech by Mr Yves Mersch, President of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg, Executive Club, Hotel Le Royal Luxembourg, 11 February 2003 Only the word spoken is authentic Royal Highness, Excellencies Ladies and gentlemen Introduction: an unusual topic for a central bank The theme of my speech tonight may seem unusual to you. Indeed, why does a public institution like the Central Bank commission surveys? Our young Bank is already well known and respected in the scope in which it operates. It holds its rank among the other national central banks. The actors of the financial center recognize its professionalism. And the public is a priori rarely directly concerned by the Bank's day-to-day activities. I will therefore present to you the reasons that lead us to take an interest in the public at large. The results, as you will see, are currently not up to our ambitions, neither for the Banque centrale du Luxembourg nor for the Eurosystem. I will give you our analysis of the situation, as well as the measures we plan to take. Finally, I will take advantage of the opportunity offered to me to comment on the latest update of Luxembourg's stability and growth programme. The need for surveys for the BCL But let's start with the reasons that push the Central Bank to be interested in its notoriety in general and in the understanding of its missions in particular. There are three main ones. First, as with any modern business, whether private or public, communication is an essential dimension for a central bank. Second, monetary policy is a part of the government's detached economic policy. It must be conducted with a long-term perspective. This justifies its conduct by an independent central bank. But this independence obviously has a counterpart. The BCL is accountable to the general public, that is, to Parliament, the financial markets and the general public. Thirdly, communication is particularly important in the Eurosystem's decentralised scheme. As Belgium did at the time of the Belgian-Luxembourg Economic Union - when the Governor regularly came to Luxembourg to tell us: "Come on! Let me tell you! "-the national central banks must make the link between the monetary policy decisions taken in Frankfurt and the citizens. Generally speaking, it's about making sure the public understands our missions and objectives. Does he agree with the monetary policy conducted in Europe? In addition, it enhances the effectiveness of monetary policies. Citizens of the Grand Duchy and the Eurosystem in general At the European level, the ECB regularly commissions surveys. Thus, a survey was carried out (by INRA) in September and October 2002 on a sample of 1000 people in Luxembourg (and the same in the other countries of the euro zone). At European level, the main finding is that the general public does not feel well informed about the Eurosystem. This perception has even deteriorated since 2000, and this also in Luxembourg. An illustration of this is given by the following result. To the question "for each of the following institutions, can you tell me if one of its main responsibilities is to maintain price stability?", the respondents answer largely in the affirmative: The ECB (80%) and the BCL (74%). However, more than two-thirds respond the same: The government, the European Council of Finance Ministers or the European Commission. It would seem that there is still a slight confusion in people's minds about the respective powers of the governments and the ECB, (the BCL respectively). This result is confirmed when we see that 62% of Luxembourg respondents believe that the ECB takes its instructions from the Commission or national governments. In the Grand Duchy, 57% of respondents believe they are poorly informed about the ECB. The ECB's objectives are not clearly understood. Admittedly, more than two-thirds think that price stability is one of them, but also: 72% believe that exchange rate management is one of them, while this task is shared with the Council and cannot be carried out at the expense of price stability; 66% believe that the creation of high economic growth is one of them, while growth is only an indirect objective (Article 105 of the Treaty); 55% think that the loan of money to the state is one of them. In view of these relatively disappointing results, a major question arises: Would the Eurosystem's communication be inadequate in terms of content (are we dealing with the right subjects?), language (is it understandable or too technocratic?) and communication vectors used. The ESCB's reaction was not long in coming. It is currently working on the unification and standardisation of the Image of the Eurosystem in all euro area countries. This policy aims to increase the visibility of the Eurosystem and the readability of its message, while respecting the specific identity of the national central banks. Luxembourg citizens and the BCL But back to Luxembourg. Parliament, representing the people (and therefore the public), has so far paid little attention to the monetary question. The Central Bank has therefore conducted surveys to determine the public's perception of its action. Of course, polls do not replace elections and therefore cannot validate or reject the decisions taken by the Central Bank. With this in mind, I would like to reiterate that the term of governor of the central bank has been limited in time. But polls allow us to situate ourselves within our country and not to ignore public opinion. It is clear that we are less well known to the general public. The BCL obviously has a less solid historical foothold than the Sveriges Riksbank (1656) or the Bank of France (1800), but some national central banks have been able to compensate for a shorter "historical", such as the Bundesbank (1957). The BCL suffers from a lack of notoriety. In January 2002, 48% of respondents were not aware of the BCL. This score rose to 74% in January 2003. By analyzing this last result by socio-professional category we realize that the "best" informed are people who have studied higher than Bac 3 (49% know the BCL) or are in the upper income bracket (37% know us). These better-than-average results were expected, but our notoriety remains very low in absolute terms. Note that there is no gender disparity. As far as age groups are concerned, the Central Bank is virtually unknown among 15-24 year olds. However, there is a positive point: among the 26% of respondents who know the BCL, 80% have a good or even very good opinion of the BCL. So the quality image is there. It remains to be made known. This development is astonishing considering the Intensive Campaign by the Central Bank for the introduction of the euro. This campaign was a real success, because according to a survey by the European Commission in November 2002, more than 90% of Luxembourg citizens say they have been well or even very well (more than 40%!) informed about the euro. The fact that the BCL focused its communication on the euro, and not on its own identity, certainly explains much of these results. Moreover, these negative figures are difficult to explain: are they due, for example, (1) to the sampling method or (2) to confusion with Banque de Luxembourg or Banque Continentale de Luxembourg or, as mentioned for the Eurosystem, (3) to inadequate communication on the part of the BCL? (1) It is too early (barely 1 year of use) to evaluate, in collaboration with our partner, the effectiveness and relevance of the survey method. Changing the questions or sample may improve the absolute values, but not the negative evolution. On the one hand, extending the series will allow us to refine the analysis of the current results. On the other hand, the BCL has begun a reflection to carry out an analytical survey on a smaller sample of the population. This survey, by complementing the existing barometers, will allow the BCL to more accurately assess the reasons for its low awareness. (2) The confusion of bank names most certainly exists and will also be evaluated by this survey. (3) As for the BCL's communication, at present, it consists of: Press releases and press conferences, generally well reported in the national press; Television and radio interviews: 55 in total for 2002; Paper publications (annual reports, newsletters and study books). These publications are mainly intended for an audience of financiers and economists in the financial centre, but are occasionally of interest to the general public (e.g. study paper n6 on pensions); and A website, which was visited by more than 100,000 contacts in 2002. These visitors were mainly looking for statistics or information about the euro or numismatic products. The actual impact of these vectors is difficult to determine. The recent controversy between the Regie Saint-Paul and RTL concerning the various studies that analyze the communication market is eloquent. This controversy has highlighted the need to set up a multi-media study in Luxembourg capable of providing quantified, correct and reliable information concerning the penetration of each media. Knowing who our target is indeed one thing. Knowing by which communication vector this target can be reached is another. However, the Luxembourg public is asking for more information. Half of the respondents who know the BCL (for the record 26%) say they are not very informed about its own activities. 78% said they would like to receive more information about this. 15-24 year olds responded favourably to 96%! People with low incomes, and therefore often those with the least education, are 100% interested. This request is apparently not satisfied by the existing communication, it is a question of finding other ways to convey our identity such as: adapt the pedagogy used for the introduction of the euro to institutional communication. The interactivity of the euro campaign has shown its effectiveness. The technical accuracy of the financial statements failed; prefer, initially, efficiency to completeness in order to fill the lack of notoriety. This amounts to choosing a main campaign theme (naturally price stability), while agreeing to deal with others later (e.g. payment systems), once awareness has improved. The difficulty then lies in the choice of a balance between: one widely popularized communication (adapting to the lowest common denominator), which would make it possible to reach the greatest number; and the safeguarding an image of excellence and professionalism of the institution. I thus initiated a reflection on the development of a communication strategy with the general public. Already, a brochure presenting the Central Bank will be published later this year. Training is an area that we also study very carefully. We have already given a lecture to economics professors across the country. They offered to contribute to the preparation of new manuals. The development of a number of courses - open to other audiences on an expensive or reciprocal basis - is also progressing, even if the Central Bank is not intended to become a training centre. We also want, like other national central banks, to invest in schools and high schools in the medium term. Such a very proactive action plan would complement the BCL's "traditional" communication strategy as I have just described it. As you can see, surveys are an essential tool for the design of our future communication strategy. Luxembourg citizens are still unaccustomed to the value of monetary stability. Our duty is to make them aware of this subject. Perhaps wage indexation makes them feel immune to inflation. It is here that I wish to go beyond the initial scope of my speech to address the Government's latest economic forecasts. Luxembourg's stability and growth programme. First of all, I would like to point out that on 27 November the European Commission adopted a Communication on strengthening the coordination of budgetary policies. The Economic and Financial Committee welcomed this document. It lays down certain principles aimed at making the application of the Stability and Growth Pact more effective - without changing it. I would also like to point out in this connection that the ECB believes that the Pact is in the interests of the Member States and that it contributes to price stability. In particular, the Commission proposes to give more importance to deficit targets that take into account business cycles. It also proposes to pay more attention to the long-term sustainability of public finances. It is in the light of these proposals that I would like to share some thoughts on the stability and growth programme that the Luxembourg Government tabled in January. This fourth programme is based on forecasts made by STATEC. The latter has developed a pessimistic scenario, an optimistic scenario and a median scenario. In view of the current uncertainty, particularly in the financial sector, the Government has based its programme on the pessimistic scenario. As a result, the GDP growth adopted by the Government reflects a concern for realism in the choice of macroeconomic assumptions. For 2002, the total government balance would be slightly in deficit. This development is mainly attributable to a deterioration in the balance of the central government, which is expected to fall from 2.6% in 2001 to -2.2% in 2002. This inflection of nearly 5 points of GDP is due in particular to the deterioration of the economic situation, which would have caused 270 million euros in tax losses and the tax reform of December 2001. The balance of local authorities would also deteriorate by 0.8% and become negative. This decline is the largest observed during the period 1990-2002. The social security balance would also develop unfavourably, with the surplus rising from 3.1% of GDP in 2001 to 2.2% in 2002. This deterioration is only partly due to the evolution of the economic situation. Indeed, most social security revenue depends on the wage bill and not directly on the economic situation. However, the wage bill increased significantly in 2002. The deterioration of the balance is therefore rather explained by various discretionary measures granted by the State. The transposition of the Rentendesch decisions has thus largely contributed to this deterioration. General government expenditure as a whole, which includes the central government, social security and municipalities, is estimated to have increased in 2002. They would have increased from EUR 9 200 million in 2001 to more than EUR 10 200 million in 2002. This 11% increase would thus have clearly exceeded nominal GDP growth, which is expected to be limited to 1.4% in 2002 according to the authors of the programme. For the years 2003 to 2005 and in the light of the latest BCL projections, the stability programme is at first sight realistic. On the one hand, revenue forecasts are based on conservative macroeconomic assumptions. On the other hand, the authorities acknowledge that Luxembourg's general government will run a deficit from 2002 to 2005, despite social security surpluses. However, a closer look highlights some inaccuracies. Let me highlight those that I believe are the main sources of uncertainty. Firstly, the programme foresees a significant improvement in the social security balance during the period under review. The surplus would rise from 2.2% of GDP in 2002 to 2.9% in 2005. This development is not really in line with the BCL's projections, which are based in particular on a pension model. According to these projections, the social security surplus is expected to be less than 2% of GDP in both 2004 and 2005, due in particular to the low employment growth in 2003 and 2004. In this context, the amount of social contributions received by the general pension scheme is estimated to increase by only about 4% in 2003 and 5% in 2004, compared with an average of 8% from 1990 to 2001. Although important in absolute terms, the pension scheme's income from wealth is also offset by a low average rate of return. The compensation reserve, which reached some 22% of GDP at the end of 2001, is mainly composed of investments less than a year old, whose return is necessarily poor. My second comment concerns the evolution of general government expenditure. As postulated in the programme, it seems difficult to implement in the absence of structural reforms. After a sharp increase in 2002, the expenditure-to-GDP ratio would remain close to 47% in 2003 and 2004, after which it would decline to 45.6% of GDP in 2005. Thus, a very significant deceleration in expenditure growth is expected to occur to ensure compliance with the expenditure targets of the stability programme. While expenditure increased on average by almost 8% over the period 1991-2001 and by 11% in 2002, it is estimated to increase by only 3.9% in 2003, 3.3% in 2004 and 2.7% in 2005 in nominal terms. Such a control of expenditure would be entirely appropriate in view, in particular, of the sharp increase observed in the recent past. However, I doubt that it can be implemented due, in particular, to the following factors: 1. Public investment is expected to grow steadily. Thus, they are expected to increase by 31.1% in 2003 according to the authors of the stability programme. 2. Under the latest collective agreement, state employees will benefit from a further increase in their salaries, at a rate of 1.6% in January 2004, following the 1.6% increase granted in January this year. 3. With the same policy, pension expenditure, which accounts for about one fifth of total general government expenditure, is projected by the BCL by 8.4% in 2003, 4% in 2004 and 6.7% in 2005. 4. Health care benefits are experiencing sustained growth due, in particular, to the cost of new medical technologies and the increase in the number of insured persons. Thus, the growth rate of these benefits would have been about 9%, on average, from 1998 to 2001. In such circumstances, it appears difficult to comply with the programme's spending targets, at least in the absence of reforms that could slow the spontaneous growth of public spending. A less favourable than expected evolution of balances could certainly be countered by an increase in revenues. However, an increase in the tax burden would affect the competitiveness of the Luxembourg economy at a time when it is already facing many challenges. A structural effort to regulate expenditure would be all the more justified since the ratio of public expenditure to GDP has risen sharply in recent years. While it reached only 42% of GDP at the end of the nineties, this ratio would have been 47% in 2002. As a result, average public expenditure per capita would have amounted to 23,000 per year in Luxembourg, about double the amount observed in the euro area as a whole. My third point on the stability programme is that it contains an overly optimistic assessment of the long-term sustainability of the private pension scheme. Thus, it is mentioned that "the evaluation carried out in 2001 by the International Labour Office (ILO) showed that the current financial situation of Luxembourg's general pension insurance scheme is solid and stable". Even under the assumptions of the ILO's least optimistic scenario, it is asserted that "the system will generate surpluses over the next ten years and as a result, the reserve, as well as its relative level, will increase". This avoids the fact that the accumulation of reserves over the next ten years will result from large arrivals of frontier and foreign workers who will cause a significant increase in benefits when they reach retirement age. Moreover, the programme conceals the fact that the ILO projections do not take into account the Rentendesch measures. Important lessons from the ILO report are also evaded. Thus, the ILO stated that under the pessimistic scenario, "there is no possibility of an increase in benefits. On the other hand, the Government should start discussing solutions very early on to fill the large imbalance between expenditure and contributions that will arise in the coming decade." The ILO also stressed that "it is not recommended to pay the "thirteenth pension", nor to increase the flat-rate increases by 10%, nor the rate of increase from 1.78% to 1.90%. These measures are very costly." The ILO further states that "Since the reality might be less favourable than the assumptions of the [...] [optimistic] scenario suggests that it is recommended to reduce the level of expenditure of the general pension insurance scheme". More fundamentally, the assessments of the sustainability of public finances contained in Luxembourg's stability programmes should be updated more regularly. The current evaluation is based on the first ILO study, carried out even before the adoption of pension revaluation measures. Eventually, the evaluation should also include special pension systems, or even the health system. Finally, the Government should detail various measures to counter the factors that are drifting the budgetary situation of the pension system. The assets currently held by the central Government are certainly capable of strengthening the sustainability of Luxembourg's public finances. In total, these reserves would have amounted to EUR 3 120 million or 14% of GDP at 31 December 2001. While this level seems appreciable, the importance of the corresponding room for manoeuvre should not be overestimated. The central government is expected to run a large deficit throughout the period 2002-2005, so that the accumulated deficit would reach 10% of GDP in 2005, or about 70% of the reserves recorded at the end of 2001. Such a situation could become problematic if the state recorded new deficits after 2005. While some reduction in the level of reserves may be justified in times of economic downturn, the funds must nevertheless have significant reserves in order to be able to finance important future projects. In addition, the central government must endeavour to maintain sufficient working capital to meet temporary liquidity needs. Conclusion My point is not alarmist. It contributes to the search for ways and means to counter the collapse of our economic dynamics. Turning a blind eye and financing a pace of spending compatible with inflows of funds that have disappeared in the hope that these sources will spring up again as before is risky for a poorly diversified economy. What if the recovery is slow to come? The cost of the adjustment referred tends to show a geometric increase. The conservative reflex seems to be amplified with the opulence of a society. It is to be hoped that, unlike our neighbours and despite the electoral deadlines, we will be able to maintain the cohesion and national consensus necessary to tackle the reforms that guarantee the sustainability of our much-envied situation. Thank you for your attention. I am at your disposal for any questions.

Title: Savings and Investment: Determinants and Consequences for Economic Growth
text: SAVINGS AND INVESTMENT: DETERMINANTS AND CONSEQUENCES FOR ECONOMIC GROWTH Speech delivered by Mr Yves Mersch, President of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg, on the occasion of the Financial One 2003 Conference. Luxembourg, 15 May 2003 Only the Spoken Word is law Ladies and Gentlemen, The topic I have to talk about is "Saving and Investing: Determinants and Consequences for Economic Growth." By way of a brief introduction two remarks are necessary: the first concerns the content of this contribution. Since the subject is so multifaceted, it is impossible for me, if only by the time allotted to me, to deal with it in its entirety. The second point is a major obstacle. It relates to the lack of statistical data on sectoral savings in Luxembourg. Indeed, Luxembourg does not have detailed statistics on savings by economic sector (households, enterprises, State,...). The absence of these data results from the absence of a financial account relating to the national economy. Building such an account is obviously a delicate undertaking; it requires the collection of data collected by different authorities as well as their cooperation, the establishment of new procedures for collecting data from economic actors and possibly household surveys. In this regard, a project to establish a financial account for Luxembourg is underway at the BCL. The first results of this process would be available in the course of 2005. This will make it possible to understand, on the one hand, the contours of the Luxembourg economic circuit, and on the other hand the importance of inter- and intra-sectoral transfers. I shall try to identify the main features of the development of national savings in Luxembourg since the end of 1995, when our country set up a data collection system for the compilation of the current account of the Balance of Payments. Since 2000, the balance of payments has been drawn up under the joint responsibility of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg and Statec. In the absence of saving data, it is through the balance of payments and national accounts that the trend from this aggregate can be extracted. Despite these problems in measuring national saving in Luxembourg and in some measures of investment, long-term trends in saving and growth seem to support the commonly accepted idea that there is a virtuous circle of saving and growth. Recent empirical research on international data has shed new light on the links between savings, investment and growth. We will use it as a basis to try to answer four questions that I consider important to our economy: Those is the relationship between economic growth and national savings? That is the link between savings and investment? Does national saving translate into domestic investment? And finally, what is the role of interest rates in adjusting savings and investment decisions? The answer to these four questions is not without consequences for the definition of economic policy. Thus, if saving leads to growth because it systematically turns into investment, then economic policy must encourage saving. However, if investment is driven by factors other than saving, and if saving is generated by investment, then economic policy must stimulate investment. This is all the more true, the objective assigned to economic policy is dictated by growth and full employment, and not by the satisfaction of particular interests. To begin with, it seems to me that it is worth recalling first of all some economic definitions of the aggregates that interest us today, in this case investment and savings. The definition of investment, adopted by economists, differs significantly from the concept popularized by the press and/or used, on a daily basis, by the general public. Indeed, the public uses expressions that refer to investment, but that cover different realities, such as "I invested in the stock market" or "my company invested in a new machine". Yet the first expression is inappropriate. It refers to financial investments. While the second covers the economic notion of investment. Investment is a fundamental economic operation; for it is he who determines the accumulation of capital, considered as an essential factor of economic growth. It is also investment that allows the improvement of labour productivity and the development of technical progress. Therefore, the most general meaning of investment consists of the value of durable goods acquired by production units to be used for at least one year in the production process. In other words, it is the flows that feed the existing capital stock. As for saving, it is defined as unused income. This simple definition covers multiple problems as soon as one wants to grasp the macroeconomic evolutions of this aggregate. Indeed, saving is often equated in the public mind with household saving alone. However, from a national accounts point of view, saving appears as the balance of the income account of different sectors, i.e. the difference between disposable income and final consumption. Thus, the savings of companies are equivalent to the self-financing capacity; while household saving represents the sum of gross fixed capital formation (home acquisition) and financial saving, consisting of investments and liquid assets. Similarly, government saving is the sum of the value of government investment and its budgetary balance. 1. The relationship between saving and economic growth Let's first look at how saving was extracted from the well-known identity of national accounts: In a closed economy, national savings must be equal to investment. We will see that in an open economy savings and investment are not necessarily equal. This is due to the impact of foreign trade in goods and services on national income. Thus, the identity of national income in an open economy is written: PNB C G I (X-M) GNP: National income GDP income from the rest of the world - income paid to the rest of the world C : Private consumption G : Public consumption expenditure I : Public and private investment X-M: The current account balance of the balance of payments From this identity, we can extract national savings. It must simply be remembered that national saving is equal to the difference between national income and private and public consumption. Thus: S GNP -(CG) I(X-M) with S National savings Public savings Private savings This last equation highlights the major difference between an open economy and a closed economy: an open economy can save either by increasing its capital stock or by acquiring external assets, but a closed economy can only save by increasing its capital stock. Thus, an open economy has more investment opportunities than a closed economy because one country's savings can be borrowed by another country in order to increase its capital stock. For this reason, the current account surplus is often referred to as net foreign investment. After this brief reminder, I would like to dwell a little on the link between national savings and economic growth. Empirically, growth and saving often show a positive correlation. In this regard, Figure 1 illustrates this relationship for Luxembourg. The correlation coefficient between the two aggregates is positive (0.305). It should be noted, however, that the level of this result is relatively low. This is probably explained by the importance of the degree of openness of the Luxembourg economy. Indeed, in an open economy, part of the national savings are invested abroad. This mechanism should result, at least in the short term, in a disconnect between economic growth and national savings. However, the persistence of a positive, but relatively weak, relationship between the two aggregates is an indicator of the imperfect mobility of capital. From a theoretical point of view, economists find it difficult to identify their links accurately. Economic theory predicts that when households have access to credit and consider the future for their consumption and saving decisions, temporary changes in income usually result in fluctuations in saving rather than changes in consumption. However, this theoretical postulate is not clearly confirmed by academic work on international data. In other words, saving cannot be called a pro-cyclical aggregate because it does not accurately track the fluctuations in income that the theory predicts. Figure 1: National saving and GDP growth rates in Luxembourg (1995-2003)1 As an indication, Figure 2 illustrates the relationship between the national saving rate and the output gap2 over the period 1995-2002. Despite a moderate correlation rate (0.55) between the two variables, there is still a positive link between the saving rate and the output gap. Indeed, there is a contraction in the saving rate at certain periods of decline in economic activity, characterized by a negative output gap, and an upward trend in saving during periods of overheating of the economy where the level of effective income grows more than potential income. The absence of a perfect cyclicality of saving does not exclude the appearance of periods when the trajectory of national saving would be in line with that of the output gap, as illustrated by Figure 2 for Luxembourg. In this regard, a few remarks deserve to be highlighted: The two series (saving and investment) have a positive correlation rate of 0.55. This is synonymous with a joint dynamic and in the same sense of the two variables; The It is worth noting that the dispersion of points reflects more or less three periods of relationship between saving and investment. A first group of points is centered at the intersection of the two axes. This is an indication of the savings rate during periods when the observed national income is equivalent to the potential income. The displayed savings rate is channelled in a range of 31% to 33%; One second group of points predominates. It is characterized by relatively high savings rates in times of positive output gap. Thus, in times of strong economic growth, national savings increase significantly. Finally a final group is associated with a high savings rate, but also with a largely negative output gap. In other words, in times of significant decline in economic activity, the savings rate shows a significant increase. This is probably due to households' uncertainty about economic prospects, which encourages them to favour savings over consumption. In other words, precautionary savings may bear the responsibility for increased savings in a phase of declining economic activity. Figure 2: National saving rates and output gap in Luxembourg3 (1995-2002) Let us now turn to the relationship between trend GDP and private saving. This relationship is more relevant from the point of view of long-term growth. Most empirical studies confirm that the increase in real income does have a positive effect on savings. However, these results are not consistent with the relationships predicted by economic theory. Indeed, from the point of view of classical consumption theory, this discrepancy is an enigma. The two main consumption patterns, permanent income (Friedman, 1957) and life cycle (A. Aldo and F. Modigliani 1964), predict a negative effect of growth on savings as individuals raise their consumption prospects in anticipation of higher future income. According to an unconventional hypothesis but somewhat reminiscent of classical thinking, households attach value to both consumption and wealth. Stronger growth improves household wealth but, because consumption and wealth are interchangeable, consumption increases less than proportionally, increasing savings. A second explanation has recourse to a kind of reverse causality: saving is systematically transformed into capital accumulation and thus into growth. This process is simply the mechanism that underlies the positive correlation between savings and economic growth observed in practice. However, according to empirical analyses, this explanation is disputed; because saving follows and does not precede growth. Therefore, proponents of this scheme conclude that the observed correlation between growth and saving reflects at least partially an inverse causal link between growth and saving, and that classical reasoning that does not take into account this two-way endogeneity risks overestimating the contribution of savings to growth. 2. Is saving a prerequisite for investing? There are differing views on the principle that saving should be a prerequisite for investment. Overall, two main principles clash: the so-called sacrifice principle, which postulates that saving must be prior to investment, and the so-called expenditure principle, which makes saving a consequence of investment. The first principle assumes, in a situation of full use of resources, that nations have no choice but to save for investment. The choice is therefore intertemporal, the sacrifice of present well-being (reduction in consumption) being rewarded with a higher well-being and income in the future. The second principle, although it maintains the possibility of prior saving, gives a stabilizing role to the banking system. Spontaneous savings that appear at the beginning of an analysis period can be allocated to investment, either "aborted" or hoarded. The aborted part, which can take the form of crowding out effect by outward investment, leads to a lack of domestic investment, which translates into lower consumer price levels. The role of the banking system then becomes crucial. Through its credits, it must fill the deficit in national savings. If the compensation is exactly equal to the aborted savings, there will be price stability, but if the amount of bank credit is higher than the aborted savings, the economy would show an acceleration in inflation. The return to equilibrium is carried out by the mechanism of the real cash, called the Pigou effect, which leads to forced savings. Despite these discrepancies, understanding the mechanism reflecting the interaction between savings and investment is necessary for at least two reasons: Like as we have just described in the previous section, it may be that the link between investment and saving is the explanatory key to the savings-growth relationship. In Assuming that capital accumulation is indeed the engine of growth, understanding the interaction between saving and investment is essential for the assessment of the classical assumption that increasing saving is the most appropriate means of promoting economic activity. This idea implicitly assumes that each country's additional savings are completely transformed into an increase in gross fixed capital formation. Thus, in a closed economy, national savings and domestic investment are necessarily equal. However, things are more complex in an open economy, such as Luxembourg, because capital flows between countries make it possible to switch between national savings and the volume of domestic investment. National savings are not necessarily used for domestic investment. In a world characterized by "perfect" capital mobility, each country's savings will flow to the country that offers the most attractive private rate of return. In this context, the increase in national saving will result in a current account surplus or a decrease in related deficits, rather than an increase in domestic investment and, in turn, an increase in economic growth. However, this reasoning should be put into perspective because empirical work reveals a strong positive correlation, in the long term, between investment and saving. According to Obstfeld (1986), the percentage of saving and investment cannot diverge much in the long run, particularly if the ratio of foreign assets to GDP is stable. The veracity of the latter hypothesis helps to explain the strong correlation between national saving and domestic investment. During the period 1995-2003 (see Table 1), national savings and domestic investment in Luxembourg fluctuated relatively. Their levels oscillate in a much wider range than that observed in the euro area during the period 1995-2001. Indeed, the oscillations in the shares of savings and investment in GDP in Luxembourg vary, respectively, from 30-36% and 21-25%, while those of the euro area are limited in a range of 21-22% for savings and 20-21% for investment. The extent of the fluctuations that characterise these two aggregates in Luxembourg is a factor of macroeconomic cyclicality. This would be due to the fact that the variability of investment automatically affects the dispersion of growth. Table 1: Investment and savings in Luxembourg and the euro area as % of GDP. Investment and economic growth From both a theoretical and empirical point of view, the link between gross domestic investment and the long-term growth rate is well established. Nevertheless, the question of the link between these two variables deserves to be detailed in the conduct of an economic policy. To measure the effects of investment on growth, it is necessary to distinguish between long-term and short-term consequences. In the long run, investment increases the productive capacity and/or productivity of the capital employed and thus allows an increase in the country's wealth. In the short term, the relationship between investment and growth goes through the multiplier and accelerator mechanisms. An increase in investment leads to growth in incomes, under the multiplier effect, and thus an increase in aggregate demand. This additional demand causes a need for new capital which then translates into investments (accelerator effect). The combination of these effects can cause steady economic growth or cyclical behaviours. This is the famous model of Samuelson's oscillator. Investment has a significant effect on the economic situation. The decomposition of GDP growth makes it possible to account for the effect of investment on growth. For this it is enough to exploit the previous accounting identity. The contribution of each factor to GDP growth is then the product of its growth rate by its weight in GDP. The application of this exercise in Luxembourg reveals that the contribution of investment, compared to the other components, is relatively less important; nevertheless, the extent of its variations [-2% to 7%], as illustrated by Figure 3, represents an important explanatory factor for the fluctuations in economic growth in Luxembourg. A priori, maintaining a more or less stable ratio of investment to GDP would result in greater economic stability. This condition appears necessary, but it remains insufficient, since steady growth depends not only on the accumulation of physical capital, but also on other factors, such as human capital, the efficient use of resources, ... Figure 3: Contribution of investment to GDP growth: 1986-2003 Attempting to stabilize economic growth through investment raises other questions, including the disruptive nature of a stimulus through investment and the nature of investment, i.e. that the action envisaged is intended to stabilize private or public investment. The answer to this question is not so simple, because private investment, apart from state tax incentives, depends on expected profitability, risk and interest rate. Logically, the only direct action variable available to the State is public investment. However, I confess that I am not really convinced of the full effectiveness of this instrument for two reasons: the first is related to the difficulties of implementing this tool for counter-cyclical purposes, mainly due to the increasingly long delays between the planning and implementation of the investment; while the second relates to the contribution of public investment to growth. This is characterized by greater stability than the contribution of private investment (see chart below). From 1991 to 2002, the contribution of private investment to growth varies from -3% to 5%, while the contribution of public investment fluctuates in a regular range of or -1%. That said, it is true that in the presence of opposite fluctuations in the two categories of investment (private and public), economic growth would be less subject to cyclical fluctuations in private investment. Figure 4: Contribution of public and private investment to GDP growth: 1991-2002 I have previously stressed the role of interest rates as an explanatory factor for the variation in private investment. This provides me with an opportunity to address the last point of my presentation, which is dedicated to the role of interest rates in reconciling savings and investment decisions. 4. The role of interest rates in reconciling savings and investment. Often, when economists talk about the role of interest rates in achieving macroeconomic equilibrium, they think first of all of the action they take in the intertemporal allocation of resources. This amounts to trying to understand to what extent their evolutions make it possible to obtain an equalization between savings and investment. We must therefore return to the arguments relating to the sensitivity of investment decisions and savings to interest rates. For investment, it is customary to distinguish between investment in housing on the one hand and the demand for productive capital of the private sector on the other. For housing investment, empirical work converges to recognize its high sensitivity to interest rate fluctuations. This is the result of a well-known effect: the maximum debt volume of a household is defined by the amount of financial charges that cannot exceed a certain percentage of its disposable income. Therefore, changes in the interest rate directly affect the creditworthiness of potential borrowers, and therefore the level of demand for credit. Thus, the evolution of interest rates exerts a mechanical influence on the level of household investment. In this context and by way of illustration, Figure 5 illustrates both the relationship between the short-term interest rates observed on the money market, the average interest rate on mortgage loans charged by credit institutions and the volume of loans newly granted for the residential sector in Luxembourg. It should be noted that a simple calculation reveals a negative correlation of -0.16 between the short-term interest rates observed on the money market and the volume of credit. The intensity of the relationship between average mortgage interest rates and the volume of loans and more important (-0.35). This is the result of a smoothed passing-on of changes in key interest rates on the rates of newly granted loans. Figure 5: Interest rates and volume of newly granted loans to the residential sector: 1996-2002 For productive investments, the action of interest rates is more complex to analyze and more difficult to assess. This explains the opposition between the results of empirical work. Indeed, judging by the published econometric estimates, it is clear that the sensitivity of investment to interest rates is low4. More generally, it appears relatively insensitive to the majority of financial variables, with the exception of the level of profits (i.e. business savings) and that economists have some difficulty in differentiating it from the classic accelerator effect or the effects related to credit rationing, particularly for small firms. That said, a number of other arguments suggest that the effect of interest rates on investment is not as small as empirical evidence claims. First, because econometric estimates do not take into account credit rationing constraints applied by credit institutions, particularly for small businesses. It is therefore not surprising that the influence of rates is difficult to highlight. On the other hand, the fact that credit institutions pass on the fall in key interest rates only with a delay, the effects of interest rates on investment can only be observed with a delay, the extent of which depends on the behaviour of the banks. In this regard, the study G. de Bondt (2002)5 reveals that almost 50% of the fall in the Eurosystem's key interest rates is only passed on to corporate loans one month late. As for the interest rates associated with consumer credit, their adjustments to money market conditions are much slower. Despite these constraints, the current process of greater integration of European financial markets will lead to a broadening of the range of assets on which economic agents will be able to take a position, but also to much greater arbitrage possibilities. The choice between financial and real assets will arise more sensitively. The increase in possible substitutions between financial assets will lead to a more marked divide between them, on the one hand, and real assets, on the other. In other words, it is a choice between physical investment and financial investment. In this context, Tobin6's Q theory provides a mechanism by which changes in stock prices affect the investment behavior of companies. Tobin's Q is defined as the market value of a company in relation to the replacement cost of its capital. When the Q falls for all companies, they will not invest because their market value is lower than the cost of capital. A strategy of buying an existing business is less costly than a strategy of starting new businesses and investing in capital. Thus, a downward shock in the stock market reduces the market values of companies and consequently the values of Tobin's Qs. This translates into a decline in investment and potentially a wave of corporate buyouts. Symmetrically, an upward shock in the stock market translates into an increase in corporate values and consequently in Tobin's Q values. This means that the profit outlook is favorable (the rise in securities is assumed to reflect anticipated profits). It is then more profitable to buy real assets (economic investment). It should also be stressed that the influence of interest rates on the situations of companies and on their investments is not only reflected in the comparison between the cost of capital and the profitability of the projects envisaged. The evolution of rates also applies to the entire stock issued at variable rates. It is not only new borrowers who are concerned, but also indebted companies. And it is not only investment projects that can be called into question, but also the solvency of a number of companies. Thus, the investment can be affected at the end of a more powerful sequence than that which is partly described by a simple investment function. It is clear that the most indebted companies are much more sensitive to interest rate fluctuations than the least indebted companies. Similarly, this effect may affect in a similar way start-ups or so-called venture capital firms that are likely to pay the price without this being the result of mismanagement or insufficient profitability, since these young companies generally have more difficult access to external sources of financing. In any case, current interest rate levels in the euro area are relatively low, making the latter effects implausible, especially if credit institutions adopt a systematic adjustment of customer credit costs to their refinancing terms. Let us now turn to the analysis of the relationship between savings and the interest rate. On this point too, uncertainties persist. From a theoretical point of view, we know that the evolution of interest rates exerts two effects on consumption: A substitution effect that is easy to account for. The change in interest rates encourages households to revise the allocation of their expenditure over time. For example, an increase in interest rates should lead them to substitute future consumption for present consumption. That is to say, it must cause an increase in savings. The income effect, on the other hand, is a little tricky to analyze. Its impact varies according to individual positions. A borrower is naturally disadvantaged by an increase in interest rates. Compared to its expenditure plan, the level of its updated resources is deteriorating, and it must, in principle, reduce its consumption. On the other hand, an agent in a lender situation is advantaged by the rise in interest rates. The improvement of its future resources allows it and encourages it to consume today a greater proportion of its income. In aggregate, households are net lenders (positive income effect); while companies are net borrowers (negative income effect). All in all, the conjunction of all these effects is theoretically ambiguous, and empirical observations do not allow a satisfactory conclusion. This provides me with an opportunity to recall that beyond these empirical questions, the phases of price instability and inflation experienced in the past were periods of very low or even negative real interest rates. That is, these periods were characterized by a significant transfer of income from savers to capital borrowers. However, the maintenance of price stability coupled with positive real interest rates has reversed leverage in favour of lenders.
