Title: The economic situation in Luxembourg and the need for staying watchful
text: THE ECONOMIC SITUATION IN LUXEMBOURG AND THE NEED FOR STAYING WATCHFUL Speech by Yves Mersch President of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg at the NOBELUX Chambre of Commerce 28 January 2004 Seule la Parole prononcee fait foi Ladies and Gentlemen, I should first like to thank the organisers for having invited me to this "Get together lunch". It is a real pleasure to address today's audience and to be able to discuss Luxembourg's economic situation with all of you afterwards. First let me draw a quick picture of the economic situation in the euro area. As a matter of fact, the last published data show a recovery in the euro area. The 0.4% GDP growth in the third quarter of 2003 evidences the strong dynamism of the world economy, which should go on in 2004. The Governing Council of the European Central Bank expects an improvement of domestic demand. Private consumption should remain steady, in particular because of the appreciation of the euro. Positive effects on the employment situation will most probably follow in due time. Productive investment will improve progressively mainly because of stronger external demand, low interest rates and financing conditions which are generally speaking favourable. Moreover, private companies' efforts to increase their productivity and profitability should support this trend. In general, the Governing Council expects a progressive economic recovery of the euro area in the coming quarters. Nevertheless, in the long term, the Governing Council remains concerned about the possibility of external imbalances in certain regions of the world, which could jeopardise the stability of the world's economic growth. With regard to prices, most recent information confirms previous economic projections. According to Eurostat, the euro zone annual inflation was 2.0% in December 2003, following a rate of 2.2 % in November. HICP inflation rates over the short term are still expected to fluctuate around the 2% level. Now, let me turn to the economic situation in Luxembourg. The activity in the industrial sector has been quite volatile in 2003. It grew by 2.3% in the first quarter of 2003 compared to the previous quarter. It then fell by 1.4% in the second quarter and finally increased by 2.7% in the third quarter. Public works are also slowing down after the end of a certain number of large-scale works. As to the construction industry, economic surveys indicate a decline in demand as shown by the guaranteed activity period, which has dropped from 3.7 months in December 2002 to 3.5 months in December 2003. In general, statistics with regard to residential building are positive. Building authorisations in particular have experienced a big increase for the last quarters, as they have been promoted by the government's will to correct the imbalance between housing offer and demand and by low mortgage rates. As for non-residential construction, future does not seem as bright. Office buildings are increasingly empty, which increases the pressure to reduce rents. The favourable trade situation in 2002 seems to have continued throughout 2003. During the first half of 2003, turnover has increased in all three sectors of trade. This growth rests on a broad basis, as practically all segments of the various sectors recorded a progression in sales in 2003. Only hotels and restaurants seem to suffer from a fall in the number of clients as evidenced by a decrease of their annual turnover. As regards the financial sector, the confirmation of good conditions on the stock markets and the recovery of bond yields have allowed the banks of the financial centre to generate a gross profit before provisions and taxes of 3 974 million euros as at 31 December 2003, which represents, however, a decrease by 7.8% compared to 31 December 2002. Faced with reduction of revenues, credit institutions have continued with their cost reduction programs in order to be able to limit the pressure on their net results. Thus, operating costs have been reduced by 3.6% (-113 million euros) over 12 months. The downward evolution of the headcount in the credit institutions reflects in the evolution of personnel costs which fell by 3.6% (-58 million euros) during the same period of time. The number of credit institutions has continued its decrease which started back in June 1996. During 2003, this number moved down from 177 on 1 January 2003 to 169 on 31 December 2003. This downward trend is partly due to the merger and acquisition process among parent banks, but also to reorganisations within banking groups. We expect this number of credit institutions to continue its decrease in the next years. The Luxembourg economy taken as a whole will experience a third year of low growth and recovery will only be slow and gradual afterwards. In the medium term, the evolution of growth will be determined by international demand which is accelerating. The clearing of uncertainties, the stabilisation of financial markets and the progression of domestic demand underlie this scenario. The growth rates of the end of the 1990s, however, will probably not be achieved. Thus, according to our projections, Luxembourg's real GDP will grow by 0.8 to 1.4% in 2003 and by 1.7 to 2.7% in 2004 and probably more in 2005. Despite recovery, economic growth will unfortunately not be strong enough to stop unemployment's growth. The unemployment rate could reach 4.5% of active population in 2004 and even 5.2% in 2005. Inflation in Luxembourg, already moderate, will decelerate slowly. On the one hand, the oil price in euro scenario has become less favourable than in spring 2003. On the other hand, measures regarding indirect taxation have been implemented and these measures will certainly prevent a more significant deceleration of inflation. Nevertheless, a progression of inflation is not foreseen. A moderate imported inflation, promoted by the rising euro-dollar exchange rate in particular, and also decelerating employment costs in the euro area and in Luxembourg will limit future growth of consumer prices. On average, inflation should remain below 2% in 2004 and also in 2005. Our conclusion according to which there will be no automatic indexation of wages in 2004 remains valid. Now I would also like to spend a few words on the budgetary situation of the Luxembourg general government. Supposing an unchanged policy, our projections show the comfortable surplus of public administrations will almost certainly make room for a financing requirement from 2003 onwards. Deficit could reach 2% of GDP in 2004 and reach 2.8% in 2005. Deterioration of Luxembourg's public finances is only partly attributable to the weakening of the economic situation. Ignoring this evolution, the balance of public administrations would remain in deficit by 2.4% of GDP in 2005. As a reminder, this corrected balance showed a 5% surplus in 2001. The deterioration of the public administrations' budget situation is mainly attributable to the increase of the expenses to GDP ratio. After having already increased a lot in 2002, this ratio would be of 47.9% of GDP in 2005, mostly because of the increase of social transfers, of the compensation of employees and of steady public investments during the period 2003-2005. As regards revenues, they reached a maximum of 47% of GDP in 2002, but they would drop to 45.1% in 2005. This evolution is mainly due to the evolution of direct taxes collected from companies, as the strong acceleration of tax collection that took place in 2002 will probably be replaced by an important deceleration in 2004 and 2005. According to the amended draft budget for 2004, the central State's financing requirement is limited to 84 million euros, despite a striking deceleration of revenues' growth. This result is attributable to a progression of total expenses limited to 2% compared to the final 2003 budget, which is itself a consequence of a 19% reduction in capital expenses. Nevertheless, it should be emphasised that the central State's deficit, as calculated following SEC 95 accounting rules, would be much higher. In the end of 2003, the Government presented the fifth update of Luxembourg's stability programme. Macroeconomic assumptions that prevailed in the programme's elaboration seem realistic. Moreover, the programme foresees the development of significant general government deficits from 2004 onwards. These deficits would be of 1.8% of GDP in 2004 and 2.3% in 2005, while the preceding actualisation banked on a light deficit in 2005. The programme, however, still seems relatively optimistic with regard to the evolution of local administrations' deficits which would peak at 0.2% of GDP in 2004 and in 2005. As evidenced in the 2004 draft State budget, the revenue from the local commercial tax, which represented almost 40% of local administrations' revenues in 2002, will indeed severely drop in 2004. Moreover, the programme rests on the assumption of a significant reduction of the expenses to GDP ratio of public administrations, which would move down from 47.7% in 2003 to 47.2% in 2005 and 46.4% in 2006. Such an evolution requires the adoption of new structural measures limiting significantly the increase in expenses. According to our own calculations, public administrations would show important structural deficits from 2004 on. On the opposite, the programme foresees positive balances during the whole period 2002-2006. In light of these budgetary considerations, I would like to conclude with an analysis of the Luxembourg social insurance system, especially with regard to the pension system and the healthcare. In the past, the social insurance system has recorded important surpluses, but according to our projections, these surpluses will decrease over the period 2003-2005 and reach 1.2% of GDP in 2005 compared to 2.9% in 2001 and to 2.4% in 2002. On the long term, and in the absence of a very high economic growth the budgetary situation of the system would continue to deteriorate. This deterioration would hit the two biggest sectors of the social system: pensions and healthcare. With regard to the private pension system, assuming notably that Luxembourg achieves a 3% annual growth on average, our long-term projections show that surpluses will continue to grow until 2015 and then they will start to decrease. Around 2040, an annual financing need would arise, and it would reach 8% of GDP at the end of the projection horizon, in 2085. By 2055, the reserves that have been built will have been used up and significant liabilities will accumulate thereafter. This shows the long-term precariousness of the Luxembourg pension scheme. As to the healthcare system, if the annual growth rate of the real expenses per protected person remains at 3.8%, which was the actual level during the period 1990-2002, social contributions would have to be gradually increased. This would entail a significant increase of labour cost for the companies in Luxembourg. Under the 3% annual growth assumption mentioned before, it would be possible to maintain the social contributions level at the 2003 level only if the annual growth of real expenses per protected person stays below 1.8%. This would mean, however, a very strong decrease of these expenses compared to the period 1990-2002. Thus, the sustainability of this system is also to be questioned. Thank you very much for your attention.

Title: Financial Stability - From the Challenges of New International Standards to the Role of the Central Bank
text: FINANCIAL STABILITY - FROM THE CHALLENGES OF NEW INTERNATIONAL STANDARDS TO THE ROLE OF THE CENTRAL BANK Speech delivered by Mr Yves Mersch, President of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg, on the occasion of the 11th meeting of the Governors of the Central Banks of the French-speaking countries 10 June 2004 Only the Spoken Word is authentic The international financial system has generally weathered well the economic adversities, financial turbulence and geopolitical shocks of recent years. Today, while hoping for calmer waters with the ongoing economic recovery, we are faced with a convergence of several important regulatory reforms. These reforms are likely to have a structural influence on the financial industry. The new international standards The interest of the new international standards for a central bank stems mainly from its role in the area of financial stability. Three main reform projects are currently underway: bank solvency rules, accounting standards and corporate governance. The new solvency framework for banks, "Basel 2", is based on three pillars :(1) of the minimum capital requirements; (2) the examination of risks by the prudential supervisor, and (3) the dissemination of information to the public. The interest of this new framework for a central bank stems from its potential impact on the risk profile and solvency of banks, and hence on financial stability. Basel 2 aims to address banks' real risks; this is a positive fact. However, greater risk sensitivity means an increased influence of the macroeconomic environment on banks' decisions. This may lead to an increase in pro-cyclicality in the granting of credit. If the norm therefore accentuates the effects of the business cycle, it increases the danger of instability. These concerns, which have been the subject of official comments by the Governing Council of the European Central Bank, have been taken into account. The final texts have not yet been put into practice. Continued attention in this regard is still required. Nevertheless, it appears that the implementation of "Basel" 2" will be carried out in a differentiated way: a) Applicable to all banks and investment firms in the European Union through a Directive; b) Applicable only to banks with international activity in the United States and certain other countries; and (c) Not applicable simply in some other countries. This raises the problem of the equivalence of the conditions of competitiveness at international level. In terms of accounting rules, the reform is moving towards a greater application of fair value. The Governing Council of the European Central Bank has expressed its cautious reservations about IAS 32 and 39 on financial instruments, with the result that the application of fair value is now limited to a limited set of instruments. The controversies surrounding fair value have indeed revealed the fundamental tension between the point of view of investors and that of authorities and companies. The former call for a day-to-day evaluation, the latter advocate a long-term evaluation. As with the solvency rules, an assessment of the impact of the new accounting rules, as well as the issue of international convergence in this area, in particular that between ias-IFRS (International Accounting Standards - International Financial Reporting Standards) and US-GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles), will be of particular importance. The third normative project is that of good corporate governance. It is a crucial element in maintaining financial stability. Financial firms are not the only ones concerned. Revelations of resounding abuses in recent years, mainly affecting non-financial companies, have revealed serious deficiencies in accounting transparency and etexterne internal control mechanisms. Fortunately, these events have not had a lasting impact on financial stability, thanks in particular to the limitation of large risks to banks. Ongoing efforts call for more formal and rigorous regulation, coupled with increased vigilance on the part of shareholders and authorities. The role of the central bank in financial stability I would like to reiterate the remarks on the prudential elements set out above that may have a systemic impact on financial stability, in the context of the need for a central bank to be integrated into an appropriate supervisory framework. Originally, the role of a central bank in financial stability results from the combination of its role as guardian of the currency and the participation of commercial banks in the process of money creation. The value of the scriptural money issued by commercial banks depends on their strength. The central bank's mission with regard to the proper functioning and stability of the sector is therefore linked to public confidence in the stability and security of the means of payment. The banking sector is a system whose individual entities are closely linked by payment systems and the interbank market. A central bank must be interested in the robustness of its counterparties. It must also ensure the proper functioning of the financial system. To this end, it assumes the role of ultimate provider of liquidity and stable means of payment. Financial stability contributes to price stability; price stability in turn contributes to strengthening financial stability. Today's financial reality is characterized by the simultaneous intensification of international trade and links between different segments of the financial industry. The removal of sectoral and national boundaries has stimulated the integration and consolidation of the sector. This new context goes hand in hand with an increase in the potential effects of financial crises. The emergence of large banking and financial groups, the large volume of financial flows, as well as the increase in direct intermediation by the market, constitute an amplification of the potential channels of contagion. These developments pose new challenges for the authorities to prevent and, if necessary, react in the event of a crisis. Indeed, a central bank will find it difficult to fulfil its responsibilities regarding monetary stability, which is directly linked to considerations of financial stability and systemic risks (including crisis prevention and management), without being involved in the supervision of the banking sector. Such involvement can be done directly or through appropriate cooperation agreements. The central bank's access to micro-prudential information is a condition for efficiency in crisis management. The consolidation of the supervision of the different financial sectors into a single institution is implemented in several European countries, such as the United Kingdom, Hungary, Germany, Austria or more recently in Ireland. These institutional adjustments have not called into question the general involvement of the national central banks in supervision. Within the euro area, some central banks have direct responsibility for micro-prudential supervision, others are indirectly involved in this task, and still others have a formal arrangement for cooperation with the supervisor. I must note that the Banque centrale du Luxembourg is the only national central bank of the Eurosystem without any legal role in the supervision of individual banks and a formal cooperation arrangement with the banking supervisor at this stage. Conclusion The new international standards should help improve the financial stability framework; they are of interest to central banks to the extent that they are likely to have an impact on the stability of the financial system; considerations of financial stability and systemic risks call for the need for a central bank to be integrated into an appropriate supervisory framework.

La mission de la banque centrale quant au bon fonctionnement et  la stabilit du secteur est donc lie  la confiance publique dans la stabilit et la scurit du moyen de paiement. Le secteur bancaire est un systme dont les entits individuelles sont troitement lies par les systmes de paiement et par le march interbancaire. Une banque centrale doit s'intresser  la robustesse de ses contreparties. Elle doit aussi veiller au bon fonctionnement du systme financier. A cet effet, elle assume un rle de fournisseur ultime de liquidit et de moyens de paiement stables. La stabilit financire contribue  la stabilit des prix; la stabilit des prix contribue  son tour  renforcer la stabilit financire. La ralit financire d'aujourd'hui est caractrise par l'intensification simultane des changes internationaux et des liens entre les diffrents segments de l'industrie financire. L'effacement des dlimitations sectorielles et nationales a stimul l'intgration et la consolidation du secteur. Ce nouveau contexte va de pair avec un accroissement des effets potentiels de crises financires. L'mergence d'importants groupes bancaires et financiers, le grand volume des flux financiers, ainsi que l'augmentation de l'intermdiation directe par le march, constituent une amplification des canaux potentiels de contagion. Ces dveloppementsne sont pas sans poser de nouveaux dfis aux autorits pour prvenir et au besoin, ragir en cas de crise. En effet, une banque centrale aura des difficults  assumer ses responsabilits concernant la stabilit montaire, qui est directement relie  des considrations de stabilit financire et de risques systmiques (y inclus la prvention et la gestion des crises), sans tre implique dans la surveillance du secteur bancaire. Une telle implication peut se faire directement ou grce  des accords de coopration adquats. L'accs de la banque centrale aux informations micro-prudentielles est une condition d'efficience dans la gestion de crise. La consolidation de la surveillance des diffrents secteurs financiers en une seule institution est mise en uvre dans plusieurs pays europens, comme au Royaume-Uni, en Hongrie, en Allemagne, en Autriche ou plus rcemment en Irlande. Ces adaptations institutionnelles n'ont pas remis en cause l'implication gnrale des banques centrales nationales dans la surveillance. Au sein de la zone euro,certaines banques centrales assument une responsabilit directe dans la surveillance micro-prudentielle, d'autres sont impliques indirectement dans cette mission, d'autres encore ont un arrangement formel de coopration avec le superviseur. Je dois constater que la Banque centrale du Luxembourg est l'unique banque centrale nationale de l'Eurosystme dpourvue d'un rle lgal quelconque dans la surveillance des banques individuelles et d'un arrangement de coopration formel avec le contrleur bancaire  ce stade. Conclusion Les nouvelles normes internationales devraient contribuer  amliorer le cadre de la stabilit financire ; elles intressent les banques centrales dans la mesure o elles sont susceptibles d'avoir un impact sur la stabilit du systme financier; les considrations de stabilit financire et de risques systmiques appellent la ncessit pour une banque centrale d'tre intgre dans un cadre de surveillance appropri.

Title: The impact of enlargement (and the future constitution) on financial services
text: THE IMPACT OF ENLARGEMENT (AND THE FUTURE CONSTITUTION) ON FINANCIAL SERVICES Serge Kolb, Director of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg Annual congress of the Union of European Lawyers 18 June 2004 Only the Word spoken is authentic: Ladies and Gentlemen, First of all, I would like to thank the organisers for inviting me to this Congress of the Union of European Lawyers to share with you some thoughts on the development of financial services in Europe. The subject of the impact of enlargement and the future constitution on financial services has been proposed to me. Indeed, these are two historic events this year that will permanently and significantly mark the identity of the European Union, one by its extension, the other by its deepening. The draft Constitution is welcomed by the Eurosystem. In its official opinion of 19 September 2003, the European Central Bank recalls that this draft simplifies, lightens and clarifies the Union's institutional legal framework. It increases its ability to act both internally and externally. It is to be hoped that this Constitution will enter into force as soon as possible. The project is reasonable. It is essentially to be seen as a consolidation of the acquis communautaire and as a logical step towards European integration, of which, I stress, the completion of the single market in financial services is an indispensable pillar. The Constitution incorporates, without modifying it, the mechanism of economic and monetary union in force since the Maastricht Treaty. It provides an adequate legislative and regulatory framework for the integration of financial services. As a lawyer, you should appreciate that, in this area, one of the most regular in economic life, a clearer definition of the legislative and administrative powers exercised by the democratically controlled institutions, represents as such a major step forward. Having said that, I would like to focus my presentation on the impact of enlargement. Single market - state of play Today, almost 50 years after the adoption of the Treaty of Rome and its common market objective, almost 20 years after the adoption of the Single Market programme, financial integration has not yet been achieved. The market remains segmented, and alas, it is still far from reaching its potential. Certainly, the progress made is remarkable. Several market segments, especially wholesale ones, have achieved a high level of integration. This is measured by price convergence and the share of cross-border transactions. Since the introduction of the euro, the money market has integrated well and the inter-bank market is no longer compartmentalised. However, national fragmentation persists, especially in capital markets as well as market infrastructures such as payment systems and securities settlement systems. The introduction of the euro in 1999, by unifying a crucial element that underpins any financial system in twelve countries, was a significant stimulus. The European Financial Services Action Plan, launched in March 1999 and ready to be completed by next year, will adapt the legislative framework to the needs of an integrated market. It is part of the Lisbon Strategy of March 2000, according to which the European Union should become the most competitive economy in the world by 2010. The political bodies therefore attach great importance to the achievement of an integrated financial market in Europe. That said, it should be noted that even in a situation where there is no longer any discrimination of economic agents, geographical or otherwise, in their access to and investment in capital, and where the rules and standards are the same for all, factors will continue to favour the local provision of financial services. Have you ever thought about entrusting your savings to a bank in Finland, for example? I think for most of you, the answer is no. Indeed, in addition to the visible barriers of regulation, taxation or standardization, there are less visible obstacles related to the natural advantage of the local service, such as familiarity with domestic particularities or the preference to carry out transactions in one's mother tongue. In short, retail markets will hardly reach the degree of internationalization of wholesale markets. Such a result will be due, it must be recalled, to the specific preference of economic agents and not to the failure of public authorities to establish the preconditions for market integration. The impact of enlargement - new Member States As of 1 May this year, ten new countries have joined the fifteen old members of the European Union. Interestingly, in the majority of these new countries, the post-communist restructuring of the 90s resulted in a financial sector largely dominated by foreign, especially European, institutions. The lack of a developed national infrastructure has imposed on these countries a policy of openness to foreign investment which, it should be noted, has largely benefited them. Today, with a deeply modernized financial intermediation structure, the citizens of these countries enjoy a much wider choice of products and much stronger financial institutions than fifteen years ago. Accession to the European Union is an important milestone in the transformation of the financial system of the new Member States. The adoption of the acquis communautaire opens up the opportunities linked to the four freedoms of the internal market (free movement of goods, persons, services and capital), even if their full realisation will have to wait for the expiry of certain transitional measures. The adoption of the euro at the end of the convergence process, which is firmly on the political agenda, is likely to give a further boost to integration, just as was the case for the former members. The impact of enlargement - old Member States As far as the old Member States are concerned, the impact of enlargement is still not very visible at present. This is not surprising: newcomers, although together represent a fifth of the population of the Union of Fifteen, account for only 5% of their gross domestic product. The accession of these countries therefore does not significantly alter the data of the Internal Market. The new members certainly constitute a market with great potential for European institutions, but only in the long term, as their real convergence with the old members progresses and their standard of living catches up. Excluding the exceptional cases of Cyprus and Malta, the eight new members of Central and Eastern Europe now reach only almost half the level of the Union of Fifteen in terms of per capita income, adjusted for purchasing power. The assets of their banks, compared to the gross domestic product of the economy, are only a third of the level of their counterparts in Western Europe. Capital markets as well as financial intermediaries other than banks, such as pension funds or insurance companies, remain marginal. The potential for growth and diversification, and thus the business opportunities for financial intermediaries, will therefore be considerable, but in the long term. In addition to their quality as a forward-looking market, a second impact of the accession of the new Member States could emanate from their attractiveness as providers of financial services. The lower costs and the lower tax burden, coupled with qualified personnel, attract the establishment of companies and could make these countries a serious competition for former members. However, despite their natural advantages, we must not forget either the factors favourable to the local delivery of services that I mentioned earlier, nor the lock-in effect of established actors. Moreover, in the current context, it is no longer as easy to create an international financial centre as Ireland or Luxembourg have done in the past. Thus, the massive relocation of financial services, for example from Luxembourg to the new Member States, is, in my opinion, currently an unrealistic scenario. The challenge of financial institutional adjustment Ladies and gentlemen, allow me to touch on one more subject which falls within our institutional tasks and which is closely linked to enlargement: the issue of financial regulation and supervision within the European Union. The opening of the financial sector of the countries of Central and Eastern Europe to foreign investment in the 90s was an important favourable factor for the deployment of large financial groups as we know it today. The accession of these countries highlights the gap between, on the one hand, an increasingly pan-European and even global financial reality, with the emergence of cross-sectoral conglomerates such as bancassurance groups, and on the other hand, the panoply of national regulations, which multiplies compliance costs for the actors concerned, creates opportunities for arbitration, slows down the integration process, and could also reduce the effectiveness of the authorities' supervision. In addition, financial integration is likely to change the channels for the transmission of systemic risk at European level. The authorities are well aware of these new challenges and adaptation efforts are ongoing. At the national level, the supervision of the various financial sectors has been consolidated in several countries into a single institution, for example in Germany, Austria, the United Kingdom or more recently in Ireland. These institutional adjustments have generally not called into question the involvement of the national central banks in supervision, which is also confirmed by the reforms currently under way in Italy. Central banks have a key role to play in overseeing the stability of the financial system as a whole and therefore a keen interest in the development and health of individual systemic institutions. This is intrinsically linked to the position of central banks at the centre of the financial system and their interest in preserving monetary policy transmission mechanisms and the soundness of counterparties, in payment systems, in fiat money or other transactions. At European level, efforts are directed in particular towards strengthening cross-border cooperation. The Union's central banks and banking supervisors signed a Memorandum of Understanding on cooperation in crisis situations at the beginning of 2003. The 2000 Coordinated Banking Directive is under revision, with, among other things, increased importance for consolidated supervision and an obligation to inform central banks in the event of a crisis. As for the reorganisation of institutional arrangements, it is based on the so-called Lamfalussy approach, after the name of the Chairman of the Committee of Wise Men who drew up recommendations in 2001 on the regulation of European securities markets. In short, the Lamfalussy approach aims to increase the flexibility and efficiency of the regulatory process by distinguishing between primary law, adopted by the Ecofin Council and the European Parliament through the codecision procedure, and secondary legislation, the implementation of which is delegated to specific committees. After the securities sector, these committees were created for the banking sector and for the insurance sector at the turn of this year. Conclusion To conclude, the enlargement of the European Union highlights the need for market players as well as public authorities to adapt to a new financial reality dictated by the blurring of sectoral and national borders and increased international competition. The arrival of the new Member States, although it does not significantly change the benchmarks of the financial market due to the still modest economic size of these countries, could nevertheless have a significant impact on the future direction of European regulation and the market. The new members of Central and Eastern Europe, being much less wealthy than their counterparts in Western Europe, have a particular interest in the proper functioning of the market and in avoiding an untimely regulatory overload. Therefore, these new countries should become a beneficial force contributing to the achievement of an efficient, sound, liberated and integrated financial market within the European Union. Thank you for your attention.

Title: The role of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg
text: THE ROLE OF THE BANQUE CENTRALE DU LUXEMBOURG by Mr Yves Mersch, President of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg In front of high school girls from the Fieldgen Private School and the Lyc8ee Technique Sainte-Anne Ettelbruck, April 11, 2005 Only the word spoken is authentic A member of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB), composed of the national central banks (NCBs) of the 25 Member States of the European Union (EU) and the European Central Bank (ECB), the BCL was created on 1 June 1998, at the same time as the ECB. Until then, Luxembourg did not have a central bank, delegating the burdens incumbent on such an institution to the National Bank of Belgium (NBB). The creation of the BCL was not, however, created ex nihilo, replacing the Luxembourg Monetary Institute (IML). While the main task of the BCL is to participate in the performance of the tasks of the ESCB with a view to achieving its objectives, it also carries out the tasks entrusted to it by its own organic law or by other laws, regulations or conventions. The BCL operates both at a supranational level, that of the euro area, and at a national level. Today, I will present the fundamental tasks of the Eurosystem and the role played by the BCL within it. The description of the BCL's participation in this work cannot be exhaustive, as the areas covered, often of a technical nature, are vast. I shall therefore confine myself to presenting in a little more detail the main objective of the Eurosystem, price stability, the definition and execution of monetary policy and the question of financial stability. Finally, I will briefly outline the other tasks carried out by the Bank. The main role of the BCL within the Eurosystem The Eurosystem, composed of the NCBs of the 12 countries that have adopted the euro and the ECB, has several fundamental tasks: the definition and implementation of monetary policy, the conduct of foreign exchange operations, the holding and management of the official foreign exchange reserves of the Member States, and the promotion of the proper functioning of payment systems. In addition, it contributes to the sound conduct of the policies pursued by the competent authorities with regard to the prudential supervision of credit institutions and the stability of the financial system. It also collects the statistical information necessary for the performance of its tasks and the issue of banknotes in the euro area. Main objective: price stability While the Eurosystem's tasks are manifold, its main objective is unique, namely price stability. However, without prejudice to the main objective, the Eurosystem shall also support the general economic policies of the Community. Since the main objective of the Eurosystem is price stability, the arguments justifying such an approach should be questioned. To put it simply, in an environment of price stability, the market allocates resources efficiently. Indeed, price variability complicates the evaluation of prices. This uncertainty accentuates imperfect information and increases the likelihood of poor optimization in individual agent decisions, i.e. the likelihood of an inefficient allocation of resources. A credible policy of price stability, focused on the medium to long term, also anchors expectations, lowering long-term interest rates, which promotes investment, growth and employment. Finally, the limitation of monetary erosion (i.e. the loss of value of money) makes it possible to maintain the purchasing power of economic agents, promoting consumption, investment and in turn growth and employment. The definition of monetary policy The Governing Council of the ECB, the decision-making body on the stance of the single monetary policy and composed of the six members of the Executive Board of the ECB and the twelve Governors of the euro area NCBs, decided to quantify price stability. This is defined over the medium term as an annual increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) of less than, but close to, 2% for the euro area as a whole. The quantification of the main objective therefore allows economic operators to facilitate their assessment of the Eurosystem's performance in achieving its main objective. The fact that price stability is defined in relation to the euro area as a whole means that the Governing Council does not act on the basis of inflation rates in individual countries. The medium-term perspective emphasizes that monetary policy has no short-term effects on prices, such as the price of oil. It also points out that the impact of a change in the official interest rate on prices is a lag in time of an average of 12 to 18 months. Consequently, exceeding the 2% threshold in the short term does not in any way constitute a trigger for automatic intervention on the official interest rate. Finally, there is no long-term trade-off between inflation and growth. Arbitrage, which exists in the short term, generates more inflation in the long term without additional growth and employment. While monetary policy inflections are having a short-term effect on overall output in the euro area, output will eventually return to a level very close to its initial level. In contrast, the impact of monetary policy on prices is more moderate in the short term, but persists over time. Any temptation to use monetary policy in the short term should therefore be avoided. It is for this reason that monetary policy must be entrusted to an independent central bank, since the political powers, in search of short-term votes in the electoral deadlines, can more easily give in to this temptation. In order to assess the risks to price stability, the Governing Council adopted a two-pillar monetary policy strategy. The first pillar includes a long-term monetary analysis and aims, in short, to monitor the growth of the quantity of money, as this is closely linked to the issue of inflation. The second pillar of the strategy is the analysis of a wide range of economic and financial indicators that can provide information on future price developments. The execution of monetary policy To achieve its objective, the central bank does not exert a direct influence on prices, but rather on interest rates. Some journalists call this the "rent of money." The single monetary policy is thus based on the setting of the level of the short-term interest rate and the volume of liquidity granted to credit institutions and, in turn, to individuals and the economy as a whole. Indeed, the change in the interest rate applied to commercial banks, decided by the Governing Council of the ECB, has an impact on the conditions offered to their own customers. While decisions on rates are centralised at the level of the Governing Council, the implementation of decisions is decentralised at the level of the NCBs, together forming the operational arm of the Eurosystem on an equal footing. It should be noted here that within the Governing Council, the principle of "one man, one vote" is de rigueur, even if the decision by consensus is preferred. The President of the BCL therefore represents one of 18 votes in monetary policy decisions. However, I would make it clear that each governor takes part in these decisions, not as a representative of his Bank or his country, but in his personal capacity, with a view to making the best decision for the entire euro area. The BCL therefore carries out operations on the financial markets (open market operations). This means, in practice, that it grants loans against securities given as collateral by BCL's counterparties, namely the credit institutions of the Luxembourg financial centre. The interest rate for short-term major loans is the most important monetary policy signal. The Eurosystem also offers credit institutions a possibility for longer-term loans and a system of borrowing or depositing funds on an overnight basis. The only regulatory instrument used by the BCL is to require credit institutions to build up minimum reserves in the form of deposits in account with the BCL. By increasing or decreasing the amount of such minimum reserves, the ECB and the NCBs influence the need for credit institutions to refinance with their NCBs. These monetary policy operations within the Eurosystem are carried by a payment system called TARGET. This system is composed of an interconnection of national real-time gross settlement (RTGS) systems. In Luxembourg, this system is called LIPS-Gross. The BCL thus ensures both the follow-up of developments in existing systems and the execution of payments. In financial markets, and even more so in the context of monetary policy operations, payment systems are inseparable from clearing and securities settlement systems. The settlement of securities transactions involves two flows: delivery of securities and payment. While initially, the delivery of securities was done in a physical form, the vast majority is now done in a dematerialized way, in the form of accounting entries. Securities are located with central securities depositories. Any credit transaction made by the Eurosystem to a counterparty must be against collateral in the form of eligible assets. This rule aims to protect the Eurosystem against potential losses and to ensure equality between counterparties. In Luxembourg, Clearstream Banking has become the national depository for bcL to receive on deposit securities pledged by commercial banks. Financial stability Price stability and financial stability are two inseparable poles. Price stability, by anchoring agents' expectations, contributes to financial stability. Conversely, financial instability can undermine price stability. Thus, for example, an exchange rate crisis can lead to a depreciation of the exchange rate and generate imported inflation. The ESCB's stability tasks are twofold: to contribute to the policies of the competent authorities on the prudential supervision of credit institutions and the stability of the financial system and to promote the smooth functioning of payment systems. In addition to monitoring and actively participating in European work, the BCL has set up macroprudential indicators to monitor the overall evolution of the Luxembourg financial system. For six months, from June to December 1998, the BCL incorporated the activity of micro-prudential supervision, i.e. individual financial institutions. The laws of 23 December 1998 entrusted micro-prudential supervision to the Commission de Superviser du Secteur Financier (CSSF). In taking this step, the legislator probably did not imagine that Luxembourg would be the only country in the European Union where this separation would lead to a total lack of bilateral coordination between micro-prudential and macroprudential supervision, the latter corresponding to the supervision of the financial system as a whole and traditionally the responsibility of a central bank. This institutional configuration has created an unpremeditated situation where financial stability no longer assumes the status of a public good, segmentation having taken precedence over coordination, against the current of financial globalization in general and further reducing Luxembourg's low weight on the international scene. Payment systems are the keystone in the irrigation of the economic fabric and financial circuits of an economy. By enabling payments made securely and on time, they contribute to good economic development and contribute to financial stability. Symmetrically, they are a significant source of financial instability. Because of the size of the amounts channelled through them, a default by a counterparty can cause a domino effect qualified as systemic risk. In view of the importance of these infrastructures for the financial system, the legislator has conferred supervision in principle on the CSSF and by exception on the BCL. Within the framework of the payment systems in which it participates, the BCL ensures that the systems comply with the international standards and recommendations in force. The other missions of the BCL The issuance and circulation of monetary signs Beyond the functions it performs, means of payment, store of value and unit of account, money is an element of social cement. This role has become all the more tangible since it was put into fiduciary circulation in 2002, a form that implicitly embodies an essential element inherent in money: trust, necessary for the acceptance of a currency. Thus, central banks have a primary function to play in the construction and maintenance of capital confidence linked to a currency: Warrant low monetary erosion in order to guarantee the purchasing power of a currency; Warrant the quality and incorporation of good security features in banknotes in order to promote their longevity and ensure protection against counterfeiting and; Insure an adequate supply of monetary signs to the economy. While the first imperative is, as we have seen, the main objective of the Eurosystem, the other two do not remain behind, on the contrary. The security features are the result of sophisticated techniques and make the euro at least as secure a banknote as the safest of the banknotes that have previously circulated in national monetary areas. The BCL issues and puts into circulation the euro banknotes, but only puts the coins into circulation, on behalf of and in the name of the State Treasury, the issuance of which is the responsibility of the latter to date. Production of statistics The BCL also plays an essential role in the collection of statistics, which is indispensable in the strategy as well as in the execution of monetary policy. For example, the BCL compiles national broad monetary indicator data aggregated at the euro area level and forming the analytical basis for the first pillar of the monetary policy strategy. It also collects and provides a large number of economic and financial statistics to the Eurosystem, used under the second pillar. In the context of monetary policy, the calculation and monitoring of the minimum reserves to be set up by counterparties with the BCL is essential. In addition, it produces statistics on the financial centre, the use of which is essentially confined to a national level. The BCL was therefore instructed by the legislator to set up, together with Statec, Luxembourg's balance of payments. Beyond a simple statistical record of the economic transactions of an economic zone with the rest of the world, the balance of payments is of major interest for economic policy. Economic analysis The BCL, like any central bank, has a research department. As such, it participates in the national economic debate. Its independence allows it to make analyses without being subjected to political pressure. Studies produced by staff or teams of researchers are the result of research carried out within the framework of the ESCB or targeted in the light of current economic debates in Luxembourg. In addition to study books, the BCL publishes its newsletter and its annual report. International cooperation and the provision of services to third parties The BCL also contributes to Luxembourg's representation at international level, like the other European central banks. The BCL's action gives priority to multilateral monetary and financial contact with a Luxembourg presence as well as bilateral contact with the countries or regions of activity of national cooperation. The BCL's involvement also covers two other areas: technical assistance and the provision of services to central banks outside the ESCB and to international and even supranational institutions. The BCL has, for example, become, through its expertise, a regular active player and appreciated in the context of seminars organized by the ATTF (Financial Technology Transfer Agency). In terms of financial services, BCL offers its know-how in the management of reserves, securities and cash for the same categories of institutions. Cooperation with the actors of the Luxembourg financial centre As an intermediary with the Eurosystem and an institution anchored in the Luxembourg financial landscape, the BCL is keen to closely involve economic actors. In order to establish a dialogue for information and consultation purposes, the BCL has set up various working committees which it organizes in the fields of statistics, market operations, payment systems, monetary signs, legal issues and information technology.

Title: Structural reforms and monetary policy
text: STRUCTURAL REFORMS AND MONETARY POLICY by Mr. Serge Kolb, Director of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg at the conference on THE POLITICAL ECONOMY OF THE LISBON AGENDA", 12 and 13 april 2005 in Luxembourg Seule la parole prononcee fait foi Over the past years, the Governing Council of the ECB has constantly stressed the need to press ahead with structural reforms in the goods, services, capital and labour markets . Central banks are convinced that structural reforms are crucial to a better performing EU economy, i.e. an economy with higher potential growth, more employment opportunities and greater resilience to shocks." Progress in structural reforms will also help to bolster consumer and business confidence over a shorter horizon" . The benefits of structural reforms in the context of monetary policy Structural reforms, in addition to their impact on the real economy, may be of relevance for the transmission of monetary policy. They may even facilitate the single monetary policy and augment its effectiveness. Structural reforms may contribute significantly to an improved economic performance in terms of adjustment to shocks, in particular by raising price and wage flexibility. As prices and wages become more sensitive to market conditions, they adjust faster than before -when rigidities prevailed -to changing economic conditions. The higher flexibility avoids the accumulation of past shocks, stabilises the economy and simplifies the issues which monetary policy must face. Structural reforms can therefore have significant consequences for the transmission of monetary policy decisions to final demand and prices. In less flexible economies changes in policy interest rates feed through to prices only after a longer time. Empirical studies on the effects of monetary policy in both the euro area and the United States show that the impact of monetary policy on prices is much faster in the US. One explanation for this finding could indeed be that prices react more flexibly in the US . More flexible labour and product markets result in an improved adjustment to economic shocks and a swifter response to given policy impulses. Hence, increased labour and product markets flexibility may clearly entail that monetary policy actions can be of a lesser magnitude and a lower frequency. For instance, increased flexibility in labour markets might mitigate second-round effects as adverse supply shocks are adjusted to with a muted increase in inflationary pressures over the short-term. The higher flexibility brought about by structural reforms accelerates the speed of the adjustment from the Keynesian" short run (adjustment via quantities rather than prices) to the classical" long run. Accelerating the adjustment to the long run has the advantage that the economic adjustment is increasingly shifted to the price and wage side of the economy. Under such circumstances, monetary policy can achieve price stability with a lesser impact on the real variables such as output and employment. More concretely, empirical observations show that an increase in competition resulting from the implementation of structural reforms in the euro area has as a consequence, among other things, that the Eurosystems monetary policy becomes indeed more effective, because the sacrifice ratio (i.e. the cost in foregone output required to reduce inflation by 1 percent) decreases considerably. Monetary policy is clearly easier to implement if output losses stemming from the compression of inflation are modest. This gain in effectiveness of the monetary policy arises from the fact that enhanced competition reduces the monopolistic power of both producers and workers, and hence these actors ability to confine their respective supplies in order to increase prices and wages . Price stability -the primary objective of monetary policy -provides guidance to economic actors as to a better allocation of production factors towards alternative uses. Price stability thus assists the structural reform efforts to realise their intended welfare-increasing effects. Also, the acceptance of structural reforms is likely to be higher when the purchasing power is maintained. And, a decrease in relative prices in some sectors ensuing from structural reforms becomes more perceptible, fostering public approval of these reforms. Price stability is thus the most important contribution of monetary policy to the structural reform process. Prices and inflation reflect by and large the competitive situation in labour and product markets. More competition in both these markets will lower relative prices and diminish wage and price pressures. This holds in particular in the services industries, which account for a major part of the economic activity in the euro area. For instance, reforms in the telecommunications sector have resulted in substantial decreases in consumer prices for telecom products . More structural reform efforts in the services industry can further ease price pressures, while establishing conditions favourable to moderate wage developments in line with productivity gains. Finally, the individual euro area Member States cannot use monetary (or exchange rate) policy anymore in order to absorb asymmetric shocks since a single monetary policy is conducted for the euro area as a whole. This entails that such shocks must be absorbed by reallocating resources within the euro area countries concerned and that the burden of adjustment is shifted to other economic policies than monetary (or exchange rate) policy. Hence, the single monetary policy by itself has increased the case for implementing structural reforms in the individual euro area countries. Challenges resulting from structural reforms Structural reforms may constitute a tricky issue for monetary policy as they might alter the fundamental relations that govern the functioning of the economy and hence also the monetary policy transmission mechanism. Changes in long-run trends in macroeconomic variables, which can only be spotted after some time, increase the degree of uncertainty surrounding the economic context in which monetary policy decisions are taken. However, a forward-looking monetary policy has to be aware of changes in potential GDP growth because of their bearing on the equilibrium real interest rate and on the adjustment path towards such a rate. Unfortunately, both potential output and the equilibrium interest rate cannot be observed and their estimates are surrounded by a high degree of uncertainty. The Governing Councils monetary policy decisions are therefore based on a two-pillar approach designed to ensure a full analysis of the risks to price stability, which takes account of all relevant information, in both the economic and the monetary pillar. Conclusions A double conclusion can be drawn from the above reflections, namely that the best contribution the Eurosystems monetary policy can make to the structural reform process is to contribute to maintaining a stable macroeconomic environment which is favourable to carrying out structural reforms, while such reforms in turn can facilitate a successful stability-oriented monetary policy by increasing the responsiveness of the economy to given policy impulses.
