There is a wide scope for a fruitful dialogue at various levels: European, national as well as inside our own institutions. Basically, one should not any more place economic and social visions in mutual opposition. They are interrelated. The schematic view according which the global economy is run by and for the rich (capitalists and bankers) against the poor (workers) is not relevant. Our globalised economies need good governance. In this context, central banks have a role to play but in a process of checks and balances with other powers. Europe has invented a new independent central bank, the Eurosystem, which has proved, after 10 years, not so bad from a social point of view, notwithstanding the recurrent criticisms. Both, the central banks and the trade unions, are in the end working for general interest. They may walk together in the difficult way ahead. We all share the same social values. The monetary union is only one step in the long process started more than half a century ago and having as its objective an ever closer union for the benefit of all. There is still a long way to go to build the European Union. I thank you very much. 21

Title: Sovereign funds: Partners for growth and stability?
text: SOVEREIGN FUNDS: PARTNERS FOR GROWTH AND STABILITY? High Level Panel Conference organised by Crans Montana Forum Palais dEgmont Brussels 2nd April 2008 Contribution of Etienne de Lhoneux Secretary General Banque centrale du Luxembourg Eurosystem (The spoken-word-prevails) Introduction Ladies and Gentlemen, I am particularly pleased to have been invited to provide a central bankers view in contributing to the debate on sovereign funds. So far the Eurosystem has not adopted an official position1 but it is fully supporting the European common approach as proposed by the European Commission and endorsed by the European Council on the 14th of March. In particular, among the five principles put forward by the Commission, we underline the importance of the commitment to an open investment environment and the respect of European and international law. The European Monetary Union was based on the free movement of capital, both internally and externally. We know that this principle does not constitute an obstacle to new measures aiming at a smooth functioning of the markets; on the contrary, the present financial turmoils demonstrate the need for better regulation and probably more active involvement of Central Banks in view of financial stability. 1 The views expressed are purely personal and do not reflect necessarily the vision of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg or of the Eurosystem. I wish to thank in particular Mrs Onenne Partsch for her precious assistance. 08/04/2008 In my capacity as central banker, I wish especially to analyse the phenomenon of sovereign funds in the light of the objectives and tasks traditionally conferred on central banks (namely, the pursuit of price and financial stability, the conduct of monetary policy, the holding and management of official foreign reserves and the conduct of foreign exchange transactions) and ask how sovereign funds fit into this picture. In this perspective, the question of the interaction between sovereign funds and central banks arises, not only at a functional but also at an institutional level. At a functional level, the question arises of how to ensure an optimal intervention of central banks and sovereign funds in order to efficiently contribute to price and financial stability: should there be mechanisms of cooperation or consultation between sovereign funds and central banks? At the institutional level, the question arises whether some of the institutional guarantees (such as independence, accountability, transparency, immunity, prohibition of monetary financing) should be made applicable to sovereign funds. The international role of the euro is expanding rapidly; it belongs to money to monitor carefully the development. The SWFs are diversifying the investment, are contributing to the development of the international use of the euro. The development of sovereign funds is often presented as a shift from central bank foreign reserve assets into sovereign funds. This is not the situation in Europe. In the euro area, one of the basic tasks of the central bank is to hold and manage the foreign exchange reserves of the Member States. The governments are only allowed to keep working balances. Management of reserves by central banks has proved to be beneficial. These reserves are essential for the performance of central banks functions; they also provide the State, in its capacity of shareholder of the central bank, with regular incomes. Sovereign funds appear to be intimately linked to central banks, not only because of the origin of some of their funds, but also because their investment strategy should contribute to the price and financial stability of the all economies and be compatible with central banks policies. 1. Economic and fiscal context of the creation and development of sovereign funds 2 08/04/2008 The creation and rapid development of sovereign funds does not come ex nihilo2 Sovereign funds have been established in a very specific economic environment namely: 1/In resources-rich economies which have been benefiting for the last few years from high oil and commodity prices. These funds have as objective to stabilise government and export revenues and, frequently also to build up financial savings for future generations; 2/In countries, notably in Asia, which have experienced substantial build-ups in international reserves. Moreover, countries with SWFs, usually have a great exposure to dollar, be it the currency of denomination of the revenues (e.g. in the oil industry), the currency to which the domestic currency is pegged or because of the dollarisation of official and/or private cross-border assets. They may be tempted by a diversification, notably in euro denominated assets. Finally, the wealth generated in these countries is so huge that it cannot be absorbed by the domestic financial markets, which are comparatively underdeveloped and immature. It is usually difficult, in these circumstances, to keep the monetary conditions balanced; these parameters create a great exposure to the turbulence of currency market, increase inflationary pressure and give rise to potential shocks to the balance of payment. Specific measures, such as the conduct of foreign exchange transactions, combined with the possible sterilisation of foreign exchange interventions may be taken in order to keep the monetary conditions balanced. The conduct of such transactions, which are not always available and/or efficient in all countries, may, however, not be sufficient to keep the monetary conditions balanced. The foreign reserves are usually invested in AAA-rated, highly liquid and relatively low yielding assets, such as Treasury bills and bonds3. It should be stressed, however, that the pace of official reserve accumulation clearly outpaces the net issuance of the most traditional reserve assets (such as US Treasury, US Agency debt, euro area government securities, UK Treasury), so that 2 IMF definition includes both Government-owned and Government-controlled funds while the OECD seems to limit the definition to Government-owned investment vehicles only, see October 2007 edition of the Investment Newsletter, OCDE 3 See ECB Occasional Paper No. 43, February 2006, The Accumulation of Foreign Reserves, p. 8. 3 08/04/2008 the increased diversification of these foreign reserves may, to some extent, be inescapable4. Some countries are tempted to move the excess of foreign reserves to sovereign funds thereby escaping strict reserves investment policy and moving towards more flexible but more risky investment strategies. Depending on the founding principles governing these sovereign funds, they may seek better returns, more diversified allocations with higher stakes in equities, currency diversification and a wider geographical dispersion. Most sovereign funds seem, for instance, to diversify their exposures globally instead of allocating their assets in specific countries or economic zones. Besides, sovereign funds may seek to diversify their portfolios among the different asset classes (including non-tradable or non-public shares) with, potentially, a longer investment horizon (central banks being mostly guided by liquidity motives in their investment policies due to very shortterm liabilities stemming from the nature of their mandate). Finally, sovereign funds may opt for investment strategies which are more risky than a typical central bank. Thanks to the greater flexibility offered to sovereign funds, these may pursue purposes, as various as smoothing fiscal revenues (in stabilisation funds in oil producing countries), intervening as second line of defence in the context of currency crisis, recapitalising the state-owned banks in China, repaying the external debt in Russia, funding investment in Taiwan, elsewhere saving part of the oil revenues for future generations. 2. Interaction between sovereign funds and central banks: functional and institutional levels Having identified that sovereign funds may be intimately linked to central banks, not only because of the origin of some of their funds, but also because of their investment strategy, they may contribute to the price and financial stability of the domestic economy, the question of the interaction between central banks and sovereign funds now arises. 4 For example, even if emerging market central banks had purchased the total net primary issuance of these traditional reserve assets in 2007, they would still have had roughly USD 742 billion left over to invest. 4 08/04/2008 At a functional level, although sovereign funds may pursue very diverse objectives (including higher return, saving oil revenues for future generations), they may also be involved in operations traditionally entrusted to central banks, such as the management of foreign reserves (e.g., GIC in Singapore), the intervention as second line of defence in the context of currency crisis (e.g., GIC in Singapore and KIC in Korea) or the recapitalising of domestic or foreign banks, which may be seen as similar to lender of last resort function. In other cases, such as in Russia, the creation of the stabilisation fund has been perceived, in its effects, as a substitute for sterilisation. It has been considered, however, that such a measure can be no substitute for sound, medium-term-oriented fiscal policies and that the current monetary and fiscal policy frameworks and instruments need to be further adjusted if progress is to be achieved in keeping inflation under control in the period ahead. These examples show that although they may be complementary with central banks tasks, interventions of sovereign funds may sometimes relieve the short-term pressure on a domestic government and deter the latter from taking the appropriate steps as far as monetary and exchange rate policy are concerned in the longer term. This brings us to the sensitive relations between monetary policy and exchange reserves (entrusted to financially, institutionally and functionally independent central banks) and the fiscal and economic policy, entrusted to the government, the latter being nevertheless, encouraged to conduct sound national fiscal policies in order to avoid undue inflationary pressures and distortion in the definition and implementation of monetary policy by the central banks. The due separation between monetary policy and exchange rate policy, on the one hand, and fiscal and economic policy, on the other hand, is usually based on the concept of independence of central banks, the latter exercising their powers and carrying out their duties without intervention of government or any other body. Such independence is, however, counterbalanced by the concept of accountability, the central bank being fully responsible for the proper discharge of its obligations, strict transparency and auditing requirements applying in this respect. It should be stressed, however, that one of the most prominent features of the sovereign funds, established as Government controlled public agencies, is, precisely, 5 08/04/2008 that they create unprecedented bridges from monetary and exchange rate policy to fiscal policy. This is clearly not acceptable since this may not only endanger the independence of central banks (potentially moving away from the latter the financial means necessary for the due performance of its obligations) but also distort the efficiency of its monetary policy and exchange rate policy. In addition, this would also discourage the home government from adopting sound fiscal measures in order to achieve, in the long term, a truly stable economic environment, conducive to lasting growth. In view of the above, and as far as the intervention of sovereign funds may overlap with traditional central banks tasks, it would be appropriate to consider creating mechanisms of cooperation (be it in the form of exchange of information, consultation or cooperation) in order to coordinate the respective interventions of the former and the latter, in the due respect of the independence of the central banks5. In any case, sovereign funds should abide by strict transparency requirements, so as to allow all relevant stake holders to identify, analyse and appropriately assess the consequences of their intervention on monetary policy, exchange rate policy, and the economic and fiscal policies of a country. Nowadays the involvement of central banks in financial stability matters is increasingly a substantial part of their activities; the slide 6 annexed to the presentation shows, outside the transparency and corporate governance requirement, some specific concerns with regard as financial stability. As positive element is mentioned the broadening of long-term investments, the contribution to the global risk sharing is the fact that typically, SWFs are not leveraged. The main concern is related to the interference of non economic motives and as a consequence, possible distorsion of price mecanisms, the inevitable risk of herding behaviour, for large amount as well as abrupt sales of assets or modification of currency distribution. In order to fulfil their tasks and monitor financial activity, central banks require highquality statistical information from the investment funds6. 5 In Norway, the Sovereign wealth fund is a remakable example; by vertu of the law, the central bank of Norway is interested with the managment of the fund. 6 This is the reason why the Governing Council of the European Central Bank has adopted last year the regulation No 958/2007 of the ECB of 27 july 2007 concerning statistics on the assets and liabilities of investment funds. 6 08/04/2008 Although this may be difficult in practice, it should also be considered whether additional institutional guarantees usually applicable to central banks in the performance of their duties (including independence, accountability and potentially, immunity of jurisdiction and of execution) should not be applied to sovereign funds when intervening in support of central banks activity. The management of foreign reserve assets by Eurosystem central banks enjoys specific legal protection. The prohibition of monetary financing makes these reserves unavailable for financing government budgets. Their management is transparent7. The Central Bank Gold Agreement provides also good example of transparency. We know that according to the US Foreign Sovereign Immunity Act 1976 (FSIA) the property of a foreign central bank or a monetary authority shall be immune from attachment and from execution, unless there is an explicit waiver by the central bank. More and more European States have adopted legislation in view of protecting foreign reserve assets in Europe. This is especially the case in Luxemburg where a new law of 2007 has granted a very generous immunity regime to foreign assets held with the Luxembourg central bank by third countries or foreign central banks8. Moreover, my central bank is, together with five other Eurosystem central banks, developing new reserve management services, in accordance with a guideline of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank of 7 April 2006, to the benefit of third countries or their central bank. 3. Conclusion Sovereign funds are a multidimensional phenomenon, which we have approached, in this talk, from the view point of the tasks traditionally entrusted to central banks. 7 Most Central Bank report their foreign reserves holdings to the IFM (International Monetary Fund) under SDDS (Special Data Dissemination Standard) and publish a annual report. 8 A new article was introduced in the Organic law of BCL by the law of 13 july 2007:  Art. 27-1.(2) No account with the Central Bank intended to be used in the context of common monetary or exchange policies or in the context of the management of foreign reserve assets held for foreign central banks or foreign States may be subjected to any seizure, sequestration or blocking order. According to the European Central Bank:  as the euro is increasingly used as an international reserve currency and in line with recent changes made to the laws of other Member States, the ECB would recommend that this provision clarifies in an unambiguous manner the protection usually granted to foreign reserves held by the BCL by inserting the words as well as of the management of foreign reserves assets held for foreign central banks or foreign States. ECB Opinion of 11 December 2006 (CON/2006/56). . 7 08/04/2008 Sovereign funds have been established in a very specific economic environment, characterised by high volatility of commodity and asset prices in markets with a strong exposure to the dollar; they have to provide certain countries with a meaningful vehicle for diversifying their investment. They have contributed to the maintenance of price and financial stability in the short term, thereby acting as a partner for both growth and stability in the short term. In the longer term and in the interest of a true contribution by sovereign funds to both growth and stability, we would recommend that stake holders, based on a thorough analysis of the global economic context in which these sovereign funds have been established and are operating, recommend and implement the necessary reform in order to effectively remedy the structural deficiencies having led to the current situation. We especially think that countries, confronted with a large surplus, could adopt structural and macro-economic reforms designed to foster domestic demand and enhance financial systems both at domestic and regional level. There is a need to reflect on the possible consequences of a shift from reserve assets to Sovereign funds vis-a-vis exchange rate policies and the conduct of efficient monetary policy. A matter of particular concern is the possible interference of non-economic motives with regard to the control by foreign government. Good governance of Sovereign funds may be inspired by central bank experience. As SWFs are typically State-owned, or at least State-controlled, their transparency and accountability should be exemplary. In any case, we would recommend the greatest caution as to the possible impact on the independence of central banks and the efficiency of both monetary policy and exchange rate policy or the intervention of sovereign funds in tasks traditionally entrusted to the latter. A possible way forward, in the absence of concrete regulatory action at international level, would be the creation of cooperation arrangements between central banks and sovereign funds so as to properly coordinate the respective intervention of the former and the latter in the due respect of the independence of central banks. The efforts of IMF and OECD in view of best practices are of course welcome. Nevertheless within the European Union it may be assumed that the European Institutions should take a leadership position in shaping the regulatory landscape pertaining to globalisation and SWFs. We must ensure that the European Union is the level at which the most efficient regulatory action is taken; a regulatory initiative at UE level is the best guarantee to avoid the fragmentation of capital markets and the protection of purely national interests. Regulatory frameworks should include 8 08/04/2008 adequate information disclosure, in particular full disclosure of asset allocation in term of currency composition and instruments of SWFs, with direct reporting to the Eurosystem. Corporate governance measures could include a regime for the golden shares as well as regulation of services of general interest. It is up to European legislator to provide adequate legislation aiming at protecting the legitimate interests both of the investors and of all our citizens. In this context, further dialogue with the Eurosystem central banks is, in my view, welcome. Thank you for your attention. 9

Title: Liquidity, adjustmen of operational frameowrks and public policy orientation
text: LIQUIDITY, ADJUSTMENT OF OPERATIONAL FRAMEWORKS AND ORIENTATION OF PUBLIC POLICIES By Yves Mersch, President of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg 16th Meeting of the Governors of the Central Banks of French-speaking countries held in Nice from 13 to 15 May 2009 Ladies and gentlemen, dear colleagues, It is a great pleasure for me to be at this 16th meeting of the Governors of the Central Banks ofFrench-speaking countries. In this regard, I would like to thank the Bank of France for its hospitality and organization, and I am delighted to have to share with you these reflections on the current financial crisis. Iwill first address the mechanisms of contagion through liquidity of the subprime crisis, and then present the changes to the operational framework made by the Eurosystem in its liquidity management policy. Finally, I will conclude witha discussion of government responses to the solvency of the banking system and recently envisaged reforms in financial regulation and supervision. (1) Themechanisms of contagion by the liquidity of the subprime crisis The losses recorded through the increase in the default rate on subprime mortgages were relatively small compared to the size of the US financial system. This initial shockof limited magnitude, however, led to an unprecedented liquidity crisis as a result of financial contagion mechanisms. While the abundance of liquidity dominated the debate before the crisis, the sudden drying up of liquidity on the market of structured products has called into question the new way banks operate, which has had the effect of affecting the heart of the financial system: the interbank market. As part of the initiation and distribution model, bankstake loans off their balance sheets by selling them to a specific vehicle (SPV) which assembles them into structured products (ABS, CDO, etc.) and resells them on the market. Securitisation therefore allows banks to increase their source of refinancing, by making illiquid assets held on their balance sheets liquid, while transferring credit risk to financial investors through an ad-hoc legal entity. This financial package 1 The complex process of providing banks with liquiditywhile at the same time satisfying investors' risk appetite has proved highly sensitive to the reversal of the housing bubble in the United States. In general, the initiation and distribution model increased banks' dependence onmarket liquidity, thereby increasing their exposure to liquidity risk, especially since this method of refinancing was based on assets which were mostly devoid of secondary markets and whose he valuation was based on the use of mathematical models. While securitisation enhanced the liquidity of the underlying receivables by transforming them into marketable securities, the financing of operators engaged in the securitisation process was crucially dependent on the continued maintenance of market liquidity. Indeed, the financial fragility of this model was masked by the abundance of liquidity that prevailed before the outbreak of the crisis. Banks have created off-balance-sheet vehicles in order to increase the return on a long-term investment by having it financed in the short term on the financial markets. ABCP conduits and SIVs, which fall into this category, hold structured products and issue asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) to refinance their illiquid long-term securities (in this case structured products). SPVs therefore play a role similar to that of banks by borrowing very short-term and financing high-yielding long-term products, with the difference that these bodies have no capital to absorb shocks (these entities were de facto outside the scope of regulation and supervision), their refinancing activity on the ABCP market being backed by credit lines granted by the banks that set them up. The viability of issuance conduits and structured investment vehicles, which take advantage of yielddifferentials between maturities in their transformation potential, is therefore based, under these conditions, on the assumption of continuous liquidity, i.e. a permanent renewal of its investment by the investor. However, when the increase in the default rate on the subprime market in the United States led to a deterioration in the fundamentals of structured finance products, the complexity and opacity of these securities and the absence, in many cases, of a market price for these instrumentsresulted in valuation difficulties. Uncertainty about the quality of these products then led to a drying up of liquidity in structured product markets (notably the RMBS market) and a refusal by investors to renew their position in the ABCPs market, which led to refinancing problems for SPVs. Off-balance-sheet structures have thus been obliged to obtain liquidity to repay them, either by drawing on the credit lines granted by banks (in the case of ABCPs) or by liquidating part of their assets, which, most often, has resulted in a reintegration of outstanding assets into banks' balance sheets (SIVs). The complexity and opacity of structured products led to a reluctance on the part of banks to participate in interbank transactions. The latter adopted a liquidity-holding behaviour both because of the uncertainties relating to counterparty risk, but also because they were unsure of their 2 own exposure through off-balance-sheet vehicles, whether on securitized receivables or receivables in the process of securitization that had to be reintegrated into the balance sheets or on structuredfinance products held on the assets of these vehicles. In doing so, liquidity in the (unsecured) interbank market dried up and rising risk premia on the money market led central banks to intervene to contain the contagion mechanisms of the financial crisis. The complexity and opacity of structured finance products and banks' increased dependence on market liquidity resulted in a self-sustaining spiralof liquidity ebbs within the financial system. This contagion phenomenon was also aggravated by the accounting of assets at market value and by the reduction of leverage, the latter mechanism being all the more important as credit growth in the euphoric phase of the cycle had been fostered by the undervaluation of credit risk by banks inherent in the transfer of receivables in off-balance-sheet structures. This situation, which deterioratedsharply in September 2008 when the collapse of Lehmann Brothers led to a deep crisis of confidence in the solvency of financial institutions, led to an unprecedented liquidity crisis as banks and other financial institutions refused to lend money to each other. Central banks then had to react by changing their operational framework and the stance of their monetary policy, while many financial institutionswere rescued by national governments. At the same time, this crisis has prompted reflections on the implementation of regulatory and financial supervision reform. (2) Changes to theoperational framework made by the Eurosystem in its liquidity management policy As the crisis developed, the Eurosystem made several changes to its operational framework in order to ease the tensions on the euro money market,i.e. managing liquidity conditions on the interbank money market with a view, as a first step, to steering very short-term interest rates towards a level close to the euro exchange rate. Nominal ission for the main refinancing operations. In particular, extraordinary amounts of liquidity were injected from August 2007 through a combination of short-term and long-term open market operations, as well asthrough internationally coordinated actions in terms of currency swap agreements. This activist policy of liquidity management, based on frontloading reserves at the beginning of the period, then gave way, in a shorttime, to the temporary introduction of an unlimited fixed-rate refinancing procedure from October 2008. This aggiornamento of our operating framework proved necessary to stem the contagion mechanisms of the financial crisistriggered by the bankruptcy of the investment bank Lehmann Brothers. Bank credit accounts for more than 70% of external private sector financing sources in the euro area. The Eurosystem has therefore favoured the banking system asthe transmission channel for its monetary policy. It is for this 3 This is because the unconventional measures taken by the Eurosystem in recent months have been described as a policy of enhanced credit support. Overall, the changes to the monetary policy operational framework, aimed at easing the conditions for access to liquidity for Eurosystem counterparties, can be grouped into seven categories. - Frontloading policy: After theonset of financial turbulence, credit institutions preferred to meet their reserve requirements relatively early in the maintenance period because of signs of a contraction in transactions onlonger-term money market compartiments. In these circumstances, the Eurosystem carried out liquidity frontloading at the beginning of the reserve maintenance period followed by a reduction in the liquidity supply so as to leave the total supply over the entire period in size. The Eurosystem has regularly allocated amounts well above the reference amount in the main refinancing operations, and subsequently carried out fine-tuning operations as soon asstrong downward pressure began to emerge on the overnight interest rate. This policy was applied until 8 October 2008, when the Governing Council announced that the main ref in-funding operations would henceforth be carried out through a fixed-rate tendering procedure, with all bids being paid at the rate applied to the main refinancing operations. - Additional longer-term refinancing operations: Tensions on the money market were observed, not only in the short-term compartment, but also in the longer-term segment, where a very low volume of transactions was reported. In order to promote a normalisationof conditions, the Eurosystem introduced additional longer-term refinancing operations in August 2007, which were gradually extended during 2008. These measures, which resulted in the conduct of four longer-term refinancing operations in each maintenance period (one for the duration of the period, two with a maturity of three months, and one with a maturity of six months), had the effect of increasing the average maturity of the Eurosystem's refinancing operations. At the end of 2008, longer-term refinancing operations accounted for almost 3/4 of the amounts allocated by the Eurosystem to its counterparties. Since the decision of 15 October 2008, longer-term refinancing operations have also been carried out through a fixed-rate tender procedure, with all bids being paid at the rate applied to the main refinancing operations. This arrangement was further extended by the decision of 7 May 2009 since longer-term refinancing operations with a maturity of one year will also be carried out during 2009 (in June, September and December). These operations will take the form of fixed-rate tenders, with all bids being filled. The rate for the first operation, to be announced on 23 June 2009, will be the same as that applied on that date to the main refinancing operations. Subsequently, the tender rate may include a premium over the main refinancing operations, depending on the current situation. 4 - The unlimited fixed-rate refinancing procedure: Following the exacerbation of tensions in all segments of the money market following the collapse of Lehmann Brothers in September 2008, the Governing Council decided, as ofOctober 2008, to introduce an unlimited fixed-rate refinancing procedure for all open market operations, with maturities ranging from one week to twelve months. This measure, which will remain in force for as long as necessary, at least beyond the end of 2009, has eased tensions on the money market; uncertainties about the supply of central currency had led monetary policy counterparties to outbid too heavily in the context of variable-rate tendering procedures. The resulting increase in banks' demand for refinancing also resulted in the emergence of excess liquidity, which was mainly reabsorbed through the use of the deposit facility, which had the effect of keeping EONIA below the rate set for the main refinancing operations. This difference between the overnight rate and the key ECB rate subsequently widened from January 2009, when the Governing Council decided to reduce the standing facilities corridor to its previous level of 200 basis points. whereas the latter had been lowered to 100 basis points in October. For example, the 6-month and one-year EURIBOR rates, which play a key role in the monetary policy transmission mechanisms in the euro area, are currently at lower levels than the rates applied to contracts denominated in US dollars and pounds sterling for identical maturities. - Cross-currency swap operations: Since December 2007, the ECB and the US Federal Reserve have put in place atemporary reciprocal currency swap arrangement under the TAF programme. As a result of this arrangement, the Eurosystem was able to lend US dollar liquidity to euro area banks in exchange for eligible collateral for its credit operations. Since the launch of this facility, the frequency, volume and maturity of these refinancing operations have been gradually increased during 2008. From October 2008, this procedure was again elaboratedsince the ECB, in agreement with the Fed, has now undertaken to supply all tenders in dollars through a fixed-rate tendering procedure for terms of up to 84 days. Since October 2008, the ECBhas also been providing liquidity in Swiss francs to banks in the euro area through a swap agreement with the Swiss National Bank. Banks in the euro area can currently benefit from fixed-rate refinancing in Swiss francs , with the maximum amount for these 7-day operations set at 25 billion per tender. - Extension of the guarantee framework: In view of the previous measures, the list of eligible assets admittedas collateral for Eurosystem credit operations was extended on a transitional basis from October 2008 (until the end of 2010) in order to increase banks' refinancing capacity. To some extent, this decision has also helped to restore liquidity to some markets, as banks have become less reluctant to buy certain securities to the extent that they can now 5 use as collateral with the Eurosystem. In terms of ratings, the critical threshold has been lowered from A- to BBB- and the composition of collateral repo has shifted significantly in favour of less liquid and riskier assets, including structured products (ABS) and non-marketable assets . Marketable debt securities issued in the euro area and denominated in dollars, pounds sterling and yen have also been accepted since November provided that the issuer is established in the European Economic Area. - Expansion of the list of counterparties to the EIB: The European Investment Bank (EIB) will become an eligible counterparty to Eurosystem monetary policy operations on 8 July 2009. From that date, the EIB will have access to the Eurosystem's open market operations and standing facilities through the Banque centrale du Luxembourg on the same terms as other counterparties. The EIB will have to meet all requirements and will have to maintainminimum reserves with the Eurosystem. In particular, this measure will improve the financing conditions for companies in the euro area. - Broadening procedures: On 7 May 2009 the Governing Council decided that the EuroSystem would purchase euro-denominated covered bonds issued in the euro area from banks. Details of the technical details of this operation will be announced after the meeting of the Governing Council on 4 June 2009. This decision, which is part of the Eurosystem's desire to continue its policy of enhanced credit support, will improve the refinancing conditions of banks in the euro area. Overall, the changes to the operational framework made by theEurosystem have resulted in an increase in the size of our balance sheet, which increased by almost EUR 600 billion between June 2007 and March 2009, representing a 65% increase in volume representing just over 6% of euro zone GDP1. During this period, the composition and risk profile of our balance sheet also changed. Appropriate risk management measures have, of course, been implemented in order to limit the risks associated with the expansion ofour guarantee system. The return to normal functioning of the money market is an essential element of the Eurosystem's exit strategy. From this perspective, lowering the key interest rate to close to zero is problematic as itcould prevent normalization as it would reduce the incentive for banks to resume operations on the interbank market. The Eurosystem also attaches great importance to maintaining the credibility of monetary policy in achieving the objective of price stability over the medium term. From this point of view, special sterilization operations will probably have to be carried out when economic conditions warrant. 1 For its part, the balance sheet of the Banque centrale du Luxembourg increased by 23.8 billion between June 2007 and March 2009, an increase of around 47% in terms of volume, representing nearly 65% of Luxembourg's GDP. 6 To conclude, theresponsiveness of central banks and the flexibility of their operational framework have played a key role in preventing the liquidity crisis from turning into a systemic crisis. From this point of view, the package of measures adopted by the Eurosystem has made it possible to ensure continuous access to liquidity for solvent institutions, and thus to mitigate the dysfunctions that have occurred on the money market. However, this role of intermediation in the provision of liquidity can only be temporary, since the Eurosystem is not intended to replace the market and provide liquidity on a massive basis over the long term. Moreover, central bank intervention alone cannot promote normalization in the functioning of the money market, since their operational framework does not address the root causes of liquidity risk, namely counterparty risk concerns and problems of information asymmetry and adverse selection. (3) Public policy direction and systemic risk management The reflection revolves around two axes, the first concerns the current solutions provided by governments to the problem of bank solvency, and the second, preventive measures designed to avoid the recurrence of the problems we are currently facing. On the latter point, prudential regulation and supervision play a key role in improving the transparency of the financial system and inproviding incentive mechanisms to limit the procyclicality of banks' credit supply behaviour.  Solvency of the banking system and public policies Central banks can alleviate the liquidity problem butthey cannot alone address the solvency problem, which is central to restoring confidence and, in so doing, ensuring the normal functioning of the circulation of liquidity in the financial system. National governmentshave assumed their responsibilities in this area, whether through the adoption of rescue plans for institutions presenting systemic risk, or through the adaptation of financial asset accounting standards. Various measures have been implemented by national governments to clean up the balance sheet of the banking system. At the level of liabilities, the measures taken by governments have been based on several tools: (1) an extension of the guarantee of the deposits deposited,so as to avoid a phenomenon of rush to deposits, (2) a strengthening of equity through the subscription of subordinated debt securities or preferential shares by the State, and (3) an improvement in the refinancing conditions of financial institutions by means of a State guarantee for interbank loans and bond market issues. At the asset level, national bailouts have focused on setting up a bad bank structure to relieve banks of their toxic assets. On this last point, the Eurosystem has also defined a set of guidelines to address the main problems relating to the implementation of this type of programme, whether at the level of the category of eligible assets, the 7 valuation and the discount to be applied according to the type of debt held, the conditions to be met to participate ... . In addition, a reform ofaccounting rules was introduced by the European Commission in October 2008 in order to limit the degree of vulnerability of banks' balance sheets to the current situation on the financial markets. Under fair value accounting, banks have hitherto been required to immediately reflect in their accounts the decline in the price of the assets they hold, so that the losses recorded automatically affected their capital position. The reformintroduced by the Commission is therefore likely to improve the stability of the financial system since it allows banks to reclassify certain assets from 'transaction' portfolios, valued at market prices, to 'bank' portfolios,valued at historical amortised cost. It also offers greater flexibility in the calculation of "fair value" for valued assets for which there is no longer a market transaction, and therefore a price reference, since it is nowpossible to estimate the value of these securities from the expected cash flows. Despite this measure, the persistent gap between EU and US accounting standards, in particular since the FASB amendment published on 9 April2009, remains a distorting in the presentation of stress tests and the balance sheet health of financial institutions, a distortion that the Commission should seek to address in the near future.  Financial regulation andprudential change The role of financial regulation and supervision is to preventively prevent a recurrence of the current situation. Different paths have already been identified in this area by international working groups (FSF, Larosiere Group, G20 ...): The initiation and distribution model highlighted the problems of undercapitalization of banks in the face of their off-balance sheet commitments. Prudential regulation must now focus on integratingoff-balance-sheet activities into the definition of the capital ratio with risks taken into account according to the nature of the assets held. In particular, the FSF proposes, in the context of Basel II, to strengthen capital requirements for structured finance products since the understanding of liquidity risk related to these products is complex. More generally, in line with the suggestions made by the Basel Committee and the ESCB Banking Supervisory Committee, currentrisk management practices need to be strengthened so that the financial institutions concerned are able to assess the related risks and, in so doing, build up sufficient reserves to improve their resilience capacity. e in the presence of shocks of a systemic nature. The regulator must therefore focus on defining incentive mechanisms to compensate for the procyclicality of the financial system. In line with the recommendations made by the FSF, this could be achieved, for example, through the introduction of thin provisioning. This ex-ante accounting provisioning, which would consist of anticipating credit risk and spreading the impact of the write-down of receivables over the entire cycle period,would represent in 8 This is a step forward in this area since it would allow banks to build up a safety cushion in times of growth. The current crisis has also revealed the need to extend financial regulation and prudential supervision to non-bank institutions whose activity involves a risk of a systemic nature, such as hedge funds, but also to strengthen the existing capital adequacy framework for insurance companies, notes the those whose activities are linked to structured products markets. In general, the introduction of a structural policy aimed at improving the transparency of the financial system and reducing information asymmetry appears to be fundamentally amental. The creation of a clearing house for CDS in the United States and the euro area is a step in this direction as it will better manage the counterparty risk related to these derivatives. With regard to the proactive roleplayed by rating agencies in the course of the crisis, a reform of the functioning of the latter is currently being studied, whether from the point of view of the conflict of interest which impacts the quality of their rating, or the creationof a differentiated rating scale for structured finance products. given the valuation difficulties and liquidity risk underlying these products. Finally, enhanced coordination and cooperation betweencentral banks and micro-prudential supervisory institutions was highlighted in order to promote better consideration of systemic risk in the prevention of financial crises. With this in mind, the report of the de Larosiere Group submitted to the European Commission recommended the establishment of a new European financial architecture through the creation of two entities designed to supervise risks and strengthen the coordination of the super vision of financial institutions within the EU: a European system of financial supervisors, which would operate on the basis of a decentralised network and which would be responsible for micro-prudential supervision, and a European Systemic Risk Board, within the General Council of the ECB and to which representatives of the European Commission and banking, insurance and securities supervisors would be invited. The latter would be responsible for collecting and analysing all relevant information on financial stability from a macro-prudential supervision perspective. In a similar vein, the Luxembourg legislature has recently assigned to the central bank the task of supervising theliquidity of the markets and its operators at both macro-prudential and microprudential level. This amendment to the statute, which now allows the BCL to fully assume its responsibilities in terms of financial stability, marks animportant step forward in terms of strengthening cooperation and exchange of information between the central bank and the authority in charge of financial sector supervision. Conclusion To conclude, the flexibility of the operational framework of the system hasmade it possible to contain the contagion mechanisms of the liquidity crisis by ensuring adequate access to refinancing to illiquid but solvent institutions; from this point of view, the euro has played an essential role in the management ofthe financial crisis. Governments 9 For their part, they have adopted measures to address the solvency problems of banks and financial institutions posing systemic risk. The combination of these interventions shouldhelp restore confidence and restore an environment in which governments, regulators and supervisors can identify and implement the reforms needed to improve the functioning of the financial system. The current crisis has also highlighted the need to integrate the objective of financial stability into the prerogatives of the central bank, which is able to develop a macro-prudential analysis framework aimed at detecting the formation of financial imbalances. At Eurosystem level, this could be greatly facilitated by the information content of the monetary pillar. The discussions under way, I am convinced, will not fail to lead to fruitful solutions that will prevent the current problems from recurring in the future. Thank you for your attention. 10

Solvabilit du systme bancaire et politiques publiques Les banques centrales peuvent allger le problme de la liquidit mais elles ne peuvent  elles seules adresser le problme de solvabilit qui est un aspect central pour restaurer la confiance et, ce faisant, assurer le fonctionnement normal de la circulation de la liquidit au niveau du systme financier. Les gouvernements nationaux ont pris leurs responsabilits dans ce domaine, que ce soit  travers ladoption de plans de sauvetage des institutions prsentant un risque systmique, ou encore au niveau de ladaptation des normes de comptabilisation des actifs financiers. Diffrentes mesures ont t mises en uvre par les gouvernements nationaux pour assainir le bilan du systme bancaire. Au niveau du passif, les mesures prises par les gouvernements ont repos sur plusieurs outils : (1) un largissement de la garantie des montants dposs par les pargnants, de manire  viter un phnomne de rue vers les dpts, (2) un renforcement des fonds propres  travers la souscription de titres de dette subordonnes ou dactions prfrentielles par lEtat, et enfin (3) une amlioration des conditions de refinancement des institutions financires par le biais dune garantie par lEtat des prts interbancaires et des missions de titres sur le march obligataire. Au niveau de lactif, les plans de sauvetage nationaux se sont focaliss sur la mise en place dune structure de dfaisance destine  soulager les banques de leurs actifs toxiques. Sur ce dernier point, lEurosystme a dailleurs dfini un ensemble de lignes directrices pour adresser les principaux problmes affrents  la mise en place de ce type de programme, que ce soit au niveau de la catgorie dactifs ligibles, de la 7 valorisation et de la dcote  appliquer en fonction du type de crance dtenue, des conditions  remplir pour y participer . En outre, une rforme des rgles comptables a t introduite par la Commission europenne au mois doctobre 2008 de manire  limiter le degr de vulnrabilit du bilan des banques face  la situation actuelle sur les marchs financiers. Dans le cadre de la comptabilisation  la juste valeur, les banques taient jusqu prsent contraintes de traduire immdiatement dans leurs comptes la baisse du prix des actifs quelles dtiennent de sorte que les pertes enregistres affectaient automatiquement leur position en capital. La rforme introduite par la Commission est donc susceptible damliorer la stabilit du systme financier puisquelle permet aux banques de reclasser certains actifs des portefeuilles de  transaction , valoriss au prix de march, vers des portefeuilles  bancaires , valoriss au cot historique amorti. Elle offre galement une plus grande souplesse dans le calcul de la  juste valeur  pour les actifs valoriss pour lesquels il ny a plus de transaction de march, et donc de rfrence de prix, puisquil est dsormais possible de faire une estimation de la valeur de ces titres  partir des flux financiers attendus. En dpit de cette mesure, lcart persistant entre les normes comptables europennes et amricaines, notamment depuis lamendement FASB publi le 9 avril 2009, demeure une source de distorsion dans la prsentation des tests de rsistance et de la sant du bilan des institutions financires, distorsion que la Commission devrait sefforcer de combler dans un avenir proche.  Rglementation financire et supervision prudentielle Le rle de la rglementation financire et de la supervision est dviter, de manire prventive, que la situation actuelle ne se reproduise. Diffrentes voies ont dores et dj t identifies dans ce domaine par des groupes de travail internationaux (FSF, Groupe de Larosire, G20) : Le modle dinitiation puis de distribution a mis en avant les problmes de souscapitalisation des banques face  leurs engagements hors-bilan. La rglementation prudentielle doit dsormais sattacher  intgrer les activits hors-bilan dans la dfinition du ratio de capital avec une prise en compte des risques en fonction de la nature des actifs dtenus. Le FSF propose notamment, dans le cadre de Ble II, de renforcer les exigences en fonds propres pour les produits de financement structur tant donn que lapprhension du risque de liquidit relatif  ces produits est complexe. Plus gnralement, dans la ligne des suggestions effectues par le Comit de Ble et le Comit de surveillance bancaire du SEBC, les pratiques actuelles de gestion du risque doivent tre renforces de manire  ce que les institutions financires concernes soient  mme dvaluer les risques affrents et, ce faisant, de se constituer des rserves suffisantes pour amliorer leur capacit de rsilience en prsence de chocs de nature systmique. Le rgulateur doit ainsi sattacher  dfinir des mcanismes incitatifs destins  compenser la procyclicit du systme financier. Conformment aux recommandations formules par le FSF, cet objectif pourrait par exemple tre atteint par le biais de lintroduction dun provisionnement dynamique. Ce provisionnement comptable ex-ante, qui consisterait  anticiper le risque de crdit et  taler lincidence de la dprciation des crances sur lensemble de la dure du cycle, reprsenterait en 8 effet une avance dans ce domaine puisquil permettrait aux banques de se constituer un matelas de scurit en priode de croissance. La crise actuelle a par ailleurs rvl la ncessit dtendre la rglementation financire et la supervision prudentielle  des institutions non bancaires dont lactivit comporte un risque de nature systmique, comme par exemple les Hedge Funds, mais galement de renforcer le dispositif existant en matire dadquation des fonds propres pour les compagnies dassurance, notamment celles dont les activits sont lies aux marchs de produits structurs. De manire gnrale, la mise en place dune politique structurelle destine  amliorer la transparence du systme financier et  rduire lasymtrie dinformation apparat fondamentale. La cration dune chambre de compensation pour les CDS aux Etats-Unis et dans la zone euro est une mesure allant dans ce sens puisquelle permettra de mieux grer le risque de contrepartie relatif  ces produits drivs. Concernant le rle procyclique jou par les agences de notation dans le droulement de la crise, une rforme du fonctionnement de ces dernires est actuellement  ltude, que ce soit du point de vue du conflit dintrt qui impacte la qualit de leur notation, ou encore de la cration dune chelle de notation diffrencie pour les produits de financement structurs, tant donn les difficults de valorisation et le risque de liquidit sous-jacents  ces produits. Enfin, un renforcement de la coordination et de la coopration entre les banques centrales et les institutions charges de la surveillance micro-prudentielle a t mis en avant de manire  favoriser une meilleure prise en compte du risque systmique dans la prvention des crises financires. Dans cette perspective, le rapport du groupe de Larosire remis  la Commission europenne a prconis la mise en place dune nouvelle architecture financire europenne  travers la cration de deux entits destines  superviser les risques et  renforcer la coordination de la supervision des tablissements financiers au sein de lUE : un systme europen de superviseurs financiers, qui fonctionnerait sur la base dun rseau dcentralis et qui serait en charge de la surveillance micro-prudentielle, et un conseil europen du risque systmique, au sein du Conseil gnral de la BCE et auquel seraient invits des reprsentants de la Commission europenne ainsi que des superviseurs de la banque, de lassurance et des valeurs mobilires. Ce dernier serait charg de rassembler et danalyser toutes les informations pertinentes concernant la stabilit financire et ce dans une optique de supervision macro-prudentielle. Cette modification de statut, qui permet dsormais  la BCL dassumer pleinement ses responsabilits en matire de stabilit financire, marque une avance importante sur le plan du renforcement de la coopration et de lchange dinformations entre la banque centrale et lautorit en charge de la surveillance du secteur financier. Conclusion Pour conclure, la flexibilit du cadre oprationnel de lEurosystme a permis de contenir les mcanismes de contagion de la crise de liquidit en assurant un accs adquat au refinancement  des institutions illiquides mais solvables ; de ce point de vue, leuro a jou un rle essentiel au niveau de la gestion de la crise financire. Les gouvernements 9 nationaux ont quant  eux adopt des mesures destines  agir sur les problmes de solvabilit des banques et des institutions financires prsentant un risque systmique. La combinaison de ces interventions devrait permettre de restaurer la confiance et de rtablir un environnement dans lequel les gouvernements, les rgulateurs et les superviseurs pourront dfinir et mettre en place les rformes ncessaires pour amliorer le fonctionnement du systme financier. La crise actuelle a par ailleurs mis en exergue la ncessit dintgrer lobjectif de stabilit financire dans les prrogatives de la banque centrale, celle-ci tant  mme de dvelopper un cadre danalyse macro-prudentiel visant  dtecter la formation des dsquilibres financiers. Au niveau de lEurosystme, cette dmarche pourrait tre largement favorise par le contenu informationnel du pilier montaire.
