Title: The crisis - from the point of view of a central banker
text: Mr Yves Mersch Chairman of Banque centrale du Luxembourg The crisis - from the point of view of a central banker Speech at the symposium of the WGZ in Luxembourg 25. September 2009 - The spoken word is valid - 1 1. Welcome Ladies and gentlemen, I gladly accepted the invitation to the symposium of the WGZ and would like to welcome you all to today's event. In my speech on "The crisis - from the point of view of a central banker" I would like topresent to you various reflections on the financial and economic crisis. 2. Development, causes and current status of the financial and economic crisis The crisis began in a localised, specialised financial market segment, intensified andultimately materialised in the global turbulence on the financial, goods and labour markets visible today. The current financial and economic crisis was triggered in the US market for second-class mortgage loans at the beginning of 2007. During the first half of 2007, the first banks ran into difficulties. Subsequently, there was turbulence on the money and capital markets, accompanied by declining liquidity and increasing volatility. At the beginning of 2008, the continued existence of various international banking institutions was in question. On September 15, the US investment bank Lehman Brothers filed for Chapter 11 creditor protection. This was followed by a crisis of confidence in the global financial markets and the interbank market came to a standstill. The crisis now spread to the real economy in its entirety. It is clear that the downward momentum of the crisis was reinforced by the global economic interdependence of financial markets, as well as structural factors which had a cumulative effect on the crisis. Of crucial importance were, for example: - Global imbalances, such as the chronic indebtedness of individual economies and their financing via international financial markets, - thesignificant erosion of the carrying amount of assets on banks' balance sheets as a result of fair value devaluation, with negative effects on their capitalisation, particularly 2 the relationship in the case of structured securities, whose lack of transparency, complexity and risk leverage are generally relatively high, - inadequacies in the analysis and assessment of risks, such as the interaction of credit and liquidity risks at institution level, resulting in a misjudgement of risk-bearing capacity, - the volumes of financial derivatives - and in particular credit derivatives - as well as off-balance-sheet vehicles, and Execution of bank-related transactions by non-banks and their risk prevention. 3. International crisis management In contrast to the global economic crisis of the 1930s, the measures taken in the current crisis are based on a high degree of international coordination and a countercyclical orientation. Unconventional measures have been taken to provide liquidity to financial markets in order tomaintain the functioning of the money and capital markets in the short term, as well as to avert a systemic crisis and, in particular, a credit crunch by the Eurosystem and other major central banks. This response was swift and decisive, using the room for manoeuvre and respecting monetary policy objectives. There were alsoeconomic policy interventions and interest rate cuts. The measures must be described in detail as follows: - Since the outbreak of the crisis in 2007, the Eurosystem has been improving the provision of liquidity by banks in additionalliquidity-providing operations by: - The standard monetary policy instrument, the interest rate on main refinancing operations with the ECB, was reduced by a total of 325 basis points to 1% within a few months from October 2008, - In order to provide foreign currency liquidity, theEurosystem, in cooperation with other central banks, has provided substantial liquidity, in particular in USD and CHF. The frequency, volume and maturity of these refinancing operations were continuously expanded during 2008. 3 - Following the collapse of Lehman and interbank trading, the Eurosystem introduced a new mode for open market operations. counterparties of the Eurosystem were provided with virtually unlimited liquidity at the key interest rate; - fixed-rate tenders with amaturity of 12 months have been introduced, - the collateral requirements applicable to financial institutions in the case of - The number of counterparties involved in refinancing operations with the Eurosystem has been increased, - A purchase programme for issued Euro Pfandbriefe has been implemented. Governments also took stabilising measures as a result of macroeconomic imbalances. They intervened in the market by recapitizing viable banks or nationalizing non-viable institutions, but also by taking measures in non-financial sectors; support programmes are estimated to total almost 24% of EURO GNP. The combined action of the measures taken has helped to cushion both the economic downturn and the impact on labour markets. One indicator is the record fall in money market interest rates in June of this year. 4. Exit scenarios In order to limit monetary policy conflicts, it is necessary to design and schedule the termination of expansionary aid programmes at an early stage. I would like topoint out that although crisis management has led to an increase in liquidity, this will not lead to inflationary effects as long as these funds are parked at banks or central banks and do not lead to a significant expansionof credit. In order to limit the potential for undesirable developments as a result of the interventions taken during the crisis, it must be necessary to initiate a suitable exit strategy in due course. On the one hand, it will involve raising the lowlevel of the key interest rate. 4 On the other hand, the reduction of other, in particular liquidity-related aid and thus also liquidity absorption is important. The system of European Central Banks has the technicalcapacity to absorb this liquidity, even beyond the many support programmes that expire automatically. The exit process must be given critical importance. In principle, three economic scenarios are conceivable in terms of timing and output: - there is a parallel increase in the money market and the economy, - the restoration of the functioning of the money market is a priority for the - The risk of price inflation increases before the stabilisation of the Money market. The overall success of crisis management must be ensured by a sensitive approach to returning to normality. Exit scenarios must be adapted to the current economic reality and should be based on a balancing of the following key points in particular: An inevitable consequence of crisis management was that the interbank market was essentially replaced by the Eurosystem as an intermediary. An exit can therefore only be carried out once the functioning of the interbank market has been sufficiently ensured again. If different institutions are still unable to refinance themselves on the money market, systemic risks due to possible domino effects persist. At any rate, it can currently be stated that excess liquidity in the banking system is still comparatively heterogeneously distributed. Accordingly, deposits of some credit institutions on sight deposit accounts with the Eurosystem have increased, while other few financial institutions remain dependent on liquidity-supporting measures by central banks. There are also risks associated with the choice of exit date in the context of the economic cycle. If this is done too early, a credit price increase can have negative spillover effects on the financial sector and the real economy, for example, leading to a "double-dip recession" after a short recovery phase. Similar developments occurredin the 1930s and 5 1980s in the United States and in the 1990s in Japan. If the turnaround is made too late, this may stand in the way of adequate monetary developments and the monetary policy objective of price stability. Afuture economic overheating or excesses in the financial markets could be substantiated in this way. In the timing of the exit, international coordination is also essential in order to avoid a W-shaped economic development of individual countries. At present, an unexpectedly rapid recovery of the French and German economies in the 2nd quarter of 2009 contrasts with a declining, albeit persistent, recession in almost all EU member states, such as in the Eastern Europeancountries. Furthermore, further economic setbacks, such as a deterioration in credit quality, cannot be ruled out and could lead to a further aggravation of the situation. The sustainability of banks' partly surprisingly positiveearnings development and macroeconomic trends does not yet appear to be assured at the present time. In particular, the high interest income can be explained by the low refinancing rates that are significantly below average in the long-term trend and a steep yield curve. Valuations have also absorbed some of the downward movement resulting from reduced depreciation. Although recent examples show that banks have access to new capital through capital markets, for example to replace state aid, it remains to be confirmed that these are not just isolated cases. Finally, effective communication and the implementation process are also relevant when exiting. In termsof confidence, it is important that the markets are also sufficiently prepared and that a monetary policy turnaround does not take place abruptly, but in appropriate, internationally coordinated steps. 5. Implications of the crisis for the Luxembourg financial centreLet me now focus on Luxembourg and present some specific findings relating to a local financial centre. The economic integration of a financial group with local units can havespecific consequences for the host country in times of crisis. 6 Financial institutions are group-controlled in many business policy matters. For reasons of efficiency, cash and cash equivalents are managed by central financial management in many corporations. Thecentral trading departments provide parts of the Group with liquid funds from the "cash pool", which is fed by liquidity surpluses from all parts of the company. If, for example, the refinancing of decentralised units is also based on customer deposits,surpluses are transferred to the liquidity pool at the end of the business day. In the event of liquidity problems, the group may withdraw liquidity from subsidiaries or not all companies may be supplied with liquidity in the same way. As a result, liquidity gaps can occur in local units. In the event of tight liquidity, the implementation of ringfencing secures the solvency of individual companies. As a result, these funds are not available in the general liquidity pool for other parts of the group, which a priori exacerbates the liquidity situation of other business units in the group. Unfortunately, I have found that the setting of group intra-group ratios by foreign banking supervisors has had an impact on Luxembourg subsidiaries, whereas in Luxembourg we have so far refrained from restricting intra-group loans. Finally, if a banking group collapses, there may be different burdens at national level. Experience has shown that the host countries of the local Group units are often particularly burdened; an EU-wide compensation scheme should be sought here. The is in line with the requirement that it should be ruled out that, owing to asymmetric burden-sharing for governments affected by banking difficulties, the overall measures taken may not correspond to macroeconomic requirements. Finally, in order to ensure the necessary liquidity at the level of the local banking centres, the introduction of a limitation of maturity transformation - for example in the form of liquidity ratios - must be discussed. The crisis management in Luxembourg was aimed at identifying existing deficits in the short term and immediately initiating measures, in particular to provide and monitor liquidity. 7 Liquidity is the monetary lubricant of economictransactions. Any restriction of the supply of liquidity to financial markets leads almost immediately to disruptions to the economy and the financial system. Since there are historically hardly any reference cases for the crisis scenario that has occurred, liquidity monitoring has beenpractically not on the radar screen of the financial supervisory authority until now. In the meantime, various governments, including Luxembourg's, have launched a process to intensify prudential supervision of liquidity. The law of 24 October 2008 entrusted Banque centrale du Luxembourg (BCL) with monitoring the general liquidity situation of the markets as well as the liquidity risks of banks, insurance companies and other financial institutions active in the financial market, e.g. in the asset management sector. The aim is to ensure a high level of transparency on an ongoing basis regarding the supply of liquidity to the financial system and the real economy in order to disclose tendencies of liquidity shortages or restrictions on the functioning of the interbank market at an early stage. It is also about maintaining the transmission channels of monetary policy measures. In view of the economic context of the liquidity situation, capitalisation and capitalisation,it is also necessary to monitor the development of the solvency and indebtedness of financial undertakings. From a macroeconomic point of view, fulfilling this task contributes to safeguarding financial stability. There is also a need to examine and, if necessary, further develop the governance, processes and procedures of liquidity management of the financial sector in Luxembourg. It is important to monitor and manage liquidity risks at local unit level in the future. For this purpose, systematic evaluations, some of which are daily reports, the implementation of stress tests and the formation of risk reserves are unavoidable. In this context, close cooperation between BCL supervision and banking supervision and insurance supervision appears to be an important component. Financial institutions in Luxembourg responded to the crisis last year by reducing their debt. 8 The impact of the crisis on the financial sector in Luxembourg was particularly evident in the decline in the volume of business by financial institutions. The banks' aggregate balance sheet total decreased by around 100 billion or 11% between June 2008 and June 2009. Paid-in capital increased by Euro 3.7 billion, or 10%, over the same period. At the same time, institutions were deleveraged: the leverage ratio - defined as the ratio of Tier 1 capital to total assets - improved moderately during this period from an average of 5.2% to 5.6%, but is distributed quite heterogeneously due to different business models: In June 2009, 14% of banks had a leverage ratio of less than 3%. These institutions account for approximately 4% of the total capital held in the banking centre and approximately 15% of total assets. By contrast, 38% of institutions have a leverage ratio of over 6%; these account for approximately 47% of the capital and 22% of the assets in the banking centre. Allow me to make a further point on possible mismatch individual economic objectives of parent companies of local units and the macroeconomic objectives of their host countries. Smaller financial institutions whose business activity consists in the provision of general financial services in the sense of a "local universal bank" regularly have a systemically important function for the payment transactions of an economic area. If this institution is acquired by international financial groups, especially those witha higher degree of specialisation, essential local services are sometimes discontinued. This can have negative implications for the functionality of a region's payment transactions. Also, the balance sheet total is often managed centrally and bad credit is transferred to balance-sheet units. Financial analysts are withdrawn from decentralized units for cost reasons and local management does not have sufficient information on its own balance sheet. Although centralised liquidity management aims to manage risks optimally, I wonder whether, as with some securitisation structures, transparency may not be lost as a result. In fact, monitoring efficiencyalso means 9 Proximity. The management in the host country must be able to take full responsibility for its balance sheet, both within the group and vis-a-vis the local supervisors. 6. Further development of the international regulatory framework The improvement of the regulatoryframework for the creation of a more crisis-resilient financial system is currently being implemented. The current political discussion at national and international level on setting new standards for banking regulation and financial supervision aims to identify and limit systemic risks in the future, as well as to substantially reduce the likelihood or extent of potential financial and economic crises. At the beginning of this month, central banks and supervisors agreed on reforms in the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, such as new global standards for capital and liquidity, as well as limits on the leverage of financial institutions. It is planned todraw up a detailed catalogue of measures by the end of the year. The capitalisation of some financial institutions has been significantly eroded during the financial crisis as a result of high write-downs. Since it was often impossible to raise new equity, governments madecapital available. By tightening capital requirements, it is now intended to ensure that banks' debt is in line with their risk-bearing capacity in the future. With regard to systemically relevant institutions, it is discussed to impose capital requirements depending on the size, interconnectedness or risk content of the business activity. This is intended to prevent large financial institutions, in particular, from being able to virtually enforce public support measures to mitigate systemic effects. In addition, a proposal on "dynamic provisioning", i.e.dem building up a capital buffer in the event of good economic development as a reserve for crisis periods, is currentlybeing discussed. In addition, institutions should observe debt ceilings in order to improve their creditworthiness. The monitoring of the debt of financial institutions should be the responsibility of the central banks. 10 In recent years, it has been establishedthat some banks had financed long-term assets largely at short notice and that the realisation of liquidity reserves - in the form of assets classified as liquidable - was only possible to a limited extent during the crisis. For this reason, central banks and supervisory authorities in Basel have come to the conclusion that minimum international requirements for the liquidity of banks in financing transactions should be defined, with the aim of limiting risks through maturity transformation. The definition of liquidity ratios will become important here. The task of monitoring systemic liquidity risks is the responsibility of the Eurosystem central banks. The Central Bank of Luxembourg will base its liquidity monitoring on the analysis of meaningful, timely and regular reports on the liquidity situation. This provides a dynamic picture of the current liquidity situation, the expected cash flows and the coverage gaps structured according to running bands. The frequency of the reports is determined by the BCL individually for each institution. Decisions on the restructuring of micro- and macro-prudential financial supervision are expected shortly. On the basis of the report presented in February this year by a group of experts led by Jacques de Larosiere, the decision was taken in favour of a new framework for European financial supervision. As a result, it will be networked and further developed on the basis of the following elements: micro-prudential financial supervision, the European System of Financial Supervision (ESFS), will consist of a network consisting of national supervisory authorities and the three new agencies for the supervision of banks - the European Banking Authority (EBA), for stock exchanges - the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) and for insurance companies - the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority" (EIOPA). Ongoing micro-prudential supervision will remainin the hands of national authorities. In addition, the EU Commission intends to provide the EBA with far-reaching powers, such as issuing direct instructions to financial institutions or intervening directly in financial markets. 11 Another task of EU financial supervision is to develop European supervisory standards for national supervisory authorities. Financial obligations for national budgets of EU Member States, such as through auxiliary actionsfor institutions, should not arise from EBA measures. By further developing and institutionalising macro-prudential supervision, systemic risks can be better addressed across countries. Based on the report of the de Larosiere Group, the creation of an independent institution, the European Systemic Risk Council (ESRB), with responsibility for macro-prudential supervision in the EU was initiated. The central task of the ESRB will be to analyse and monitor systemic risks, to draw attention to significant risks and to make recommendations for action. However, the implementation of these recommendations should lie with national authorities. The European Systemof Central Banks (ESCB) will have a key role to play in setting up the ESRB, providing analytical, statistical, administrative and logistical support from central banks. The Board of the ESRB would be composed in particular of the 27 Governors of the General Governing Council, the ECB President and his representative, as well as the Chairmen of the three new European Supervisory Authorities to be established with voting rights and, per country, a representative of the national supervisory authorities without voting rights, which alternate according to topic. The effectiveness of the ESRB requires close cooperation between micro- and macro-prudential financial supervision of national and EU authorities. This also implies the need at national level to organise cooperation between financial supervisors and the central bank for joint preparatory work for the ESRB. In addition, close cooperation is to be established with international institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and the Financial StabilityBoard. 7. Conclusion Let me end with a few basic considerations. 12 Although some uncertainty remains, there are now indications that the recession has bottomed out. A moderate recovery with positive growth is expected for 2010. However, it can be assumed that this growth will not be sufficient to fully compensate for the economic downturn in the foreseeable future. Thereis a risk that the long-term development path of growth potential has been seriously affected by the crisis. There is currently no credit crunch. Rather, the decline in lending is due to the recenteconomic downturn and reduced demand for credit due to lower corporate investment. The future of the Luxembourg financial centre in the coming years will be marked by the inevitable consolidation of thebanking sector in the banks' home countries, such as Germany. This will have an impact on the number of institutions domiciled in Luxembourg, but not necessarily on the volume of business. One lesson from the financial crisis should be that excessivedevelopments on financial markets sooner or later lead to macroeconomic imbalances, which in turn cause considerable damage to confidence as well as considerable economic costs. Since these are consequently also borne by the financial community, its employees and shareholders, I would like to promote the recognition that the current process of further developing the regulatory framework for the financial markets creates a win-win situation for all parties involved. In addition, financial stability is a public good to which monetary policy institutions and financial supervision in particular are committed. In order to ensure this asset on an ongoing basis, the instruments will have to be adapted continuouslyand flexibly to developments in the financial sector in the future. The prerequisite for this is an up-to-date information base on developments on the financial market and an efficient organization of the institutions of financial supervision as well as their close cooperation, both at national and international level. The latter should also include, for example, cross-border cooperation in the event of distress of multinational financial companies. 13 Thank you for your attention. 14

September 2009 - Es gilt das gesprochene Wort - 1 1. Begrung Meine sehr verehrten Damen und Herren, der Einladung zum Symposium der WGZ bin ich gerne gefolgt und begre Sie alle recht herzlich zur heutigen Veranstaltung. In meiner Rede zum Thema Die Krise - aus der Sicht eines Zentralbankers mchte ich Ihnen verschiedene Reflexionen zur Finanz- und Wirtschaftskrise vorstellen. 2. Entwicklung, Ursachen und aktueller Status der Finanz- und Wirtschaftskrise Die Krise begann in einem lokal begrenzten, spezialisierten Finanzmarktsegment, verschrfte sich in Schben und materialisierte sich letztlich in den heute sichtbaren globalen Turbulenzen auf dem Finanz-, Gter- und Arbeitsmrkten. Die aktuelle Finanz- und Wirtschaftskrise wurde Anfang 2007 in den USA am Markt fr zweitklassige Hypothekenkredite ausgelst. Whrend des ersten Halbjahrs 2007 gerieten erste Banken in Schieflage. Title: Central banks and macro-prudential stability
text: Central banks and macro-prudential stability by Mr. Serge Kolb Member of the Management Board 17th Meeting of Central Bank Governors of French-speaking Countries May 13-14, 2010 Montreal, Canada The informative role of the recent crisis  For economists, shocks are often seen as exogenous phenomena to the real or financial sphere. It's something that comes from elsewhere (from heaven maybe!). This approach is equivalent to the Solow residue for productivity or the introduction of shocks into general equilibrium models. This brings me back to aggregate risk analysis. The latter are currently modelled as exogenous factors with linear processes. However, the recent crisis has shown that risks have developed within the financial sphere. And their amplification is explained by the interdependence of actors and markets. In other words, they are endogenous to the system and their accumulation would be dictated by a complex and non-linear process. In this context, it is essential to improve our understanding of the emergence and accumulation of risks within the system.  The seconde let of the crisis is the importance of the interaction between the financial and real spheres. Real shocks are relegated to second place and the reaction of many has given the impression that the nature of the The recent crisis was a new phenomenon. However, the world has experienced multiple crises of the same nature (crisis of 1929, Asian crisis, banking crisis in the Nordic countries, real estate and banking crisis in Japan). What all these crises have in common is the accumulation of financial risks. The accumulation of risks in the financial sector is not neutral for the real economy. The reverse is also true.  The third element revealed by the crisis is the revival of Minsky's thesis on the explanationof the credit cycle. According to recent studies, it appears that the excess volume of credit allocated to the economy during the period 2002-2007, a period of favorable cycle, contributed significantly to the crisis and the reversal of the cycle. Moreover, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision recently proposed the adoption of a macro-prudential instrument that consists of the establishment of a capital buffer for banks, the level of which will depend on the ratio of outstanding loansto the GDP of each country.  Excessive debt and risk-taking through investments in complex financial products have played a significant role in the fragility of the financial sector. The dispersion of risk by theso-called securitisation and/or business model, in this case the originate-anddistribute model adopted by certain institutions, was illusory. The maintenance of links with SPVs (special purpose vehicles) through largeoff-balance-sheet liabilities was a determining factor in explaining the liquidity problems after the outbreak of the subprime crisis.  All these elements have revealed that the existing system of micro-prudential supervision is insufficient. Its effectiveness has even diminished in the face of the complexity and speed of financial innovation. Moreover, the pure microeconomic approach is in no way adapted to the detection of systemic risks likely to affect non-institutionalinstitutions. financial in an individual way, but the financial systems as a whole.  The recent crisis has provided considerable impetus for macro-prudential supervision. And theongoing reforms of the supervisory architecture at EU level will enable the system to be based on two pillars, which are micro- and macro-prudential supervision. A two-pillar system, but what will be the content of the newmacroprudential pillar?  Before giving an overview of the future role of central banks in macroprudential supervision, let me dwell for a moment on some of the underlying difficulties in implementing such an approach.  The multiplicity of definitions attributed to financial stability is corollary to the absence of a commonly accepted definition. As a result, financial stability remains a vague economic concept. However, it is importantto stress that everyone agrees that financial stability is by no means synonymous with immobility. Rather, it reflects the absence of abrupt and significant movement that could destabilize the system as a whole. It is to beassessed through the analysis of systemic risk.  The objective can be broken down into two elements: - improve the soundness of the financial system ("resilience") - mitigate financial cycles ("lean against the financial cycle") The BCL adopted theEurosystem's definitiation: "Financial stability is a situation in which the financial system, which encompasses financial intermediaries, markets and market infrastructures, is able to withstand shocks and absorb financial imbalances, thereby minimising the likelihood of the emergence of disruptive factors that could jeopardise an efficient allocation of savings". Despite the attractiveness of this definition, it requires additional elementsto arrive at a macroeconomic model incorporating this notion of stability. Given this difficulty and the multidimensional nature of financial stability, the various studies are limited to an approximation of financial stability by sectoral variables, such as probability of default, market risk,... Nevertheless, it would be difficult to accept the idea that the adoption of a single variable would be able to capture all the factors of instability. This creates an additional difficulty, which is the delimitation of the boundaries of the content of macro-prudential supervision and the instruments that may be adopted. Why central banks need to be involved in macro-prudential oversight Why are central banks, whose main mission is price stability, concerned with issues related to financial stability and macro-prudential supervision? There are many reasons for theneed for central bank involvement. The first are substantive arguments: The recent crisis has revealed that the money or interbank market is a powerful channel for the transmission of liquidity shocks. And any dysfunctionin this market would have an impact on the level of interest rates and the availability of liquidity that could affect the effectiveness of monetary policy. Moreover, during the crisis, central bank money replaced that of the interbank market. The second important argument, which should merit future research, relates to the optimality of monetary policy in the presence of a fragile financial system. In other words, how can the search formonetary policy optimality be reconciled with financial instability? It seems that in times of turbulence and/or crisis, the objective of stabilizing the financial system dominates that of price stability. Nevertheless, it must be borne in mind that the objectiveof price stability is in no way in opposition to financial stability. Finally, financial innovation and the growing role of financial markets have favoured the dominance of new channels of monetary policy transmission compared to traditional channels in an intermediation system in which thecredit or interest rate channel was dominant. Indeed, financial markets, the importance of risk-taking, regulation,... have become important channels in the transmission of monetary policy. This development has led some economiststo suggest that financial asset prices should be included among the objectives of central banks. This would imply the adoption of contrarian actions by central banks in times of asset price bubbles ("lean against the wind"). However, this issue is subject to much skepticism and it continues to punctuate debates between orthodox and heterodox without any consensus and/or convergence of views on the relevance of the models to be adopted. As for the rules being prepared in Basel in terms of equity requirements, leverage and liquidity, they will certainly have an impact on the transmission mechanisms of monetary policy. It is a new channel that can be described as the 'regulation constraint channel'. The second category of elements in favour of the involvement of central banks in this area are arguments of form. It consists in the fact that: Central banks are responsible for supervisinginfrastructures (payment systems, securities settlement systems,...). In many cases, they have responsibility for micro-prudential supervision and, in some cases, they have a particular responsibility for supervising the liquidity of markets and participants. Finally, they have developed experience in financial stability or macro-prudential analyses; Such knowledge is reflected in many specific publications or in financial stability journals. What role for central banks to ensure macroprudential stability? After describing the case for central bank involvement in macroprudential supervision, the natural question that follows relates to the role to be attributed to central banks. Everyone agrees that the main task of central banks in this area would be to identify potential risks at aggregate level through the establishment of a system ofadvanced risk detection indicators, the choice of macro-prudential instruments and the issuing of warnings and recommendations in the presence of systemic risk. In this context, two major problems need to be solved: The first relates to thechoice of macro-prudential supervisory instruments, while the second concerns the potential conflict between monetary policy and financial stability requirements. Macro-prudential instruments The Committee on the Global Financial System at the Bank for International Settlements recently conducted a survey of 33 central banks to count the macroprudential instruments adopted in the different countries surveyed. It appears from this survey that the instruments used are rather micro-prudential in nature, but have a systemic purpose and therefore aggregated at the level of the entire sector concerned, in this case the banking sector. It also seems that the instruments adopted ineach country are dictated by the characteristics of their own economy. In other words, it would be difficult to adopt the same instruments for all countries. For example, it is more appropriate to adopt the ratio of credit to GDP in countries where the intermediation sector is dominant in the financing of the economy (bank-based system), whereas in a country where financing through the financial market is important (market-based system), other criteria will bemore appropriate. Furthermore, the choice of instruments should take into account the importance of interactions between macro-prudential policy instruments and sector-specific instruments. Indeed, macro-prudential policy and its instruments are in permanent interaction with the various components of economic management (monetary policy, fiscal policy, and sectoral specificities). This dynamic can generate conflicts between the objectives of the macro-prudential policy and those of fiscal or monetary policy. I will confine myself to monetary policy. Macroprudential and monetary policy: a potentially conflictual relationship In principle, the success of monetary and macroprudential policies is the ultimate goal. It is synonymous with price stability and financial stability. However, the conduct of these two policies is not an easy task. It requires a deepening of the coordinationof the two policies and potentially fine-tuning to minimise divergent actions. For example, in the presence of an acceleration in the volume of credit to the economy induced by rapid growth in aggregate demand, both policies are likely to act in the same direction. However, in the presence of a positive productivity shock, monetary policy is likely to become less restrictive due to lower inflationary pressures, while macro-prudential policyis likely to become more restrictive in response to the accumulation of financial risks induced by lower interest rates and the improvement in financial assets due to the productivity shock. A second source of conflict can beattributed to the lever of action of each policy. For monetary policy, it is the regulation of aggregate demand, while macro-prudential policy favors the conditions of credit supply. This divergence is potentially conflictualinsofar as the regulation of credit supply conditions affects the amplitude of the financial cycle and thus the effectiveness of the interest rate instrument in adjusting aggregate demand. In this context, it seems to me that the reconciliation of the two policies will depend on the degree of involvement of monetary policy in regulating the financial cycle. Finally, it should be stressed that the new approaches, which are beginning to take shape, will still require significantinvestment at both academic and institutional levels in order to put the new concepts on a solid footing.

Title: EBA day 2010 - Introductory remarks
text: Introductory remarks by Pierre Beck, member of the BCL Executive Board on the occasion of EBAday 2010 Euro payments conference and exhibition Luxembourg, 26 - 27 May 2010 Ladies and Gentlemen, First I would like to say how honoured I am to speak to this distinguished audience. 1. Why is SEPA still so important? Although I do not expect that there is still a need to convince the audience and the public at large of the benefits of SEPA, I nevertheless wish to underline the multiple challenges that SEPA has represented and still represents. SEPA is one of the most complex industry wide projects that the financial sector has carried out in recent years. From a political viewpoint SEPA is rather simple, not to say self evident: why indeed should a payment in a monetary union and in a single market area be more complex, slower and more expensive than a similar payment in a domestic context? To be in compliance with this very basic principle, it meant however that payment instruments, procedures and payment systems, which were very efficient in a national environment but not interoperable, needed to be harmonised and interconnected or extended to a European-wide reach. This raised not only technical issues but also legal ones and the European Member-States agreed in 2007 on the Payment Services Directive to give the whole endeavour the necessary legal support. Most of this work is well underway, but a lot of implementation work needs still to be achieved. 1 Therefore SEPA remains an important and sensitive project, especially in these days of crisis and economical uncertainty. SEPA is together with the Euro notes and coins a tangible element of economical integration for European citizens and corporates. A partial success of SEPA would not be satisfactory for the European integration. SEPA covers foremost retail payments. As such it is of relevance for consumers and the corporate sector, especially for SME. The benefit of SEPA for SME are the following: (i) fees of cross-border payments at a similar level than those of domestic payments (ii) legal certainty all over Europe, (iii) speed of execution, and (iv) standardization which makes the processing of payments easier not only for the banking sector but also for a corporate on both ends of a payment transaction. SEPA will thus be a strong support for increased cross-border trade within the monetary union. 2. Why is SEPA not yet there? If one looks at the progress made in the various SEPA work streams, it seems that there is more progress achieved in small countries than in the large ones. This might be due to the fact that smaller countries have more incentives, because they have a higher share of cross-border activity. 2.1. SCT These incentives worked well for SCT where existing products (like the crossborder payment) were replaced by the European Credit Transfer. 2 (source ECB internet site) The red line on the chart shows the share of SEPA credit transfers (SCT) in the inter-bank domain as a percentage of the total volume of credit transfers (CT) - that is credit transfers in the "old" as well as in SEPA format. The higher the value of the indicator, the higher the usage of the newly introduced SEPA product. The value of the SCT indicator has increased significantly in March 2009 due to the start of operation of a new system in Slovenia which will replace an existing one; most of the traffic has already migrated to SCT. Although the relative increase of SCT is reassuring, the overall share of SCT is still far from being satisfactory and will require a close monitoring to make sure that an appropriate dynamic will remain. The next slides present the share of SEPA Credit Transfer (SCT) transactions as a percentage of the total volume of all credit transfer transactions initiated in a country (i.e. credit transfer in the legacy format as well as SCT). The first slide presents the situation in the euro-area countries whereas the second deals with the non euroarea EU countries (euro transactions only). 3 Indicators of the usage of SCT as a percentage of all CT transactions per country (euro area countries) Indicators of the usage of SCT as a percentage of all CT transactions per country (non-euro area countries) It is worth noting that in general large countries have more difficulties than the smaller countries to generate high SCT volumes. There are however exceptions in 4 particular UK and DK which have reached a remarkable level of SCT usage. It seems to indicate that those countries which modernise their payment infrastructure switch in one go the core of their payment infrastructure to SCT. 2.2. SDD - The use of the SEPA Direct Debit is still insignificant. This is due to the fact that direct debits did not really exist on a cross-border level until now. The new scheme SDD is hence a new product which might be the reason why it is difficult also for small countries to implement. Furthermore, some countries have not yet launched this new instrument (for instance France  plans to start migration in 2010, Spain in June, the Netherlands in July, etc.) - An important date in this respect will be the November as regulation 924/2009 (repealing Regulation 2560/2001) will force banks (i.e. payment service providers) that accept national direct debits in euro to accept incoming SDD trans- actions ensuring the compulsory reachability of SEPA Direct Debit transactions. 2.3. Cards The European central banks have encouraged the payment card industry to setup a truly European card scheme. The industry has responded with three initiatives: - EAPS: a common initiative of existing card schemes - Monnet: an initiative of banks - Payfair: an initiative closer to the retailers These initiatives take different approaches, have different focuses and are at different levels of maturity. EAPS processes transactions, Payfair has successfully tested its processing in controlled retail environments and Monnet has set the year end for a go / no go deadline for its project. Each initiative has pros and cons but have in common to be confronted to the cost of entry to market in an environment of capped income flow and high fraud levels. Recent statistics show that in several countries, fraud has been on the increase. This is the case for two main types of transactions: - cross-border transactions account for 3 to 6 % of the transactions but for 50% of the fraud, 5 - card-not-present transactions, i.e. web-based, account for 5% of transactions but sees fraud growing very quickly. Fraud increases despite the migration to the EMV security standard (which is also at the basis of SEPA for cards). The ECB SEPA indicators show that EMV migration for cards and point-of-sales terminals has reached respectively 70% and 80% at the end of 2009 in the EU, but covers dissimilar situation ranging from 10% to full-migration. In the euro area, only 50% of the transactions at POS are EMV-based Cross-border fraud is largely due to the lack of global coverage of the EMV standard and the liability shift which penalises the weakest link in card processing. The fraud issue has become a global question, leading to further considerations such as the need or not of the magnetic stripe on the SEPA cards and the geographical reach of a European scheme. To sum up, in the field of SEPA for cards, we note the following facts: The dominance of big non European players (mainly in credit cards but also entering debit cards), the fraud issue and the slow progress of new initiatives. 3. New technologies Security of payments, especially when it come to cards, in the remote environment is even less satisfactory. There is a need to increase consumers confidence in ecommerce and the related payment transactions. Technical innovation and new user-friendly but secure access channels will give SEPA new impetus (see e/m-SEPA) and answer the need for sufficient security. It can even change European payment habits and increase efficiency when combined with other improvements like e-invoicing. Benefits could be fully reaped only if solutions are widely available and interoperable. Hence the Eurosystem, the community of central banks which are in charge of the euro, is prompting the banking community to issue a framework for electronic payments, which provides for online payments with a payment-guarantee for web-retailers based on a SEPA Credit Transfer. This framework should contain minimum operational and technical requirements and ensure interoperability among e-payment schemes. Ideally, each bank in SEPA is a member of (at least) one SEPA compliant e-payment scheme and any account holder in SEPA can make SEPA e-payments. The approval of the SEPA e-Payments Framework is planned for June 2010. 6 Another major event coming up the next month will be the first meeting of the SEPA Council. It will gather all the stakeholders of SEPA, i.e. consumers, merchants, SMEs, corporates, public administrations, the Commission and the ECB, with the Eurosystem in restricted representation. The objective of the SEPA Council is to foster consensus on the next steps towards the realisation of SEPA. 4. Conclusions This short update on SEPA and on side-issues linked to the migration to SEPA displayed several topics which will be discussed in the panel discussion later on. The Eurosystem welcomes the fact that the industry looks beyond SEPA to upgrade present systems and procedures and to innovate, but we also support its endeavour to optimise the financial supply chain for both sides: buyers and sellers. Finally, as a representative of a central bank which has recently been entrusted with the supervision of the liquidity management of various financial institutions, I note with satisfaction that this conference aims to provide the audience with a better understanding of liquidity management and its link with the payment activity. Ladies and Gentlemen, I thank you for your attention and whish you fruitful discussions. 7

Title: Towards a strengthening of global financial stability: lessons from the crisis for Europe
text: Institut d'Etudes Europeennes et Internationales du Luxembourg Fourth Norbert von Kunitzki Memorial Lecture "Towards a strengthening of global financial stability: lessons from the crisis for Europe" by Yves Mersch President of the BCL Luxembourg, 7 February 2011 Excellencies, President of IEEI, Director of IEEI, Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to begin by thanking the IEEI for the invitation to deliver a speech in memory of Norbert von Kunitzki. On this very day when we accompanied to his final resting place Edmond Israel, another friend and influential thinker, I would like to pay tribute tothe memory of N. von Kunitzki who passed away prematurely. Our country is sorely lacking in these free, learned and critical spirits, able to form a personal opinion, based on extensive and multidisciplinary knowledge and capable of calculatingthese teachings to the dimension of our environment of the greater region. I was recently able to borrow from Norbert one of these images and formulations of which he had the gift: "Is God Luxembourgish?" (title of a series of articles). 1 A few years ago, Norbert and Edmond spontaneously accompanied me in the launch of the association "The Bridge Forum Dialogue", convinced of the need for us Luxembourgers to open our windows widely and to take advantage of the international wind toventilate our fixed convictions. It is with this in mind that Norbert has also worked within the IEEI and I would like to pay tribute to the Institute's action in bringing together in Luxembourg the greatest minds, particularly in economic matters and international relations. More than three years after the first turmoil in the interbank markets, we see that we have faced the most serious crisis since the end of the Second World War. As the crisis is not over, we still lack the hindsight to draw up a complete list of lessons to be learned from these events. My intervention will deal with the causes of the financial crisis, the political reactions to the crisis, and its likely consequences. As a member of the Governing Council of the EuropeanCentral Bank, I will draw on European experiences and challenges and on the role of monetary policy in particular. 1. Causes of the crisis As Socrates said in his time, if you want to understand a phenomenon, you must start by giving it a name. My definition of a market failure is a situation where the market fails to allocate its resources efficiently. "A market failure tends to occur: (1) information orinformation literacy is imperfect or asymmetric; 2) when goods and services are differentiated; 3) when resources are stationary; 4) when market participants 2 operate in non-competitive markets (monopole, oligopoly); 5) when goods and services cannot be supplied in sufficient quantities to supply the market; 6) when external costs and benefits (externalities) are not taken into account and have to be borne by society as a whole instead of only by market agents; or 7) when public services are provided by private agents who demand economic benefits in return1.  As regards the causes of the crisis, it goes without saying that a systembased on the theory of 'rational expectations' and 'efficient markets' has collapsed. These concepts formed the intellectual basis of the political trend supporting continuous financial deregulation for more than 30 years. Our general equilibrium models are able to reflect reality perhaps in the long run and in peaceful times, but have not been able to anticipate crises, failing, imperfect, inefficient and not at all self-regulating markets in theshort and medium term. A first dimension of the research aims to make corrections and additions to the models. They are enriched by the frictions inherent in finance, the fact that all economic agents are perfectly rational are called into question, the limits of arbitrage are recognized, whichshould ensure that prices reflect at all times the fundamental price of a credit asset, i.e. cash flow adjusted for the risk price, the opacity of certain markets and an asymmetry of information are recognized. This imperfect information mainly concerns counterparty risk in the face of accounting standards capable of hiding the essential. Minsky and Kindleberger are interested in applying their description of boom-bust cycles to financial innovations. The effect of the indebtedness of actors on the price behaviour of the assets themselves is examined. A second dimension recognizes that economics must borrow from other disciplines. Behavioural finance integrates the teachings ofhuman scientists to chip away at the rational agent hypothesis. This research, which applies to both individuals and financial institutions, investigates the consequences of 1 The "causes of the crisis" section is largely inspired by de la Dehesa,Guillermo (2010): Twelve market and government failures leading to 2008-09 financial crisis, occasional paper n80, Group of Thirty, Washington. Not all direct citations are indicated as such for better readability. 3 Such as excessive self-confidence, good self-image, group thinking or conformism, dispersion of responsibility, particularly in relation to securitization. The third dimension is econophysics. Itis inspired by Mandelbrot's teachings of physics or fractional mathematics. This is the most fundamental criticism since it doubts the existence of a single balance that accounts for everything. Isn't our understanding of markets as limited as that of all the complex systems around us? Aren't there multiple changing equilibria according to chaos theory? This work has found power laws that invalidate the distribution of probability in finance. They observe the presence of very large institutional investors in relatively illiquid markets. They see interference, loops, interdependencies. They note that in fact most transactionsare not carried out by the agents themselves but by persons acting for those with different interests. So economic agents are not similar but heterogeneous, so it is futile to try to compress everything into a single systemof general equilibrium. A new ABM (agent-based models) school, at the intersection of economics, game theory and computer science, based on multi-agent systems has emerged. I retain that markets far from being perfect, agents far from being rational and limited knowledge make a lot of uncertainty and invite a lot of modesty in our economic "science". According to Frank Knight, uncertainties are unknown unknowns, as opposed to the unknowns we have identified and call risks. I close this degression on economic thinking and return to the causes of the crisis. Among the economic activities, it is the banks,I am thinking above all of the investment banks, which are primarily responsible for the failures observed. Four characteristics make banks key players in a market economy: 4 First, billions of payments requiring remittances are made daily by banks. They manage the payment systems that underpin economic transactions. Second, banks and other financial intermediariesborrow small amounts from depositors or other savers to lend large sums to investors, thereby exposing themselves to interest rate, maturity transformation and counterparty risks that make them highly vulnerable to abrupt changes in economic conditions. Banks are therefore a particularly risk-taking public service. Thirdly, these entities undertake tasks which are necessary and essential for the proper functioningof the economy, passing on savers' resources to investors and transferring risk from those who cannot afford it to those who willingly accept it. They are expected to have the information required to carry out thisintermediation. Fourth, banks are essential for the implementation of monetary policy. Monetary policy is the most appropriate economic policy to mitigate the impact of fluctuations and economic cyclesand to maintain price stability. By taking excessive risks, banks have failed in their role as intermediaries, which requires a very high level of confidence on the part of depositors and investors. However, thefirst failure is to be attributed to the US government, which has tried to encourage very broad access to household property by allowing each American family to obtain mortgages without taking into account their level of income or their ability to repay, thereby creating a problem of "adverse selection" by which results are the opposite of those desired because of information asymmetries. 5 Central banks have also had their share of responsibilitywith excessively long periods of artificially low interest rates, encouraging excess liquidity that has inflated prices in various asset classes, including stock markets and real estate. The European Central Bank is a tiny saint in this church. Interest rates have never been as low in Europe as elsewhere, and I vividly remember that several heads of state rebuked the European Central Bank when it raised them after the last cycle. Investors are also to blame for their previously unmatched greed. Some investors managed very large portfolios of bank, pension or insurance assets and hedge funds and were therefore expectedto have a great deal of investment expertise - expertise as high as the commissions they received. How is it possible that so many of these "expert" investors agreed to buy these structured products withdouble or triple A ratings without understanding their content because of the incredible mathematical complexity characterizing their structure? The only reason they bought these products was that they allowed a higher return thanx traditional products rated AAA- or AA-, which appears to be a real contradiction in terms of financial theory. Another failure observed at both the market and government level was related to credit rating agencies thatassess the risks of bankruptcy and non-one-time repayment associated with assets issued, bought and sold in the markets. These credit rating agencies were privileged in that they could not be prosecuted. In other words, they were not responsible, judicially or administratively (unlike the auditors), for the notes they gave because they were protected by the First Amendment of the US Constitution: their employees were consideredmere "financial reporters" exercising their freedom of expression. 6 Another weakness of the crisis was the failure of supervisors. In most cases, the largest bank failures and recapitalisationswere observed in countries where supervision was not carried out by the central bank but by the government. However, market failures cannot be attributed solely to economic agents, whether in the private or public sector. Instruments, corporate policies and controls were deficient. Look for example at the famous "originate and distribute" model in the so-called "subprime" mortgage or subprime credit market. On the one hand, most of the loans were not issued by banks but by agents and brokers working on commission, who were not subject to supervision and who only needed a local licence to work in the sale of financial products. Thus, their sole objective was to get families to sign loan agreements and pocket the commission without worrying about whether or not these families had the means to repay their loan. On the distribution side, many bankssecuritised loans and resold them as complex products to driving vehicles, which led them to believe that they were thereby avoiding any credit risk - a belief which was generally proved to be false in mostcases, as banks often granted lines of credit to these vehicles. In other words, banks created a parallel, off-balance-sheet accounting system that transformed short-term resources into risky long-term assets that were neither regulated nor subject to any supervision. Investors who bought these same structured products based on "subprime" loans agreed to bear the risk and the financing of these loans, because the risk wasundervalued. If the Federal Reserve System and the European Central Bank had forced banks to reintroduce these securities into balance sheets (which should never have been removed initially), banks would have had to use capital they didnot have. That would have 7 resulted in an even greater credit crunch than we have seen. What is most significant of all is that without these complex products and the parallel system created, never would a malfunction in the US securitised subprime credit market have affected European banks with such intensity. An even more significant problem is that "many banks have failed to manage their risks. Sometimes, as I mentioned earlier, they acted under pressure from shareholders who wanted a greater return on investment; sometimes the remuneration system encouraged excessive risk-taking. Other times, the heads of financial institutions thought that their long-term financing would remain cheap given the low level of interest rates . Good risk management starts with common sense and prudence, not complex models understood by a handful of physicists or mathematicians. I now come to the problems linked on the one hand to the incredibly rapid development of OTC derivatives markets,both for interest rates and the foreign exchange and lending markets, which have reached historic levels; and on the other hand to the shortcomings of the Basel II accord, which allowed for increased leverage in the largestbanks. who knew that they would be recapitalized by governments in the event of a solvency problem and who were therefore incentivized to take more risks than a bank or an intermediary who could not be rescued. In a nutshell, the combination of these loopholes has allowed the entire financial industry to make profits too soon, too easily and without proper risk management. This coincided with far too much indebtedness in theprivate and financial sector. Tensions escalated and culminated in the financial crisis that began in the summer of 2007, with a severe worsening in September 2008 when the collapse of the US investment bank Lehman Brothers brought theglobal economy to the fore. 8 edge of the abyss. After the rescue of the financial intermediation system, a transfer of debt from the private to the public sector in 2010 triggered a crisis of sovereign signatures, particularly in peripheral Europe. 2.Political reactions The financial crisis and the ensuing economic meltdown called for unprecedented political responses from fiscal and monetary authorities around the world. Some differences in the economic and financial structuresand institutional functioning of the euro area compared with the United States have led to separate specific measures - aimed at achieving the same objectives, however. Let me explain what these structural differences are based on: First of all, the economic structures of the euro area and the United States are very different. Small and medium-sized enterprises, for example, play a major role in the European economy. In addition, the public sector represents a large part of the European economy and is a major shareholder in some banks. Overall, the eurozone economy is less flexible than that of the United States. Wages and prices are more rigid. Let me give you a concrete example: the frequency with which prices change in the euro area and the United States. In the euro area, a trader changes his prices on average after 13 months. Studies show that the lead time is 11 months for producers. In the United States, these durations are less than 7 months and slightly more than 8 months, respectively. While this low flexibility may be a disadvantage in the event of positive supply shocks, such as technical innovations, in the event of a crisis, this relative European rigidity has provided protection against excessive negative expectations that would have led to a deflationary spiral. 9 - Secondly, there are also profound differences between the structure of the US and European financial systems. The lackof funding for non-financial enterprises, in particular, is striking. European small and medium-sized enterprises do not have direct access to the capital market but need loans to finance their activities. Inthe euro area, bank financing accounts for about 70% of a company's total external financing. In the United States, on the other hand, companies are much more dependent on market-based sources of financing, which account for 80% of total external financing. I would like to add that the universal banking model is the predominant investment model in continental Europe, unlike in the United States where - well before the crisis - investment banks played the most important role. In its responses to the crisis, the ECB has always taken into account the particular structure of the euro area economy. In the interests of efficiency, it has focused its measures on the banking sector and on the liquidity provision. In the US, on the other hand, the central bank focused on capital markets and bought assets directly from capital markets  an appropriate strategy given US companies' dependence on capital markets rather than bank loans. The ECB's action on the banking sector applied to the three stages of the crisis in Europe: - Ample liquidity supply when tensions on the money markets were felt in the summer of 2007; - Historical declinein interest rates from October 2008, when the economy began to enter recession. To support the granting of credit to the real economy, the ECB has also resorted to unconventional measures to relieve financing pressuresin the banking sector; - Interventions in certain market segments to ensure the proper functioning of the monetary policy transmission mechanism, starting from 10 as severe tensions began to emerge in sovereign debt markets. These strong and innovative measures have supported financial intermediation in the euro area. In addition, they have helped to maintain the availability of credit for households and businesses, while being in line with the ECB's primary mandate to maintain price stability over the medium term. 3. Longer-term objectives 3.1 A healthy financial sector Beyond the crisis, the financial sector must become more resilient, the massive debt burden must be alleviated, and excessive debt levels must be curbed in the financial, private and public sectors. In the long term, for a sound and sustainable economic and financial system, we must strive for a financial industry free of excessive risk and for the deleveraging of households and governments with excessive levels of debt. Financial sector regulation and supervision should reduce an institution's likelihood of default. An increase in the quality andquantity of capital, a minimum liquidity ratio and a leverage limit, as called for by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, aim to improve the banking industry's ability to absorb shocks from financial andeconomic stresses, whatever their source. Finally, I would like to point out that although these rules are a priori effective in limiting banks' credit risks, they cannot replace a much closer supervision by supervisorsof banks' risk-taking practices. As I noted earlier, the crisis was more about a combination of risky and opaque practices than a failure of the traditional universal banking model. 11 In this sense, this new framework alone cannot prevent a new crisis such as that observed in 2007-2008. It must therefore be accompanied by a major overhaul, underway in the EU, in three areas: - At the institutional level - At theregulatory level; and - At the level of crisis management and resolution mechanisms. As financial stability is currently affected by sovereign risk, particularly in the euro area, I will also discuss the lessons we need to learn now from the sovereign debt crisis. (a) Institutional reform At institutional level, a new framework for micro- and macro-prudential supervision, the European System of Financial Supervision, entered into force on 1 January. The European legislation that gave rise to this new framework was based on the report of a high-level group of experts chaired by Jacques de Larosiere. This new architecture aims to address a major shortcoming to light of the financial crisis: insufficient interaction and coordination between national supervisors, on the one hand, and the vulnerability of the financial system to interconnected, complex, sectoral and cross-sectoral systemic risks, on the one hand, from the tre part. In order to address these shortcomings, the new system includes a European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB), responsible for macro-prudential supervision, which brings together the governors of the 27 central banks of the European Union and is chaired by the President of the ECB. The ESRB recently held its inaugural meeting in Frankfurt. It will prevent or mitigate systemic risks by monitoring and analysing risks to financial stability, issuing early warnings of heightened systemic risks and, where appropriate, making recommendations on measures to address these risks. 12 Risks. The new system also includes three European supervisory agencies for banking, insurance and markets. These agencies will network and interact with existing national supervisory authorities to ensure the financial soundness of financial institutions themselves and to protect users of financial services. They will combine national supervision of financial institutions with specific tasks at European level which will make it possible to increase consistency in the application of the rules and to promoteharmonised regulation. (b) Regulatory reform In Europe, the Commission has put on the table a series of proposals aimed at strengthening the regulation of financial services, including greater transparency in the financial sector,better prevention of market abuse, strengthened supervision, including supervision of credit rating agencies and stronger protection for depositors. For certain reforms, such as the one on improving the quality andquantity of own funds, which I have already mentioned, or the one on accounting standards, European legislation will be brought into line with internationally established standards. It is crucial that these regulations are implemented in a harmonised manner at international level in order to avoid any distortions and opportunities for regulatory arbitrage that could seriously affect overall financial stability. I would add that the economic forums or international decision-making bodieswhich now play a greater role in setting standards for the financial sector would benefit from being more open to international financial centres, whose contribution to the new regulatory architecture could be majeure. (c) Crisis management and resolution mechanisms Because despite the strengthening of the institutional and legal framework for supervision and regulation, bank failures remain possible, it is essential to put in place crisis management and resolution mechanismsaimed at minimising the impact of a bank failure on the financial system and on the taxpayer. In the EU, the idea of a 13 The mechanism for managing a cross-border banking crisis is still at the gestation stage. Recognising that the costs of uncoordinated crisis resolution increase with the degree of interconnectedness and integration of financial institutions, the European Commission presented a Communication on a draft European framework for crisis management in the financial sector. A European solution remains particularly complex in the current state of European integration, in particular in relation to issues related to burden-sharing, intra-group transfer of assets during the crisis period, and the heterogeneity of the insolvency framework in the EU. In this context, it may be more realistic to pave the way for an intermediate solution: a national cross-border crisis management frameworkcombined with a binding process for information exchange. The establishment of national resolution funds funded by contributions from banks would reduce moral hazard and strengthen financial stability, bycurbing contagion and avoiding the urgent sale of assets sold off, thereby protecting taxpayers' money while facilitating the resolution of failed banks. In this context, the BCL has proposed an original framework for exante resolution funds that would involve the establishment of a pre-financed private structure combining the function of deposit guarantee funds and resolution funds, which are two sides of the same problem. At the end of the week, I will have the opportunity to see Commissioner Barnier to propose a date for discussing these issues with the Luxembourg public in the Bridge Forum Dialogue. 3.2 Fiscal Challenges On the basis of recent experience, we need to look carefully atthe role of excessive indebtedness. After the collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008, the accumulation of private debt stopped, but the problem of excessive debt was not resolved. Economic rescue plans, the impact of 14 Automatic stabilizers and the necessary support to the financial sector have resulted in a powerful lever of public budgets at levels never seen in peacetime. Public debt in the euro area will have increased by more than 20 percentage pointsfrom 2007 to 2011. The corresponding figures for the United States and Japan are between 35 and 40. Debt-to-GDP ratios are approaching 90% in Europe, 100% in the US and UK, and 200% in Japan. The debt burden must bealleviated and new excessive debts must be curbed. This is particularly crucial in Europe, where the single monetary policy must be supported by sound public finances. The sovereign debt crisis that has plagued the euro area for the pastyear has its roots in three shortcomings that have characterised European economic union since its creation: lax budgetary policies, inadequate macroeconomic policies, and the lack of mutated surveillancebetween Member States. The recent proposals to reform European economic governance and the introduction of the "European Semester" on 1 January for ex-ante surveillance of Member States' structural and budgetary policiesare certainly going in the right direction and the Council at the beginning of March should exceed in ambition the proposals of the Commission and the Van Rompuy Group of 2010. It is essential not to limit ourselves to the recovery of deficits alone, but to endorse a pact of structural reforms aimed at improving the competitiveness of the euro area. Indeed, macroeconomic imbalances are at the root of fiscal imbalances. Finally, it should be possible to review the sovereign crisis management framework developed in 2010 and reinforced in 2013 by the establishment of a permanent mechanism, the European Stabilisation Mechanism, in order to further increase market confidence in the euro area's ability to cope with the current risk. In particular, the current European Financial Stability Facility should be able to be competent to purchase sovereign bonds directly. This is in no way incompatible with the rigorous pursuit of beef consolidation effortsand reforms. 15 of all euro area countries, which are essential to lay the foundations for long-term sustainable growth. Conclusion After stabilizing the overall economy since the beginning of the financial turbulence, we arefaced with the challenge of returning to greater stability, which will be achieved through different paths. Given the massive debt burden in industrialized countries, growth potential and short-term growth rates will be weakened by the necessaryfiscal consolidation efforts. However, long-term, sustainable growth can only be achieved once fundamental economic imbalances have been addressed and structural reforms initiated. In Europe, governments need to show more commitment and ambition in their fiscal consolidation efforts. Stricter rules and higher minimum capital thresholds for the financial industry will make the system stronger and healthier. Buteffective regulation also requires field supervision based on competence and proximity. A fair balance will thus have to be found between the different levels of regulation and supervision: national, with the strengthening of national monitoring activities and the establishment, which is essential, of national resolution funds; European, with the necessary intensification of cooperation and coordination between supervisors and regulatory harmonization, facilitated by the implementation of the Member States. ace of the new European architecture; and comprehensive, with consistent and reasonable implementation of international banking standards avoiding market distortions and comparative disadvantages of some actors over others. Thankyou. 16
